A3: Scheduled rolling-heal plan - implement scheduled small drains (10-15min) per shard during off-peak for 2 weeks to allow safe slab rewrite without customer-impacting restarts. Owner: SRE Team (lead: Daniel Kim). Due: 2025-11-26.
A4: Eviction heuristics patch - add ghost-detection heuristic: treat entries with refcount < 0 or missing eviction timestamp as high-priority reclamation candidates. Owner: Elena Garcia. Due: 2025-12-02.

Motivation: Close a set of subtle incompatibilities between our /v1/chat.completions adapter and OpenAI's behavior that have been causing developer friction in streaming function-call flows and stop/logprobs handling. This PR implements a compact 'parameter normalizer' layer and a streaming framing/backpressure handshake to make the adapter tolerant of real-world clients and OpenAI-style payloads. Summary of changes: - Parameter normalizer: unify and sanitize incoming params (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, n, presence_penalty) and map them to our internal API consistently; accept both string and numeric encodings, preserve explicit nulls, and prefer client-provided values for edge cases. - Role aliasing: accept and normalize role names coming from clients ("assistant", "system", "user", "tool", and legacy aliases like "ai" or "bot"); ensure role is preserved in both final and streaming envelopes. - Stop sequence deduplication: support stop as string or array; expand single-string stops into an array; dedupe overlapping sequences (e.g. ["\n\n", "\n\n\n"]) and maintain order stability to match OpenAI semantics. - Sparse logprobs: add an opt-in sparse_logprobs mode that mirrors OpenAI's sparse token-level logprob structure when requested; keep heavy-weight computation behind an explicit flag to avoid perf regressions. - Streaming framing & backpressure: introduce a light handshake in the stream start (sent as first SSE/delta) that communicates our token framing and heartbeat expectations; implement backpressure signaling for HTTP/2 clients to avoid partial JSON objects when a client pauses mid-stream. - Function-call streaming support: improve chunking for function_call.name/arguments so that streaming deltas assemble deterministically into valid JSON payloads even across reconnects; final chunk action inserts a stable end-of-function marker to make reconstruction robust. - Response envelope parity: normalize streaming deltas to include a minimal structured 'choice' envelope (id, index, finish_reason) so downstream OpenAI-compat consumers don't need ad-hoc heuristics. - Tests & docs: add unit and integration tests for the normalizer, streaming handshake scenarios, and a new example in the docs showing a robust client reconnection strategy. Summary:

This handbook defines the governance model, operational runbook, and self-service flows for granting, reviewing, and revoking access to Redwood’s internal tools across roles and teams. It is intended for people-ops, engineering managers, security reviewers, and tool maintainers. The goal is to make tool access predictable, auditable, and fast while minimizing over-permissioning.

Key Principles:
- Least privilege by default: users receive the minimum role required to do their job.
- Role-driven access: we prefer role-based assignments with ephemeral exceptions.
- Self-service first, manual oversight when necessary: automate safe, common grants.
- Clear ownership: every tool has an owner and an escalation path.
- Auditable lifecycle: provisioning, reviews and deprovisioning are tracked centrally.

1) Scope and Definitions
- Tool: any internal SaaS, self-hosted service, or repo that requires explicit credentials or permissions (examples: AWS consoles, Jira admin groups, prod Grafana, CI pipelines).
- Role: a named collection of permissions (e.g., developer-readonly, infra-operator).
- Access Request: a request submitted to the Access Portal for a role or tool-specific permission.
- Exception: temporary access outside standard roles; must have an expiration and approver.

2) Ownership and Responsibilities
- Tool Owner (team-specified): maintains the role catalog, documents required permissions, defines safe self-service gates, and responds to escalations.
- People Ops: owns onboarding/offboarding orchestration, periodic review cadence, and highest-level policy.
- Security: defines acceptable exception policies, approves high-risk tools, and performs audits.
- Manager (requester approver): verifies business need and ties access to role/mission.

3) Access Model (high level)
- Role Catalog: canonical list of roles for common tools; stored in the Access Portal.
- Self-Service Roles: low-risk roles that can be assigned instantly (examples: docs-edit, ci-reader)
- Request-and-Approve Roles: medium-risk roles requiring manager approval (examples: staging-deploy, metrics-writer)
- Manual Approval Roles: high-risk roles requiring security review (examples: prod-admin, billing-admin)

4) Standard Provisioning Flow (Self-Service preferred)
1. User initiates request via Access Portal (or CLI).
2. For self-service roles: immediate grant recorded in audit log; user notified.
3. For manager-approval roles: manager receives approval email and must respond within 48 business hours; if approved, provisioning executes automatically.
4. For security-approval roles: security reviewer staged; expected SLA is 3 business days.
5. All grants include metadata: requester, approver, justification, expiration (if exception), and ticket ID.

5) Approval Matrix (sample)
| Tool Category | Example Tools | Typical Role Name | Approval Path | Max SLA for Approval | Expiration Policy |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Low risk | Docs, Internal Wiki | docs-edit | Self-service | Instant | Persistent (attached to employment) |
| Medium risk | Staging CI, Dev DB | staging-deploy | Manager | 48 business hours | 90 days (auto-renew) |
| High risk | Production infra, Billing | prod-admin | Manager + Security | 3 business days | 7 days (explicit extension only) |

6) Exception and Emergency Access
- Emergency access (e.g., incident mitigation) uses the Fast-Track Exception flow:
  1) Requester files an incident-tagged access request with justification and incident ID.
  2) On-call approver (manager or designated incident commander) may grant a 4-hour temporary token via the Access Portal.
  3) Security must be notified within 1 hour and will follow up to convert to a formal exception or revoke.
- All emergency grants are logged and retroactively reviewed as part of the incident postmortem.

7) Deprovisioning and Offboarding
- Standard offboarding timeline:
  - Day 0: account disabled for interactive access within 4 hours of HR offboarding signal.
  - Day 1: short-lived API tokens invalidated; persistent service accounts rotated if necessary.
  - Day 7: cloud console roles removed; scheduled backup of any outstanding owner responsibilities.
- Manager responsibility: reassign ownership before final removal.
- Audit: people-ops runs weekly deprovisioning reports, security runs monthly verification.

8) Periodic Access Reviews
- Quarterly review for all high-risk roles.
- Biannual review for medium-risk.
- Annual review for low-risk.
- Review process: automated report produced by Access Portal -> owner validates or initiates deprovisioning -> people-ops enforces changes within 7 business days.

9) Tool Onboarding Checklist (for Tool Owners)
1. Identify required roles and map to least-privilege sets.
2. Document roles in the Role Catalog section of the owner page.
3. Define which roles are self-service vs require approval.
4. Provide an onboarding runbook with contact points and SLOs.
5. Register tool owner and escalation email in the Access Portal.
6. Provide a test account and verification steps for the access flow.

Overview
This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) describes Redwood Inference's end-to-end triage for procurement items that require legal review or cross-functional escalation. The goal is to reduce cycle time, ensure appropriate risk controls for contracting and billing, and provide clear ownership and SLA targets for each review tier.

Scope
- Applies to all vendor engagements, SOWs, license purchases, hardware leases (including GPU reservations), SaaS subscriptions, and professional services agreements initiated via Procurement.
- Excludes low-value purchases that follow the corporate purchasing card (P-card) policy (see Finance policy: /confluence/finance-and-legal/procurement/p-card-guidelines).

Definitions
1) Low-risk procurement: Purchase value <$25k, no data access, vendor uses standard market terms, no cross-border data transfer.
2) Medium-risk procurement: $25k–$250k, includes limited data access (non-sensitive), or requires limited bespoke terms (payment schedules, warranty clarifications).
3) High-risk procurement: >$250k, access to customer data or models, on-prem or network connectivity required, escrow/KMS requirements, change to indemnity/limitation clauses, or vendor requested data residency exceptions.
4) Contracting Owner: Procurement lead assigned to the purchase.
5) Legal Triage Owner: Commercial counsel assigned to initial review.

Decision Matrix (quick reference)
| Value band | Data access | Special clauses requested | Initial path | SLA (initial review) | Escalation
| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| <$25k | None | Standard T&C | Procurement approval | 2 business days | Procurement Manager
| <$25k | Non-sensitive | Minor clarifications | Procurement + Legal FYI | 3 business days | Legal (if changes requested)
| $25k–$250k | Non-sensitive | Payment / warranty edits | Legal triage | 5 business days | Senior Counsel
| >$250k or any sensitive data | Any | Any bespoke confidentiality / KMS / escrow | Legal + Security + Finance | 10 business days | GC + Head of Procurement + Security

Procedure (step-by-step)
1. Procurement Request Intake
   a. Requestor opens a PR in the Procurement system (Jira/Workday) with required attachments: vendor quote, SOW, standard T&C, and vendor risk questionnaire.
   b. Procurement Owner tags the request with one of the risk bands and assigns Contracting Owner.
2. Automated Pre-checks (Procurement)
   a. Validate vendor is in the approved vendor list and has completed KYC.
   b. Run vendor risk scan (third-party risk tool) — attach report.
3. Legal Triage (Commercial Counsel)
   a. Counsel performs 3-screen review: (1) identify material exposures (indemnity, liability caps, warranty, IP, data access); (2) verify billing & rev-rec implications (see RevRec checklist below); (3) recommend standard redlines.
   b. Counsel applies template responses from the Clause Library for common items (data transfer addendum, limited indemnity, software license grant).
4. Cross-functional Review (when required)
   a. Security: Required for any network connectivity, data access, KMS/escrow, or on-prem deployments. Security lead must sign off within 3 business days of assignment.
   b. Finance: Required for contracts with atypical billing cadence, revenue-sharing, or subscription modifications; Finance must verify revenue recognition implications and billing trigger alignment.
   c. Product/Platform: Required for technical SOW accuracy and operational acceptance criteria for managed services.
5. Negotiation & Approval
   a. Procurement leads negotiations on non-legal commercial terms; legal negotiates legal language.
   b. For high-risk contracts, the final approval requires sign-off from Head of Procurement, Commercial Counsel, and Director of Finance.
6. Execution & Post-signature Controls
   a. Store executed contract in the contract repository (DocuSign + ContractDB) and tag with metadata (see Contract Metadata section).
   b. Trigger supplier onboarding checklists: finance onboarding (AP routing), security onboarding (vulnerability scan), and ops onboarding (service acceptance).

Contract Metadata (required fields stored in ContractDB)
- contract_id: unique Redwood identifier (e.g., RDW-CTR-2026-000123)
- vendor_legal_name
- purchasing_owner: "team/person"
- commercial_owner: "Procurement lead"
- legal_owner: "Commercial counsel"
- start_date / end_date / renewal_terms
- not_to_exceed_value / committed_spend_line_items
- billing_trigger: invoicing cadence and event that triggers rev-rec (see billing examples)
- data_classification_and_controls: none | non-sensitive | regulated | restricted
- kyc_status: complete | incomplete
- escrow_or_kms_required: yes | no
- confidentiality: internal | restricted | customer-only
- signed_copy_link: internal URL to storage

Revenue Recognition & Billing Checklist (Finance items to confirm before legal approval)
- Identify performance obligations and the billing trigger for each (e.g., access to API endpoints vs. delivery of physical hardware).
- Confirm whether contract changes the timing of revenue recognition (advance payments, non-refundable fees, milestone billing).
- Map invoicing cadence to subscription terms; attach billing examples: 
  Example 1: Monthly subscription — bill in arrears on 1st of following month; revenue recognized ratably over month.
  Example 2: Annual prepay — bill at execution; revenue recognized ratably over 12 months.
  Example 3: Hardware + installation SOW — hardware recognized at delivery; installation revenue recognized over acceptance period (SOW acceptance).

Service Level Targets for Reviews
- Procurement initial intake validation: 1 business day.
- Legal initial triage (see Decision Matrix): 2–10 business days depending on band.
- Security review when required: 3 business days.
- Complete negotiated contract to signature for medium-risk: target 15 business days; high-risk: target 30 business days.

Escalation Contacts

## Summary
This page defines the plan for customer-facing documentation for the Quantization Profile Library (opt-in). The goal is to help customers safely enable quantization profiles per route, understand limitations and compatibility, run appropriate evaluations, interpret observability signals, and roll back quickly if needed.

This is an internal planning doc for Redwood Docs + DevEx and will be used as the source of truth for docs IA, required examples, and cross-team review gates.

## Audience and use cases
**Primary audiences**
- Software engineers and ML engineers integrating Redwood routes who want to reduce cost/token.
- Platform teams managing production change control (audit logs, RBAC, rollbacks).

**Customer use cases we need to support in docs**
1. Enable an approved quantization profile for a single route (hosted API).
2. Enable profile for a route with region/tier constraints (Dedicated + multi-region hosted).
3. Validate quality and latency before expanding traffic.
4. Diagnose output changes, elevated fallback rate, or latency regressions.
5. Roll back (route-level disable; global kill-switch is internal-only but mention its existence at a high level).

## Goals (docs)
- Make it clear this is **opt-in** and **route-scoped** (v1), with baseline behavior unchanged when disabled.
- Provide a simple “happy path” enablement flow with copy-pastable examples (Console + API/SDK).
- Set expectations on **compatibility constraints** and **fallback behavior** (deterministic, baseline precision fallback).
- Provide a lightweight but concrete evaluation best-practices section that customers can follow without needing Redwood internal harnesses.
- Provide troubleshooting steps tied to the actual product signals customers will see (Console warnings/errors, request metadata, audit history, and dashboard panels).

## Non-goals (docs)
- Do not position this as automatic tuning/recommendations (out of scope for v1).
- Do not publish internal-only implementation details (artifact signing specifics, internal service names, kill-switch runbooks).
- Do not promise universal profile coverage across all models/GPU SKUs.

## Product language and terminology
We need consistent, customer-friendly wording:
- **Quantization profile**: A versioned, Redwood-validated configuration for running a specific model variant using a specific quantization method/precision combination.
- **Profile library**: The set of published profiles per model variant. Customers choose a profile for a route.
- **Route-level enablement**: Profiles are enabled per route, not globally for all tenant traffic (v1).
- **Fallback**: If a request is incompatible (hardware/sequence length constraints) or profile application fails safe checks, Redwood serves using baseline precision for that request (or route) while emitting an event.

Avoid ambiguous language:
- Avoid saying “Redwood automatically picks the best profile.”
- Avoid “lossless” claims. Use “aims to preserve quality” and emphasize eval/monitoring.

## Information architecture (public docs)
We will publish a small cluster of pages under: **Optimize → Quantization Profiles**.

### Page 1: Overview (concept + safety model)
**Proposed title:** “Quantization Profiles (Preview/Beta)” (or “Quantization Profiles” once GA)

**Outline**
- What quantization profiles are and why they reduce cost.
- Opt-in and route-scoped behavior.
- High-level lifecycle: published profiles, versioning, deprecations.
- Safety model summary:
  - Compatibility checks before enablement.
  - Deterministic selection.
  - Fallback to baseline.
  - Auditability and change history.

**Callouts**
- “Start with a canary route; expand after evals.”
- “Not all models/regions support all profiles.”

### Page 2: Enablement guide (Console + API/SDK)
**Proposed title:** “Enable a quantization profile for a route”

**Required elements**
- Console walkthrough (with screenshots once UX is final):
  1) Navigate to Route → Performance/Optimize → Quantization
  2) Choose model variant + eligible profiles
  3) Read compatibility warnings
  4) Confirm change (modal) and review expected impact
  5) Verify enablement and view change history

- API example (REST) for updating route config
  - Show setting `quantization_profile_ref` to a specific profile ID/version.
  - Show how to reset to `default` / disable.

- SDK examples
  - Python and TypeScript: configure route setting; retrieve route state; handle incompatibility errors.

**Verification steps**
- Confirm in Console that route shows “Enabled” and which profile is selected.
- Show how to verify in request metadata (e.g., response headers or trace attributes) that a profile was applied vs fallback.
- Show where to find fallback/latency/cost deltas in dashboards.

### Page 3: Compatibility + limitations
**Proposed title:** “Compatibility, constraints, and fallback behavior”

**Include**
- What compatibility depends on:
  - Model ID + model variant
  - Deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private as applicable)
  - GPU class/SKU (expressed as customer-friendly names)
  - Max context / sequence length limits
  - Region constraints (if/when supported in route policy)

- Customer-facing compatibility matrix
  - If we can’t maintain a full matrix, we must at least publish:
    - “Supported GPUs by profile type” (e.g., INT8 supported on X, FP8 on Y)
    - “Max supported context per profile” for popular models
  - Decide format: table in docs + downloadable CSV updated weekly (recommended).

- Fallback semantics
  - Define what happens when incompatible:
    - If enablement time: block with clear error and remediation.
    - If request time: safe fallback to baseline; emit a signal; no infinite retry loops.

- Limitations / known caveats
  - Output differences are possible.
  - Some profiles may be labeled “Experimental” with narrower guardrails.
  - If customers pin to a profile version, it won’t change unless they update.
  - If we ever add “recommended” aliases, document that aliases may move and how we prevent silent changes (see Open Questions).

### Page 4: Evaluation best practices
**Proposed title:** “How to evaluate quality and latency before rollout”

**Customer-friendly guidance**
- Suggested evaluation approach:
  - Identify representative prompts (production samples + edge cases).
  - Run baseline vs profile-enabled comparisons.
  - Use A/B sampling (e.g., 1–5% traffic) with a rollback threshold.

- What to measure
  - Quality: task-specific metrics (pass@k, exact match, ranking metrics) + human review where appropriate.
  - Latency: p50/p95 decode latency and time-to-first-token.
  - Cost: cost/token and throughput.

- Rollout strategy
  1) Enable in staging on a non-critical route
  2) Canary in production (small % traffic)
  3) Expand gradually with monitoring

- Provide explicit “stop conditions”
  - Elevated fallback rate
  - Increased error rate
  - Statistically meaningful quality regression on a defined slice

**Note:** We cannot publish Redwood’s internal thresholds verbatim if they are considered sensitive, but we can publish recommended guardrails (e.g., “predefine acceptable deltas and require sign-off”). We will align with Selene Huang (quality guardrails) on what’s safe to disclose.

### Page 5: Troubleshooting + rollback
**Proposed title:** “Troubleshooting quantization profiles”

**Structure: symptom → likely cause → how to confirm → resolution**

Required symptoms:
- Console says profile is incompatible
  - Common causes: wrong model variant, unsupported GPU class, context length exceeds profile limit.
  - Resolution: choose another profile; reduce max tokens/context; use baseline.

- Output quality changed unexpectedly
  - Confirm: compare baseline vs profile, check whether fallback occurred (mixed behavior can look inconsistent).
  - Resolution: disable profile; run eval; contact support with request IDs.

- p95 latency increased
  - Confirm: look at per-route latency panels; check TTFT vs decode; check batching/caching changes.
  - Resolution: disable profile; adjust route concurrency/batching; consult Redwood support.

- Elevated fallback rate
  - Confirm: dashboard panel + route events.
  - Likely causes: requests exceed profile constraints; region/GPU mismatch; deployment drift.
  - Resolution: tighten route constraints; pick compatible profile; disable.

- 5xx errors after enabling
  - Confirm: error class; check if errors correlate with specific profile version.
  - Resolution: disable; provide audit event ID and request IDs to support.

Rollback instructions (customer-actionable)
- Disable at route level (Console + API snippet).
- Verify disablement and that requests are using baseline.

We should also include:
- “What information to include in a support ticket” checklist:
  - Org/tenant ID
  - Route name/ID
  - Model + variant
  - Profile ID/version
  - Region/deployment mode
  - Approx timeframe
  - Request IDs/traces
  - Observed metrics (fallback rate, p95 latency)

## Required code/examples (public docs)
We will maintain a single authoritative set of snippets and import them into the docs site.

**REST (pseudo)**
- GET route settings (show current model + quant state)
- PATCH route settings to set profile ref
- PATCH route settings to disable / reset to default

**Python SDK**
- Update route quantization setting
- Validate compatibility result handling
- Verify applied profile via response metadata

**TypeScript SDK**
- Same as Python, plus typing for errors.

Docs dependencies:
- Final field names and error shapes must match control-plane API.
- Confirm the exact response fields that indicate `applied` vs `fallback` vs `disabled`.

## Console UX copy and warnings (alignment)
We will mirror Console language in docs to minimize confusion.

Warnings to standardize:
- “This change may affect output quality. Evaluate before ramping traffic.”
- “This profile is only compatible with <constraints>. Requests outside constraints will fall back to baseline.”
- “Pinning a profile version ensures deterministic behavior until you change it.”

We will coordinate final wording with Tessa Morgan (UX lead) and Kenji Nakamura (rollout/controls designer).

## Review, launch gating, and update cadence
**Reviewers required before docs merge**
- Applied ML: Arjun Desai (profiles lead) + Selene Huang (guardrails)
- Runtime: Noah Patel (runtime architect)
- Platform/Console: Chloe Martin (Console backend lead)
- SRE/Release: Connor O'Brien (rollout lead)

**Release stages and docs behavior**
- Beta/allowlist:
  - Docs are public but clearly marked “Beta” with known limitations.
  - Include a “Contact Support to enable” note if feature is behind an allowlist.

- GA:
  - Remove Beta banner.
  - Publish compatibility matrix link and clear deprecation policy.

**Update cadence**
- Compatibility matrix and profile coverage: weekly updates (aligned with profile publishing cadence).
- Troubleshooting section: update after each beta incident/support trend.

## Success criteria (docs)
- ≥80% of beta design partner enablements completed without synchronous Redwood help.
- Reduction in support tickets that are purely “how do I enable/disable?” (shift to higher-signal issues).
- Median time-to-rollback for customers (self-serve) < 10 minutes after following docs.
- Docs telemetry: high completion rates on enablement guide; low bounce on troubleshooting due to missing information.

## Open questions
1. **Alias semantics:** Will we expose “recommended/latest” aliases in v1 GA or only pinned profile IDs/versions? If aliases exist, we must document how we prevent silent changes (e.g., aliases only change on customer action vs Redwood updates).
2. **Customer-facing compatibility matrix:** What is the minimum viable matrix we can keep current without excessive operational load? (Proposal: publish for top 10 models + major GPU classes first.)
3. **What can we safely publish about quality thresholds?** We should align with Applied ML on whether to include specific numeric deltas or keep it as qualitative guidance.
4. **Request metadata surface:** What is the final customer-visible mechanism to confirm applied profile (headers, response fields, trace attribute)? This must be stable.

- (DevEx) Monica Patel: finalize Python + TS snippets and ensure they match SDK releases.
- (Console) Chloe Martin: confirm final Console labels, error strings, and change history UX for screenshot capture.

Summary

This playbook defines the consent model, telemetry categories, mandatory redaction/minimization pipeline, and operator runbooks for tenant telemetry in Redwood private deployments (VPC and on‑prem variants). It is intended for field operators, customer success, and security stakeholders responsible for evidence artifacts required by regulated customers.

Applicability

- Applies to all private deployments managed by Redwood (VPC-private and on‑prem packages).
- Scope: runtime telemetry (service metrics, request traces, model metadata), operational telemetry (container metrics, host telemetry), and optional diagnostic dumps (heap, core, model weights metadata).
- Does NOT apply to customer application payloads that are explicitly forwarded through service proxies; those are covered by the customer data contract and separate redaction templates.

Telemetry Categories and Examples

1) Essential operational telemetry (always-on, low-cardinality)
   - Examples: instance_cpu_pct, gpu_util_pct, disk_iops_95, process_up
   - Purpose: SLO monitoring, alerting, capacity planning

2) Request-level telemetry (controlled sample rate / hashed identifiers)
   - Examples: request_latency_ms, tokens_generated, model_variant, route_name
   - Note: fields that could be PII/PHI must be redacted or hashed.

3) Diagnostic payloads (customer opt-in)
   - Examples: full request/response payloads, model KV cache snapshots, internal debug stacks
   - Must be opt-in and time-limited; stored in restricted buckets with customer approval.

Consent Model and Customer Controls

- Default mode: minimal telemetry (category 1 + aggregated request-level metrics with strict hashing and no payloads).
- Optional modes (customer selects during onboarding):
  1) "diagnostic-opt-in" (retains full request/response for T days)
  2) "enhanced-sampling" (higher sample rate for request-level metrics only)
  3) "no-external-telemetry" (local-only telemetry; no telemetry leaves VPC except for aggregated SLO telemetry if contract allows)

- Consent artifacts: a customer must sign the Telemetry Consent Form (template in Appendix) and specify: retention_days, sample_rate, redaction_profile_id. This metadata is stored in the deployment manifest under /etc/redwood/telemetry/consent.json and is surfaced in the control-plane UI.

Data Redaction & Minimization Pipeline

Overview:
1) Ingest filter (node-level): rejects known high-sensitivity fields before serialization.
2) Redaction transform (service-level): applies JSON path redactors, regex scrubbers, and structured PII detectors.
3) Hashing/Tokenization (metric-level): deterministic hashing of tenant identifiers using HMAC-SHA256 with tenant-specific key (rotated per policy).
4) Sink selector: routes telemetry to correct storage class (aggregated metrics store, restricted object store, local-only storage).

Redaction Profiles:
- profile-basic: remove keys named ["password", "ssn", "credit_card", "medical_record"], mask 80% of long strings, remove attachments > 128KB
- profile-strict: profile-basic + remove any field matching regex patterns for emails, phone numbers, and base64 blobs
- profile-none (diagnostic-opt-in only): no redaction beyond size caps

Sample redaction table (in prose):
- Field: request.user.name -> Action: drop
- Field: request.user.email -> Action: redact local-part, keep domain (e.g., xxxxx@company.com)
- Field: request.prompt -> Action: truncate to first 512 characters, then apply NER PII scrubber

Operator Runbook: Toggle, Audit, and Emergency Redaction

1) Verify consent manifest
   - Command: sudo cat /etc/redwood/telemetry/consent.json\   - Expected: valid JSON with keys: tenant_id, profile_id, retention_days, sample_rate, approved_by
\2) Switch deployment to 'local-only' for a tenant (example, safe mode for regulatory hold)\   - Steps:
     a) In the control plane: open tenant config -> Telemetry -> select 'no-external-telemetry' -> apply
     b) CLI fallback: redwoodctl tenant update --id <TENANT> --telemetry-mode local-only
     c) Validate: curl -sS http://localhost:9100/telemetry/status?tenant=<TENANT> | jq '.mode' should return "local-only"

3) Enforce emergency redaction for a window
   - Purpose: immediate purge or redaction when a customer requests removal for an incident
   - Steps (operator):
     1) Create a redaction job: redwoodctl telemetry redact --tenant <TENANT> --pattern "/request/payload" --mode truncate --reason "DSAR" --until 2026-07-01
     2) Monitor job: redwoodctl telemetry jobs get --id <JOB_ID>
     3) Generate evidence bundle: redwoodctl telemetry jobs export --id <JOB_ID> --output /tmp/evidence-<TENANT>.tar.gz

4) Audit logs and evidence retention
   - All toggle and redaction operations must be logged to the restricted audit log (immutable) with fields: operator_id, action, tenant_id, timestamp, justification_id.

Acceptance Tests & Evidence Requirements

Before handoff to customer, run the following checks and attach evidence to the onboarding package:

- Acceptance checklist (automated):
  1) consent.json present and schema-valid
  2) sample_rate applied (verify by synthetic trace generator with 1K requests)
  3) redaction profile enforced (submit synthetic PII and assert it is removed)
  4) local-only mode test (if requested)

- Evidence bundle contents:
  - consent.json (signed copy)
  - telemetry-config.yaml at deploy time
  - sample sanitized trace (redacted)
  - audit log entries showing operator approval

Upgrade & Rollback Considerations

- Upgrades that change redaction behavior must be treated as a migration: any profile changes require (A) migration script that reprocesses retained diagnostic payloads or (B) documented customer opt-in to reprocessing.
- Backward compatibility: new profiles must include a compatibility mapping and a migration tool: redwoodctl telemetry migrate-profiles --from old-id --to new-id --dry-run
- Rollback CPs: If a control-plane upgrade introduces a bug that lifts redaction rules, initiate emergency rollback and run the emergency redaction steps above. Preserve an evidence bundle that shows the rollback window and actions taken.

SLOs and Monitoring

- Telemetry integrity SLO: 99.9% of agent heartbeats per minute.
- Redaction correctness target: 100% synthetic-PII detection in test harness within 24 hours of deployment.
- Audit latency: toggles and redaction jobs appear in immutable audit log within 10s.

Context:
description:
Context: We're seeing tail-latency spikes and intermittent GPU OOMs in multi-tenant serving when long sequences lead to large KV residency. Current paged/blocked KV designs reduce average memory but cause sudden allocation pressure and head-of-line stalls when many long-context requests overlap.

Problem statement: We need a practical runtime-level strategy that: 1) bounds per-request KV working set growth using a windowed retention model, 2) signals and smooths load to upstream scheduling to avoid synchronous OOM cascades, and 3) provides a deterministic fallback path that preserves latency SLOs for short requests while allowing long requests to continue with degraded throughput.

Proposal summary: Implement a "bounded-window KV" mode that splits KV residency into fixed-duration windows (logical time slices of attention history) with the following features: 
- Soft retention limits per-request (N windows) with an LRU-like priority inside each window.
- Adaptive backpressure signals exposed to the scheduler: soft_shed and holdback tokens that throttle batching and admission for requests that would push resident set above a dynamic high-water mark.
- Graceful OOM fallback: when hard limit is reached, use a prioritized partial-eviction strategy (drop older windows for low-priority requests while preserving most-recent window + KV prefix cache for high-priority/latency-sensitive traffic).

Why different from existing approaches: Unlike slab-only or chunked allocators, windowed retention encodes temporal locality at a coarse granularity that simplifies eviction math and gives predictable worst-case resident set sizes. Combining this with explicit backpressure tokens reduces synchronous eviction storms that previously caused cascading tail latency.

Design links and artifacts: 
- Design doc (internal Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Bounded-Window-KV-Design
- Simulation notebooks (Drive): https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1-window-sim
- Microbench harness (GitHub): https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-kv-sim/pull/67

Implementation plan: 
1) Runtime data structure: implement per-request window table metadata (compact 16B entries per window pointer) and a global residency counter that tracks resident bytes per-window-weighted.
2) Admission controller: expose tokens from an admission service that inspects current residency vs. dynamic target and returns admit / delay / shed directives. Integrate with batching pipeline to delay low-priority requests before they enter KV allocations.
3) Eviction policy: prioritized window eviction with per-request priority and age heuristics. Implement fast path that can drop entire oldest windows without touching inner-page structures to keep CPU costs minimal.
4) Fallback path: for requests delayed or partially-evicted, route to a best-effort streaming execution that sacrifices throughput (smaller KV context, truncated attention) but keeps token latency within SLO for the top-k critical requests.

Performance targets: 
- Keep P95 token-level latency increase < 10% for latency-tier traffic under memory pressure test harness.
- Reduce frequency of GPU OOM events to < 1 per 10M tokens in stress tests.
- Maintain aggregate throughput > 75% of baseline for mixed workload in degraded mode.

Trade-offs and open questions: 
- Granularity of window: 64-token windows vs 256-token windows — larger windows give higher retention efficiency but coarser eviction control. Simulation suggests 128-token windows hit a good sweet spot for typical request distributions.
- Admission latency vs batching benefits: delaying requests to avoid OOM can reduce batch sizes and hurt throughput for some workloads. We plan conservative holdback thresholds tuned per-customer tier.
- Memory accounting complexity: per-window accounting gives predictable bounds but increases meta-data overhead; we aim for <0.6% memory overhead at 1M concurrent windows.

Acceptance criteria:

Admission controller returns admit/delay/shed and integrates with existing batching pipeline
Eviction path can drop whole windows atomically without per-token ops

OOMs reduced to <1 per 10M tokens in stress harness

Purpose and scope:

2) Collect and preserve evidence for security and compliance audits with tamper-evident retention controls.
3) Standardize acceptance tests and artifacts to reduce delivery time and avoid rework.

SLOs and performance thresholds (tenant-facing):
- Availability: 99.95% monthly for tenant inference endpoint (measurement: synthetic probes from customer region + control-plane logs).

- Error budget: 0.05% of requests may return 5xx or timeouts; any breach requires incident runbook and customer notification within 1 hour.

Context:
description:
PRD-style acceptance and behavioral specification for: (A) deterministic structured output envelopes during streaming, (B) robust tool/function-orchestration semantics when downstream tool calls fail or time out (soft-fail modes), and (C) observable signal set for debugging degraded emissions. This ticket captures requirements, tradeoffs, and concrete acceptance tests for engineering to implement and QA to validate.

background:
Teams integrating function-calls and streaming structured output have encountered brittle failure modes: partial JSON emissions, stuck streams when a tool times out, and unclear signals in telemetry for root-cause. Previous specs focused on schema handshakes but did not fully specify soft-fail policies (when to continue vs abort), how to surface partial-but-valid objects, or required observability for production troubleshooting.

goals:
1) Define deterministic envelope semantics so consumers can parse incrementally and resume/reconcile partial objects. 2) Specify soft-fail modes for tool invocation: best-effort, fallback-only, and abort. 3) Establish acceptance tests for streaming + tool failures that exercise backpressure, resumability, and idempotent retries. 4) Define telemetry and SLI/alert thresholds to detect degraded emission reliability.

scope:
- Streaming text and structured frames emitted from Redwood API. - Function/tool invocation lifecycle (invoke, success, failure, retry). - Soft-fail policies and configuration. - Acceptance criteria and end-to-end test matrix (simulated tool latencies/failures).

out_of_scope:
- Changes to client SDKs beyond minimal parsing guidance. - New RPC transport protocols. - Billing/quotas changes related to retries (handled by a separate billing review).

tradeoffs:
- Strict abort-on-tool-failure yields highest data correctness but reduces availability; soft-fail increases availability at the cost of accuracy. We recommend defaulting to best-effort-with-degraded-indicators for hosted API and offering strict-abort configuration for enterprise Dedicated/Private deployments. - Emitting placeholder fields vs removing the field: placeholder maintains schema shape for parsers but may surface misleading data. We prefer placeholder objects with explicit 'soft_fail' enum and provenance metadata.

acceptance_criteria:
AC-1: Incremental Envelope Parsing: Streaming responses are emitted as ordered 'frames' where each frame is a top-level JSON object stringified and newline-delimited. Consumers can reconstruct the final object by concatenating frames and applying frame-level 'commit' markers. In tests, a slow client that disconnects and reconnects using resume token can re-sync and reconstruct a consistent object state.
AC-2: Soft-Fail Modes: System exposes three modes: 'abort' (default for strict endpoints), 'best_effort' (continue emitting remaining structured fields, include 'soft_fail' markers), and 'degraded_fallback' (switch to cheaper model or cached result then emit). Implementation must allow per-route configuration. Acceptance tests must validate each mode against simulated downstream tool failures.
AC-3: Partial-Object Validity: When a tool call fails and mode is 'best_effort', the emitted structured object must remain JSON-parseable at frame boundaries and include an explicit 'provenance' map with keys: source_variant, tool_status, tool_error_code, soft_fail=true. Test harness validates JSON validity after each frame and final reconciliation produces a documented 'incomplete' state.
AC-4: Function-Invocation Idempotency & Retry Signals: Tool gateway must return idempotency token on initial invocation. Retries (automatic or client-initiated) must attach token to avoid duplicate side-effects. Acceptance tests include simulated at-least-once delivery and assert idempotent behavior for a provided sample tool (mock webhook that records invocations).
AC-5: Timeouts & Backpressure Behavior: When a tool exceeds configured timeout: - in 'abort' mode, the stream emits an error envelope and closes (status=closed, code=TOOL_TIMEOUT). - in 'best_effort', emit soft-fail metadata and continue. System must not indefinitely block other concurrent streams; load tests will simulate N=500 concurrent streams with 10% slow tool responses and verify 99th percentile latency SLOs remain within target with degraded outputs accounted for.
AC-6: Observability Signals: For every streaming emission that includes a soft-fail, the following telemetry events must be emitted: tool_invocation.start, tool_invocation.end (status), stream.frame.commit, stream.soft_fail.marker, stream.resume.attempt (if consumer reconnects). Each event includes trace_id and frame_offset. Acceptance: Kibana dashboards show these events for a 1-hour test run and an alert rule triggers when soft_fail_rate > 0.5% over 5 minutes for production routes.
AC-7: Compatibility with Existing Schema Negotiation: Handshake must include 'preferred_envelope' and 'resume_token' semantics. Acceptance tests exercise older clients by verifying graceful degradation: if preferred_envelope is unsupported, server falls back to newline-delimited JSON frames and includes a compatibility header explaining the downgrade.
AC-8: Test Harness & E2E Test Cases: Provide automated tests that simulate network partitions, tool errors (500, 429, 504), tool latency spikes, and partial stream consumption. Tests must assert that consumers receive either a valid final object or a documented incomplete object with soft_fail metadata in all tested modes.
AC-9: Docs & Examples: Console docs must include examples for parsing frames, handling soft_fail metadata, configuring per-route mode, and troubleshooting guide with representative log queries. Acceptance: docs reviewed and approved by Developer Experience and Design reviewers and linked in PR.
AC-10: Security & Compliance: When soft-fail includes tool error payloads, sensitive fields must be redacted per PII policy. Acceptance: static analysis and a sample audit record confirm PII redaction for tool error messages containing email/SSN-like patterns.

test_cases:
TC-1: Best-effort tool timeout: Start streaming generation that triggers a tool lookup that sleeps for 8s (config timeout 2s). Mode=best_effort. Expect frames including 'tool_status':'timeout' and 'soft_fail':"true"; final object parseable. Verify telemetry events emitted.
TC-2: Abort mode on rate-limit: Simulate tool returning 429. Mode=abort. Expect error envelope and stream close with code TOOL_RATE_LIMIT. Verify client-observed close code and server-side logs reference idempotency token.
TC-3: Resume after disconnect: Consumer reads first N frames then disconnects. Server persists resume_token. Consumer reconnects with token and receives frames from last commit point through final. Assert final object equivalent to continuous stream.
TC-4: Fallback variant switch: Mode=degraded_fallback. Downstream model returns non-responsive. Server emits warning frame, switches to cached summary variant, emits final object with 'source_variant':'cached-summary' and 'tool_error_code' annotated. Verify SLO accounting attributes.
TC-5: Idempotent webhook verification: Mock tool endpoint records invocations. Trigger multiple retries with the same idempotency token. Verify single recorded invocation and correct response to client of 'duplicate-suppressed' marker.

monitoring_and_telemetry:
Minimum telemetry must include trace_id, route, model_variant, frame_offset, resume_token, tool_invocation.id, tool_status, tool_error_code, latency_ms. Dashboards: streaming-frame-latency, soft-fail-rate, tool-timeout-trend. Alerts: soft_fail_rate>0.5% over 5m, resume_failure_rate>0.1% over 15m.

notes:
Implementation must include a clear config surface (route-level parameter 'tool_failure_policy' with enum values) and safe defaults for public API. Provide migration notes for existing routes currently using legacy streaming format.

logs_and_metrics:

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: aggressive prefetching + apigw hedged retries caused connection and work-queue pileup leading to thread exhaustion in the serving runtime.
What we checked: thread counts, ulimit/nproc, runtime threadpool settings, recent config sweeps. No recent runtime code deploys in us-east at incident start; a config bump to prefetch.window_size was rolled out globally at 17:55 UTC (INT-331002 linked).
Findings: rtm-04 hit process-level thread limit (nproc soft limit reached) while other nodes showed high accept-queue lengths. The apigw retry backoff was not honoring the reduced capacity threshold; hedged retries amplified work.
Possible contributory factors: customer workload with large batches (size 256) producing many short-lived threads per request path; the dedicated autoscaler lagged behind request surge.

[01:39] Maya: when you say cache lives on server side — is it encrypted and is it surfaced in logs?

[01:58] Jordan: nice. back to streaming — can we do chunking instead? we have a websocket-based client that prefers discrete messages
[02:05] Priya: yes, you can consume via websockets or SSE and you can buffer into logical chunks client-side. the responses are the same, it's just transport. we also support callback webhooks if you want server-to-server delivery for completed outputs
[02:18] Samir: ok demo time if that's cool

[02:44] [02:44] STREAM OUTPUT END

Run a tightly-scoped customer workshop that produces a validated Zero-to-POC Canvas, draft success criteria, and a concrete 30/60/90 rollout plan. Designed for mid-sized product teams evaluating Redwood Dedicated or Private deployments.

Format options (choose one):

- Standard (3 hours): full canvas, slide walkthrough, interactive mapping wall, and breakout spike design. Recommended for first full-day engagement.

Purpose
Quick personal scratchpad capturing experiments and heuristics for reducing exemplar overdominance in few-shot prompt sets (what I call 'attenuation') — aim: keep exemplar signal useful but avoid literal copying, brittle token-level overfit, and instruction hijacking.

Background / rationale
- Problem: when small numbers of exemplars are highly similar or strongly formatted, model tends to: copy exact phrasing, overfit label tokens, or treat examples as hard rules instead of cues. This shows up as hallucinated metadata, hallucinated reasoning steps, or brittle failures on paraphrase inputs.
- Goal: heuristics that are cheap to test in hosted/Dedicated flows; prefer prompt-side fixes (no fine-tuning) that interact well with Redwood runtime features: prefix caching, batching, and token-budget SLOs.

Experiment log (chronological)
1) baseline 3-shot (A)
- Template: \"Instructions: Paraphrase to plain English. Example 1 -> Q: \"What is the meaning of life?\" A: \"Life means...\"\" (simple exact format)
- Observed: 36% verbatim reuse for unique phrases, 18% hallucinated numeric claims.

2) example-noise (B) — tiny perturbations
- Apply light paraphrase to exemplars (tense swap, synonym replace). Keep labels same.
- Observed: small reduction in verbatim copying (~22%) but occasional polarity flips (because paraphrase introduced negation in two examples).

3) anchor-token dilution (C)
- Insert neutral anchor sentence before each example: \"(Example for style only; ignore facts.)\"
- Observed: Large drop in factual hallucination (13%), but model ignored label formatting more frequently -> answer brevity decreased.

4) exemplar-weighting via explicit meta cues (D)
- Prefix: \"Examples are guides, not rules. Provide your own phrasing.\" and add \"EXAMPLE_START\" tokens between examples (unique sequence).
- Observed: Better paraphrase diversity; lower exact-match. Slight latency + token usage increase (anchor tokens counted).

5) negative-exemplar (E)
- Include 1 negative example showing what *not* to do.
- Observed: helped on structure errors but introduced confusion when negative example had contradictory label tokens.

Quick takeaway: combination of paraphrase augmentation + explicit \"guidance\" prefix seems promising. Anchors reduce hallucination but cost tokens.

Prototype heuristics (to test systematically)
- ShotRotation: rotate order of exemplars per request to avoid position bias (cheap, interacts badly with caching — needs route-aware cache bypass).
- SoftParaphrasePool: maintain pool of 5 paraphrase variants per exemplar; sample 1–2 per prompt. Reduces verbatim reuse.
- AnchorLite: single short anchor token phrase (\"Style guide: be original.\") vs full sentence; measure delta/loss ratio.
- ExampleContrast: for categorical tasks, include 1 borderline example to widen model boundary; for generative tasks include 1 counterexample to show failure modes.
- TokenBudget-aware truncation: if request close to budget, automatically switch to AnchorLite + 1-shot.

Failure modes observed / notes
- Instruction hijacking: too many meta-cues cause model to treat prompt like a multi-step instruction list and follow the wrong step. Keep meta-language short.
- Contradictory anchors: negative examples that contradict label vocabulary can flip final labels. Use neutral phrasing for negatives (show format, not content).
- Caching/cold-start interaction: rotating exemplars defeats prefix caching; for high-QPS routes, prefer static exemplar unless you have hot cache invalidation.

Motivation: reduce alert noise and per-request cost attribution overhead for long-tail token spikes by introducing a 'telemetry lattice' for low-cardinality cross-layer linkage and a deferred aggregation path to compact frequent short-lived series. This PR implements a sample-first path-sampling strategy that preserves token-level latency/cost fidelity for high-value routes while preventing cardinality explosion for low-volume routes.

What changed (summary): added a lightweight trace-linking propagator (rw.telemetry.lattice) to stitch gateway request paths to runtime spans, implemented a deferred aggregator that batches metric writes at host-local level and flushes on configurable windows to the central TSDB, introduced sampled token-cost histograms by request_path, and added a new dashboard + tuned alert rules. Also includes an e2e synthetic spike test and rollout flags for staged canary.

Key design notes: telemetry lattice uses a stable 64-bit path-hash encoded in trace baggage and a short-lived sample ID for high-fidelity attribution when sample==true. Deferred aggregation reduces immediate Prometheus series churn by aggregating micro-bursts into a small set of summarized buckets before export. Path-sampling policy: always-sample for routes with route.metadata.telemetry.priority == high, probabilistic sample (1%) for medium, and adaptive sample for low (rate-limited with burst tokens).

Implementation highlights: 1) observability/metrics: token_latency_by_path (histogram_v2) and token_cost_sampled(counter with labels: path_hash,sample_id), host-local deferred_aggregator that coalesces writes, 2) tracing: propagator/propagator.go adds baggage entry "rw-tele-lattice", runtime side attaches sampled token_cost meta to the trace when present, 3) dashboards: dashboards/request-telemetry-lattice.json shows sampled vs aggregated cost and series-count impact, 4) alerts: alerts/adaptive-slo-rules.yaml replaces a static threshold for token-burn with an adaptive baseline keyed on historical p95/p99 for the route and a minimum absolute floor to avoid missing hard regressions.

Testing and rollout: unit tests added for aggregator flush logic and propagator encoding, e2e test telemetry_spike_test.go simulates synthetic bursts across 50 routes and validates series count reduction and attribution signal retention. Feature gated behind config flag telemetry.lattice.enabled and rollout guideline: 10% canary -> 50% -> all, monitor series_count and alert_firing_rate.

Backwards compatibility: non-sampled requests carry only the path_hash which is low-cardinality; no downstream schema changes required for existing dashboards.

Notes to reviewers: focus on cardinality and exporter performance, confirm that the sampling rates/flags are adequate, and validate the adaptive alert thresholds won't hide emergent regressions.

decisions:
Use an overlay spinner that sits on top of the button content (semi-transparent layer) to prevent layout shift across different label lengths
Maintain the visible label for non-icon buttons when loading but switch copy to developer-provided 'loadingLabel' if supplied; otherwise fall back to original label with aria-live announcement

Purpose and scope:
This is a portable playbook-style doc for planning the span timeline (waterfall) surface in the Console trace viewer. Focus: practical interaction patterns for exploring long requests, span grouping, quick filters, and debug-friendly annotations. Intended audience: product, frontend, SRE, and UX who will ship the first iteration (MVP) for Q1 roadmap.

High-level goals (why):
- Help engineers quickly pinpoint latency hotspots in multi-model requests (KV cache misses, routing fallbacks, model switch latencies).
- Make it cheap to triage production incidents without switching to raw logs (link out when needed).
- Provide a compact summary view plus progressively revealed detail (progressive disclosure).

Constraints and assumptions:
- Must work for traces up to 10kms (long traces) and 200 spans without freezing the UI.
- First pass will support server-side timestamps + durations; no distributed tracing correlation yet (future).
- Prefers purely client-side rendering with virtualization for rows.

MVP surface (what to build):
1) Compact timeline (collapsed spans by default):
   - Row per span group (service.action) with count and aggregated duration range (p50/p95).
   - Tap/expand to animate open slot into full span rows beneath.
   - Visual cue for long-tail spans: thin red overlay on portion > threshold.

2) Span detail flyout:
   - Header: span name, service, duration, start offset, tags (key/value), request id.
   - Tabs: Metadata (headers/attrs), Logs (linked), Events (KV/cache hits), Raw JSON (copy).
   - Quick actions: "Copy timing", "Open in logs", "Create ticket" (prefill fields).

3) Filters & quick probes bar (persistent top strip):
   - Text search over span names + attributes (syntax: name:token, tag:key=value).
   - Prebuilt quick filters: long > 500ms, error spans, model-fallback, cache-miss.
   - Toggle: group-by-service / group-by-operation / show-only-errors.

4) Time-slice scrubber and zoom controls:
   - Mini-waterfall overview (Sparkline) with a brush to zoom time ranges.
   - Keyboard shortcuts: shift + drag to select, +/- to zoom, space to play animation.

Interaction notes and micro-flows:
- Expand flow: click on row -> row animates open -> fetch per-span details (lazy) -> arrow to first child span -> keyboard focus goes into expanded region.
- Inspect-range: user highlights a time window in the scrubber -> timeline reflows showing only spans intersecting window; counts of hidden spans shown as collapsed badge.
- Multi-select: shift+click selects multiple spans -> aggregate action bar appears with suggested next steps (trace compare, export, make ticket).

Wireframe description (ASCII sketch for devs):
[Header bar: trace id | duration | region | download]
[Quick probes bar: (search) | [long>500ms] [errors] [cache-miss] [group:service]]
[Mini-sparkline scrubber]\\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
| Row 1: auth-service.login (grouped) | #####-----   120ms p95    | [v]        |
| (expanded) child spans:           | [span bars with offsets and red warning]             |
| Row 2: routing (service)          | --###------- 40ms p95     | [v]        |
| Row 3: model-serving (group)      | -----####--- 420ms p95    | [!]        |
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Footer: selected span details / copy buttons / open link to logs]

Accessibility and performance notes:
- All interactive elements must be keyboard focusable; aria labels for span durations e.g., 'span x duration 220ms start 1.3s'.
- Use row virtualization and canvas-based mini-waterfall rendering to reduce DOM counts.
- Defer heavy JSON formatting until user opens Raw JSON tab.

Open questions / discussion items (to resolve in grooming):
- How do we represent concurrent spans that overlap heavily? (Option A: stacked lanes per service, Option B: layered single lane with translucency). Decision needed by next sync.
- Should group-by default to service or operation? Metric: fewer clicks for common debug path.
- What threshold values for quick filters are product-configurable vs hard-coded?

Backlog & acceptance criteria (scoped for first 2 sprints):
- RW-2241: Timeline base rendering + virtualization
  - AC: Load traces with up to 200 spans, initial render < 300ms, maintaining 60fps scroll.
- RW-2242: Expand/collapse row groups with lazy span fetch

- Client: use react-virtualized for rows, canvas for sparkline. Avoid full JSON parse until flyout open.

description:
Context: Multi-tool call patterns at scale expose a tradeoff between per-request latency and downstream execution overhead when we naively fan out tool invocations. Customers reported jitter in streaming handshakes when several tool results were injected concurrently (see ENG-8921). Motivation: Smooth out spikes from parallel tool warmups and avoid duplicate retries while preserving deterministic injection order (for structured output consumers and OpenAI tool-calling compatibility). This PR implements a lightweight coalescing invoker that introduces a configurable grace period (default 10ms) to allow closely timed tool calls from the same top-level request to batch their execution, plus deterministic merge points for tool-result injection and a coordinated retry protocol that reduces duplicate tool executions. Key changes and design: 1) Grace-window coalescer (api/invoker/coalescer.py): collects tool call intents for a single request context for up to grace_period_ms before dispatching a prioritized execution set. Grace window is short (default 10ms) to keep tail latency bounded; tunable via request-level config. 2) Deterministic mergepoints (runtime/invoker/mergepoint.go): tool results are assigned stable sequence slots at dispatch time so downstream structured output assembly is order-deterministic even if tools finish out-of-order. This preserves existing structured-output expectations and OpenAI function-call ordering semantics. 3) Coordinated retry token (protocol/invoker_retry.proto + runtime): introduces a small idempotency token coupled with a coordinator lease to avoid concurrent retries launching duplicate side effects when multiple workers observe timeouts. Token acquisition is optimistic; fallback retry uses backoff and escalates to a single-quorum retry owner. 4) Streaming handshake stabilizations (api/gateways/openai_compat_stream.go): when streaming a response that will include tool-result injections, the gateway now waits for mergepoint assignment and streams slot-wrapped fragments to clients. We added a lightweight client-side marker in TS SDK so OpenAI-compat clients can present partial structured frames while preserving tool-call streaming expectations. 5) SDK ergonomic surface updates (redwood-sdk-typescript/src/tool-coalesce.ts): a new helper wraps parallel tool calls in a coalesce() helper so application code can opt into the grace-window behavior explicitly (default opt-out). 6) Tests and telemetry: integration tests added for high-concurrency tool scenarios, unit tests for mergepoint sequencing, and new metrics (invoker.coalesce.window_ms, invoker.mergepoint.latency, invoker.retry.quorum_falls) for Console dashboards. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is opt-out via the coalesce helper; internal routing will enable coalescing for customer-tiered policies where cost/perf tradeoffs favor batching (Dedicated plans). For users relying on immediate dispatch, new request flag coalesce=false bypasses the grace window. Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag 'invoker_coalesce_v1'. Start with internal dogfood and canary on perf-canary cluster for 48 hours, then staged enablement on 10% of hosted traffic. Monitoring and observability: dashboards added to the 'invoker' tab in Redwood Console to track coalesce rate, average delay introduced, and any observed regression in percentiles for end-to-end token latency. Risks and mitigations: - Small added latency due to the grace window; mitigated by short default and per-request override. - Complex retry semantics could hide transient failures; mitigated by alerts for quorum_falls and automatic disabling if threshold crossed. Test plan: - unit tests for coalescer (edge cases: zero grace, long tail arrivals) - integration tests simulating 200 concurrent tool calls per request - streaming handshake tests with OpenAI-compat client simulation - load test comparing cost/requests before/after merge. Documentation: docs/api/tool-coalescing.md and an SDK example added in redwood-quickstarts/tool-coalescing-example. Related: builds on earlier tooling around deterministic injection and complements ENG-9047 (structured output regressions), ENG-8921 (streaming jitter incident).

Ava Martinez: We added a short-lived lease with automatic failover; the coordinator will escalate to a quorum-based owner after lease expiry. Added tests to simulate owner crash (see test_invoker_coalesce.py).

Motivation: We have diverging streaming ergonomics across Python/TS/Go SDKs and subtle auth-retry edge cases that manifest as half-open streams or token race conditions during refresh. This PR unifies three areas: 1) a minimal, consistent 3-way auth handshake for stream starts and reconnects; 2) a small, opinionated consumer surface that makes backpressure and heartbeats explicit but ergonomic; 3) a single, test-backed retry policy and token-refresh hook that avoids duplicate requests during auth rotation.

Summary of changes (high level):
- Introduce a lightweight stream handshake: CLIENT_HELLO -> AUTH_OK -> SERVER_READY. Implemented in each SDK with shared semantics and compatibility fallbacks for older servers.
- Consumer ergonomics: new thin abstraction that replaces ad-hoc iterators/callbacks. Python exposes StreamConsumer (AsyncIterator + context manager) with buffer_size and heartbeat_ack semantics; TS exposes createStreamConsumer({onMessage, onComplete, bufferSize}) and an async iterable wrapper; Go exposes StreamReader(ctx) that implements io.Reader-like semantics for single-message reads and a Cancel() helper.
- Auth/retries: unified RetryWithAuthRefresh policy across SDKs. Retries are jittered exponential with token refresh hook invoked once per logical request; transparent idempotency guard added for non-idempotent unary calls.
- Backwards compatibility: consumers detect old handshake flows and fall back to legacy behavior for servers that do not return AUTH_OK. Migration warnings are surfaced at runtime (single warn log per process).
- Tests: added unit tests for handshake transitions and integration e2e stream tests in a local harness that simulates mid-stream token expiration.
- Version bumps: python 0.12.0, typescript 1.9.0, go 0.8.3.

Why this shape: the platform-level serving runtime already relies on explicit stream lifecycle events; exposing a small, consistent surface across SDKs reduces footguns (double-sends during reauth, leaked goroutines or pending async generators) and improves observability for consumers.

Migration notes:
- Python: replace raw async for msg in client.stream() with: async with client.stream_consumer() as c: async for msg in c: ...; short-lived code paths still supported but deprecated.
- TS: prefer createStreamConsumer over stream().iterator() when you need backpressure controls.
- Go: use NewStreamReader(ctx) to ensure reads cancel cleanly on token refresh.

The allocator issues soft "credits" (soft reservations) based on pre-commit, historical consumption, and SLA tier. Credits drive probabilistic routing decisions: prefer dedicated when credits >= cost_estimate, gradually bleed to hosted when credits are low.

Goals:
- Reduce unexpected hosted spillovers for customers with reserved capacity while allowing controlled, observable backfill to hosted for short bursts.
- Maintain latency SLOs for P0/P1 tenants and keep unit cost predictable for reserved customers.
- Provide a transparent, debuggable fallback mechanism to hosted and to lower-cost model variants.

Design highlights:
1) Credit allocator
- Each tenant has a credit balance updated continuously: credits += reserved_rate * time_window - actual_consumption_cost. Credits are bounded and never drop below a soft negative floor.
- Credit tiers: GREEN (>75%), AMBER (25%-75%), RED (<25%). Routing preference score = base_affinity * f(credit_tier) * tenant_priority_scale.

2) Probabilistic routing with hysteresis
- For each request compute P(dedicated) = sigmoid((score - threshold)/temperature). Add request jitter and short-term moving-average smoothing to avoid flapping.
- Hysteresis windows vary by tier: GREEN (30s), AMBER (2m), RED (10m).

3) Variant shadowing and demotion
- If hosted or lower-cost variant is selected, send a shadow copy to a demoted variant for quality monitoring (no charge to tenant). Shadowing includes: prompt/response hashing, deterministic knob to redact sensitive fields, and TTL for cache.
- Maintain per-variant quality deltas; if demoted variant drops below quality delta threshold for >N requests, automatically escalate to human-in-the-loop review and revert demotion if necessary.

4) Graceful hosted backfill policy
- Backfill is allowed for short bursts if predicted dedicated wait time > backfill_threshold and tenant in RED/AMBER. Backfill must carry metadata (origin:dedicated-backfill, credit_balance, fallback_decision_id) for observability and billing reconciliation.
- Introduce a backfill budget per-tenant per-day to limit cost exposure from hosted spillover.

5) Preemption & recovery
- Dedicated slots are preemptible by a request to reclaim credits: reclaiming triggers a soft-fence preventing re-routing to hosted for a brief cooldown, and emits an event to the tenant alerting them to degraded capacity.
- Recovery path replenishes credits based on committed onboarding schedule and usage smoothing.

Telemetry & observability:
- Emit these metrics at request-level and aggregated: routing_decision(reason), credit_balance_gauge, time_in_tier, backfill_event_count, variant_quality_delta, failed_shadow_rate, cost_delta_per_hour.
- Dashboards: tenant-level SLO heatmap, backfill budget burn-rate, variant-regression alerts.
- Traceable IDs: every decision must surface fallback_decision_id and policy_version in logs to enable postmortems.

Acceptance criteria:
- Simulated 48-hour stress test shows >60% reduction in unexpected hosted spillovers for tenants with >50% reserved commits compared to baseline routing.
- No increase in P0 99th p99 latency beyond 5% during simulated burst tests.
- Integration tests for credit accounting, backfill tagging, and variant shadowing coverage >90%.

Rollout plan:
1) Canary: enable credit allocator for 2 internal tenants and one low-risk external tenant (1 week).
2) Monitoring: create dashboards and an automated guardrail that disables backfill when budget burn-rate exceeds 120% of expected.
3) Progressive exposure: +10% of tenants per day with automated rollback on regression.
4) Post-rollout: 2-week observation then adjust tier thresholds and hysteresis windows based on real traffic.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How to reconcile multi-region commitments where tenant reserves span multiple hemisheres? Proposal: maintain per-region credits with cross-region transfer cap. This adds complexity but preserves locality.
- Determining cost_estimate for long-running streaming requests. We propose a moving-window model that predicts token consumption after N tokens.
- Privacy: shadowing preserves request fingerprints but must redact PII; integrate with KMS and redact rules from private deployments.

Why: teams keep asking for predictable unit costs and simpler fallbacks they can reason about. Full-blown QoS systems are heavy. We can give product teams a set of interaction tiers (micro, standard, deep) tied to routing policies, response shapes, and model variants so they can opt-in per route.

Problem statements:
- Product teams: need predictable per-interaction cost buckets without lifting infra complexity.
- Platform: wants transparent SLOs + simple rollout knobs to degrade gracefully under load.
- UX: different flows have different tolerance for latency/verbosity. No single "one-size" model fits all.

Design principles (rough):
- Primitive, composable: tiers are small metadata tags attached to a request.
- Declarative routing: config-driven mapping from tier -> model variant, cache behavior, batching policy.
- Observable: pronounced telemetry (p50/p95 latency by tier, cost per token by tier, quality regression alerts per tier).
- Safe defaults: "standard" tier matches current default behavior; micro/deep are opt-ins.

Tiers (first pass):
- micro: cheapest. short max tokens, high quantization profile, aggressive prefix cache, fallback to canned snippet when generation fails. Use for UI hints, autosuggest, quick facts.
- standard: baseline. balanced latency/cost. default model family and mid quantization. good for general chat, assistant replies.
- deep: quality-first. higher token budgets, less quantization, larger model family, enable structured-tool-calls and longer context. Use for long-form writing, code gen, final answers.

User stories:
- As a product engineer, I want to mark route /search/hint as "micro" so my feature stays within the free tier budget and I can cap per-session spend.
- As platform SRE, I want an emergency policy that turns existing "deep" requests to "standard" when GPU queues exceed 80% for 2m.
- As a growth PM, I want to A/B test deep vs standard for onboarding flows to measure conversion lift per dollar.

Acceptance signals / metrics:
- Per-route cost per 1k requests by tier (trendable).
- Latency SLO compliance per tier (p95 < tier-defined target).
- Quality regression alerts: micro/standard/deep compare eval set deltas.
- Adoption: percent of new routes assigned a tier within 30 days of creation.

API surface sketch (for devs):
- request param: interaction_tier: "micro" | "standard" | "deep" (optional, default standard).
- server-side config: route->tier override map, emergency downgrade policy, batch/caching hints.
- response metadata: served_tier, model_variant, quant_profile, billed_tokens.

Operator/Runtime implications:
- routing layer needs fast check for route-level override + per-tenant default. Could be implemented as a small routing cache with TTL.
- autoscaler signals should consider weighted qps by tier (deep = higher GPU weight).
- caching: micro tier should prefer aggressive prefix/KV caching; deep should sometimes disable prefix cache for freshness.

- Phase 0: instrument only. Add served_tier metadata in responses for 2 weeks on internal traffic.
- Phase 1: opt-in routes. Provide SDK flag and console toggle for "micro"/"deep" per route. Collect cost/latency.

Context:
description:
Introduce a headroom controller that uses short-horizon workload forecasts to proactively provision and maintain throughput guarantees for Dedicated capacity. The controller combines forecasting, conservative step sizing, and circuit-breaker safety limits to reduce SLA violations and avoid oscillatory scale behavior during traffic spikes and diurnal patterns.

background:
Current autoscaler reacts to observed metrics (p95 latency, tokens/sec) and applies conservative steps with cooldowns. We observe two issues: (1) transient spikes cause reactive overprovisioning or missed SLOs before scaling completes, and (2) cost-inefficient oscillations when traffic rapidly changes. Several related tickets implemented safety envelopes and conservative stepping, but none incorporate predictive headroom. Customer complaints from three enterprise Dedicated tenants noted latency regressions during predictable marketing spikes.

proposed_solution:
Build a lightweight forecasting module (exponential smoothing + seasonality detector) in the autoscaler service to predict 1-30min horizon throughput and tail latency proxies. Compute a headroom target: predicted_peak * safety_margin + min_capacity. Use an adaptive controller that translates headroom delta into scale actions with a PI-inspired controller, but capped by per-tenant hard limits and global fleet safety windows. Integrate a circuit-breaker that prevents scaling above emergency ceiling unless sustained over 2 minutes. Provide knobs: forecast_horizon, safety_margin_pct, max_step_percent, cooldown_s, and emergency_ceiling. Expose metrics and a dashboard and add canary rollout to 5% of Dedicated clusters.

decisions:
Use single-model ETS (error-trend-seasonality) style forecasting implemented in Go for low latency and deterministic resource use
Forecast horizons: default 5 minutes; configurable up to 30 minutes per project
Controller algorithm: PI-inspired mapping of headroom delta to steps with exponential backoff on repeated failures
Safety limits: per-tenant floor/ceiling plus a cross-tenant emergency ceiling enforced by fleet controller
Circuit-breaker triggers require predicted headroom > emergency_ceiling OR observed sustained p95 breach for >120s
No immediate autoscale-down on short negative forecast spikes: require sustained 3x check intervals before reduction

tradeoffs:
Forecasting reduces missed SLOs for predictable patterns but introduces risk if model overestimates — mitigated by hard emergency ceilings
Adding forecasting increases autoscaler complexity and CPU usage; we chose simple ETS to minimize compute and maintenance burden
Longer forecast horizons improve anticipation but increase false positives; default is conservative (5m) and configurable
PI-style controller is easier to reason about than full RL or optimization but may be suboptimal for complex multi-tenant interactions
