body:
Context and motivation:
This PR addresses a recurring class of incidents where aggressive fast-path kernel selection and lower-precision execution (fp16 / int8) produced rare but hard-to-detect correctness deviations for edge prompts. At the same time, customers expect throughput and lower cost. We need a runtime mechanism that lets us enable high-performance paths without risking silent correctness regressions in production.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a 'safelock' gating layer in the kernel selection path. The safelock prevents switching to a fast path unless a set of runtime validators pass (numerical consistency, kv-cache integrity checks, and recent success window).
- Introduces a precision toggle API (per-model, per-deployment) with three modes: strict (fp32 only), balanced (fp16 with strict validators), aggressive (fp16/int8 allowed once warmed).
- Adds a lightweight runtime validator harness: stochastic correctness probes run as background requests against canary inputs to compute divergence metrics (token-level mismatch rate, logit-delta distribution). Validators are cheap and attach metadata to requests that triggered path selection failures.
- Changes KV cache eviction policy to be conservative when cache-warmness is below threshold; combined with safelock it avoids invalidating cached KV frames that fast kernels rely on.
- Integrates safelock signals with the continuous-batching scheduler: until a deployment's validators reach a success threshold, scheduler prefers conservative batching and disables cross-model micro-batching that can expose interleaving bugs.
- Adds observability hooks: metrics (safelock.blocked_count, validator.mismatch_rate, precision.switch_count, kv.eviction_suppressed) and a dashboard stub.
- Adds a feature flag runtime.enable_safelock (default true for new deploys) and model config fields precision_mode and validator_policy.

Design notes and rationale:
- The safelock is intentionally conservative: it is designed to minimize customer-visible regressions at the cost of initial throughput until a model warms. We prefer false negatives (staying on slow path) over false positives (silent incorrect outputs).
- Validators are probabilistic and run only on a small fraction of traffic (configurable). We do not rely on end-user prompts alone; the system feeds a small canary corpus that includes known edge cases and adversarial tokens used in previous incidents.
- KV-cache eviction suppression is implemented as an additional guard in the eviction worker: if cache_warmness < 0.7 and safelock.enabled, eviction respects a soft TTL and only evicts when memory pressure exceeds a higher threshold. This prevents state churn that invalidates prefix caching assumptions used by some kernels.

Commits (high-level):
- feat(runtime): add safelock kernel gating and validator harness (A. Kumar)
- feat(config): model precision_mode and validator_policy proto + defaulting (A. Kumar)
- fix(kv): conservative eviction path and warmness estimator (R. Patel)
- perf(scheduler): integrate safelock signal into batching decisioning (L. O'Connor)
- test: end-to-end validator integration tests and canary job (E. Tan)
- docs: runtime safelock/precision-mode doc, migration notes (doc team)

Files touched (high-level):
- runtime/kernel_selector.cpp/h (safelock implementation, gating checks)
- runtime/precision_policy.proto (new model-level config)
- runtime/validator/ (background probe harness, small canary corpus)
- serving/scheduler/continuous_batcher.cpp (respect safelock signals)
- serving/kvcache/eviction_worker.cpp (suppressed eviction path)
- metrics/registry (new metrics added)
- tests/e2e/validators_integration_test.cc (new suite)
- docs/runtime/safelock.md (operator-facing guide and flags)

Small illustrative snippet included in the patch (non-executable):
"""
if (safelock.enabled() && !validators.passed_recently(dep)) {
  // force fallback to conservative kernel + fp32 path
  selectKernel = KernelSelector::conservative(model, seq_len);
} else {
  selectKernel = KernelSelector::fastpath(model, seq_len, precision_mode);
}
"""

Benchmarks / numbers:
- Baseline (main, before PR) on rtx-a100-80gb, long-tail tests: median latency 48ms, p99 180ms, throughput 2200 tok/s.
- With safelock enabled (default config) immediately after deploy: median latency +6% (51ms), throughput -8% (2024 tok/s) while validators warm.
- After 30m of live traffic and validator success: median latency +1% (48.5ms), throughput -2% (2160 tok/s).
- Aggressive mode (opt-in, warm): throughput +12% over baseline; we see a measurable cost win.
- We ran a correctness sweep against our regression corpus (n=1200 prompts) showing token-level mismatch reduced to <0.02% for balanced mode; in aggressive mode mismatch rises to ~0.6% on the corpus (expected, opt-in).

Testing and CI:
- Added unit + integration tests for validator harness and eviction behavior.
- Added synthetic stochastic tests that simulate rare floating-point edgecases.
- CI: initial pipeline had one flaky test (eviction_worker race) failing on Linux-asan; fixed in second commit. Final CI: all checks passed (build, unit, integration, perf-smoke).

Review discussion (highlights):
- Marco: "I like the safelock abstraction; can we ensure the validator corpus is editable by SREs without code changes?"
- Aisha: "Yes — validators read a canary file from /etc/redwood/validators/corpus.json and we added operator docs. SRE can update via configmap for k8s deploys."
- Eve: "Concerned about metric cardinality when we annotate every request with validator metadata."
- Aisha: "We emit aggregated counters and histograms; only a small sampling logs request-level debug traces behind a flag."
- Liam: "Scheduler changes look sane. Need additional canary rollout plan for enterprise customers with strict SLAs."
- Aisha: "Added rollout doc and an opt-out label on deployment config; default for existing deployments is unchanged (safe-mode learned)."

Edge cases / known tradeoffs:
- There is an initial throughput hit until validators warm. We mitigate by sampling only a small portion of traffic for validators and allowing manual warm-up (canary traffic injection).
- Aggressive precision_mode is opt-in; customers should enable only after verifying on internal test prompts. We include a CLI tool for running the validator corpus locally against a deployment.
- The KV eviction suppression increases memory use under some failure modes; we documented emergency knobs and introduced an automatic disable threshold if memory pressure remains high for 10s.

Migration / operator guidance:
- New deploys: safelock enabled by default. Operators can set runtime.enable_safelock=false to revert (not recommended).
- To opt into aggressive precision: update model config: precision_mode=aggressive and monitor validator.mismatch_rate.
- Dashboards: added a starter Grafana dashboard (docs link) and alerts for validator.mismatch_rate > 0.1% and safelock.blocked_count being unexpectedly high.

Backward compatibility:
- All config fields default to conservative behavior; no breaking changes. Models without precision_mode set continue to use fp32 until they pass validators.

Post-merge actions / follow-ups (linear):
- ENG-4983: add automated warmup job to inject synthetic canary traffic during deploy windows (follow-up).
- ENG-5122: add per-customer precision analytics and billing impact report.

Merge outcome:
- Final status: merged via squash. Branch merged to main after approvals from Marco, Eve, and Liam. CI green at merge.

If you want to test locally: run tools/runtime_cli --run-validators --config test/configs/precision_local.yaml against a dev deployment; run scripts/kv_warmup.sh to pre-fill the kvcache with the canary prefix set.

Thanks to Rohan Patel for eviction work, and the QA team for extended regression runs.

Patch size: moderate; favors safety and observability over aggressive micro-optimizations up front.

Context:
Purpose and scope:
This runbook captures the operational design and step-by-step procedures for key lifecycle management (cloud KMS, HSM-backed keys, and customer BYOK), rotation patterns, and formatted audit export to the SIEM. It is intended for security engineers, platform engineers (private/dedicated), and on-call SREs who will perform rotations, evidence collection, and incident responses related to encryption-at-rest.

Non-goals:
- Specifying vendor-specific API docs (those are linked in the artifacts section).
- Replacing the Verified KMS onboarding checklist — this complements it with operational playbook material.

Overview of crypto hierarchy (recommended model):
- Root/Signer (offline or HSM-protected root key): only used to sign intermediate keys and for bootstrapping. Extremely high entropy, stored in FIPS-validated HSM or offline guard.
- Master Key (MK): KMS-managed single-purpose key used to encrypt/unwrap key-encryption-keys (KEKs). Rotated infrequently; stored in cloud KMS or HSM with strict RBAC.
- Key-Encryption Keys (KEKs): Per- tenancy (customer or environment) keys used to wrap Data Encryption Keys (DEKs). KEKs live in KMS/HSM and are subject to rotation policies independent of DEKs.
- Data Encryption Keys (DEKs): Short-lived keys used for envelope encryption of object data (S3, blockstore, DB column encryption). DEKs are generated by the service, encrypted with KEK, and stored alongside ciphertext.

Why envelope encryption: improved rotation and small blast radius — DEKs are cheap to rotate and do not require re-encrypting blobs when KEK rotates (only rewrap operation).

RBAC v2 for keys (mapping to roles):
- key-admin: create/delete/grant/revoke KEKs and manage key policy metadata. Should be restricted to Security Eng and Platform Admins. (Granting on a per-key resource basis.)
- key-operator: initiate rotate/rewrap operations, request key usage metrics, and run emergency revocations. Intended for SRE on-call + rotation automation service accounts.
- kms-viewer: read-only access to key metadata, audit entries, and rotation history; used by auditors and compliance reviewers.
- crypto-service (machine/account): service principal used by runtime to perform encrypt/decrypt operations — scoped to specific KEKs via least privilege.

Access controls and constraints:
- No human accounts with direct encrypt/decrypt rights on production KEKs unless explicitly approved and logged.
- All changes to key policy must require multi-approver workflow via ticket (JIRA-SEC or ServiceNow) with a signed justification field.

Rotation policy matrix (recommended default):
- Root/Signer: rotate only on explicit key compromise or re-keying cycle every 5+ years (with offline ceremony).
- Master Key (MK): 18–36 months, or immediately on suspected compromise.
- KEK (per-tenant): 6–12 months; automated rewrap of DEKs recommended during low-traffic windows.
- DEK: TTL 24 hours to 90 days based on workload sensitivity; for high-volume object stores, prefer short TTL (7–30 days) and frequent rewraps.

Rotation step-by-step (KEK rotation, automated):
1) Pre-checks:
   - Confirm current KEK metadata and last_rotation in KMS.
   - Verify successful snapshot/backup of key metadata snapshot (S3 location: s3://redwood-sec-key-metadata/yyyymmdd).
   - Check outstanding re-wrap tasks and in-flight writes; consult per-route write-latency dashboard.
   - Ensure automation runbook is in a healthy state (CI job green).
2) Create new KEK version in KMS/HSM using secure API. Tag version with rotation-correlation-id and timestamp.
3) Update service principal grants for the new key version (if using explicit version grants).
4) Enqueue rewrap job that will read ciphertext metadata, call KMS unwrap with old KEK -> DEK, then wrap DEK with new KEK, and write back wrapped value. Jobs are sharded and rate-limited to preserve latency SLOs.
5) Monitor rewrap progress, look for rewrap-failure counts and backoffs. Failures trigger automatic re-try with exponential backoff and eventual pager escalation to on-call.
6) After >= 95% rewrap completion, update key policy primary-version pointer to new KEK version. Keep old version alive for 30–90 days for rollback and emergency decrypt.
7) Post-ops: generate evidence bundle (audit logs, job run IDs, manifest of rewrapped object IDs) and export to secure evidence store.

Manual emergency rotation (compromise suspected):
- Immediate steps: set KEK to disabled state for new wraps (maintain unwrap to allow decrypts if needed), create incident ticket, notify CS/Legal if customer keys involved. For BYOK, escalate to customer contact according to contract.

BYOK specific flows and customer-supplied HSMs:
- Onboarding requires: customer intent form, key rollover policy acceptance, and KMS import key ceremony recorded in Confluence page.
- BYOK keys are treated as external-key IDs — Redwood stores only wrapped DEKs. Key operations with external HSM require dedicated connector host in customer VPC or HSM proxy with mutual-auth TLS.
- Rotation for BYOK: coordinate schedule with customer; do not perform unilateral rotation of a customer-supplied root. Documented SLA window must be observed.

Audit log schema (key events) — canonical fields (JSON log entry):
- timestamp: ISO8601 string
- event_type: one of [KEY_CREATE, KEY_ROTATE, KEY_VERSION_CREATE, KEY_DISABLE, KEY_ENABLE, KEY_DELETE, KEY_UNWRAP, KEY_WRAP, KEY_POLICY_CHANGE]
- resource_id: kms://<region>/<key-id>
- actor: <principal-id or service-account>
- actor_type: human|service|external-customer
- action_id: UUID (correlation across services)
- request_id: cloud-kms-request-id (if available)
- outcome: success|failure|partial
- reason: free text (failure reason / policy change note)
- correlation_tags: list of tags (rotation-correlation-id, ticket-id)
- old_version: version-id (if rotation)
- new_version: version-id (if rotation)
- rewrap_manifest_loc: s3://... or null
- sampled_trace: diagnostic trace id or null
- raw_event: raw provider event (if available)

Example log (single-line JSON):
{
  "timestamp": "2024-11-05T22:14:31Z",
  "event_type": "KEY_ROTATE",
  "resource_id": "kms://us-east1/ke-abc123",
  "actor": "svc-key-rotation@redwood-infra",
  "actor_type": "service",
  "action_id": "b3a85d6f-4c2b-4a9d-8e1c-3d9f7a9d2fbb",
  "request_id": "cloudreq-9922",
  "outcome": "success",
  "reason": "scheduled-rotation",
  "correlation_tags": ["rotation-20241105", "JIRA-SEC-1290"],
  "old_version": "v1",
  "new_version": "v2",
  "rewrap_manifest_loc": "s3://redwood-sec-key-manifests/rewrap-20241105.json",
  "sampled_trace": "trace-7a9e",
  "raw_event": null
}

SIEM export mapping guidance:
- Ingest each canonical audit log into the SIEM as a single event with the following mapped fields: time, src_principal (actor), event_type, resource, correlation_id (action_id), outcome, tags, message.
- Enrich events with identity attributes from IAM (team, manager, risk_score) and with customer ids for tenant-scoped keys.
- Create SIEM detection rules for abnormal activity patterns:
  - Multiple KEY_UNWRAP calls from different service principals for the same resource within a short window.
  - New key-version creation without a preceding JIRA ticket tag.
  - KEK rotates outside maintenance window.
  - Unexpected external-customer key access from internal VMs.

Evidence automation (post-rotation evidence bundle):
- Components to collect automatically after a rotation or emergency action:
  - Audit log slice covering action_id and +/- 24 hours.
  - Rewrap manifest (list of objects rewrapped and shard ids).
  - KMS provider raw response payloads and request IDs.
  - CI/CD job run ids and artifacts (automation run logs).
  - Signed PDF of rotation approvers (if manual approvals present).
- Automation job will package the above into a signed tarball, compute a SHA256, upload to s3://redwood-sec-evidence/<action_id>/evidence.tar.gz and emit an evidence-created audit event.

Testing, validation and rollback:
- Canary run: pick a low-traffic tenant and perform a KEK rotate + rewrap. Validate decrypt success on sampled objects for 48 hours. Use automated smoke tests (github.com/redwood-infra/tests/key-rotate-canary).
- Rollback: if rewrap fails en masse, revert primary-version pointer to previous version and abort further wrap jobs. Keep failure manifest for investigation.

Monitoring and observability:
- Key metrics to publish: rewrap_progress_percent, rewrap_error_rate, key_usage_per_minute, key_latency_p50/p90/p99 for wrap/unwrap calls, key_policy_change_count.
- Dashboards: per-region key counters, tenant-impact view, and a security incidents dashboard that surfaces any disabled keys or rapid version churn.

Operational playbook checklist (pre-rotation):
- [ ] Confirm maintenance window and customer notifications (if tenant scoped).
- [ ] Snapshot key metadata.
- [ ] Ensure rewrap jobs have capacity and throttles configured.
- [ ] Backup evidence store writable.

Post-rotation checklist:
- [ ] Rewrap >= 95% completed or documented exception list.
- [ ] Evidence tarball produced and verified.
- [ ] Post-rotation smoke tests green.
- [ ] Update key inventory and rotation calendar.

Compromise handling (short runbook):
1) Immediately mark key as disabled for new wraps and log action.
2) Create incident ticket with correlation_id and contact list.
3) If customer key (BYOK), notify customer per contract and follow agreed escalation.
4) Start forensic capture: full audit slice, host traces, and rewrap manifest.
5) If necessary, perform emergency rewrap to new KEK and reject old version; expedite evidence export for compliance.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Do we require HSM for all MKs by default or only high-sensitivity tenants? (propose: high-sensitivity and enterprise with SLA >$Xk/month)
- Retention policy for old key versions beyond rollback window (30/90/365 days?)
- Integration point for RBAC v2 authorization checks in the KMS proxy — pre-check or delegated to provider?

Next steps (action items):
- Lina: draft BYOK onboarding form for customer agreements (due 2024-11-20).
- Diego: implement SIEM enrichment pipeline prototype (P0) and push PR.
- Samir: add rotation canary to infra tests and schedule monthly runs.

- Rewrap job implementation: github.com/redwood-infra/rewrap-service (PR-487 linked above)
- Evidence automation template: CONFLUENCE-SEC/Evidence-Automation-Template
- Incident escalation contact list: CONFLUENCE-SEC/Incident-Contacts

Notes and contextual snippets (working):
- Consider adding rate-limit bucketing per-tenant to rewrap workers to avoid noisy-tenant storms.
- We should index rewrap-manifests by tenant and time for quick e-discovery.
- Long-term: explore native HSM signing for root key ceremonies and publish an offline attestation record.

Context:
Purpose
This doc is a combined architecture + operational runbook for our routing policy engine and control-plane components across multi-region deployments. It is intentionally practical: short diagnostics, commands, and mitigations embedded in architecture context so on-call engineers can both reason about root cause and act quickly.

Scope
- Components: routing-policy-service (RPS), control-plane-api, policy-store (etcd/consul), route-agent (edge sidecar), regional health aggregator, and the global policy router.
- Cross-region concerns: affinity, KV replication lag, split-brain on leader election, and fallback model variant routing.
- Not included: serving-runtime GPU node-level debugging (see serving-runtime/sre-runbooks).

Architecture notes (brief)
- Control plane (control-plane-api + policy-store) is the single source of truth for routing policies, rollout stages, and region weightings. It exposes a versioned API used by route-agents to fetch policies on startup and at policy-change webhooks.
- Route-agents run in each region and maintain an in-memory policy cache and local evaluation engine for low-latency routing decisions. Agents watch the policy-store via streaming endpoints and apply delta updates.
- Policy evaluation order: explicit-route (customer pin) -> canary -> weighted-routing -> geo-affinity -> fallback. Policies are deterministic and evaluated top-to-bottom.
- Rollouts: canaries are enabled by rollout rules stored in the policy-store. Each rollout has a name, window, and metric criteria (latency and error thresholds).
- Health checks: agents report region-level health via health-aggregator which updates a region-status index used by global router.

Common incident scenarios + runbooks
1) Control plane API unresponsive (HTTP 5xx or timeouts)
- Symptom: config change fails; route-agents show repeated fetch retries; recent deploy of control-plane-api; alerts: PLAT-CONTROL-API-ERR.
- Quick checks:
  - Check SLOs/dashboard: control_plane_api_request_latency_p50/p95, control_plane_api_error_rate (Dash: Platform / Control Plane / API)
  - kubectl -n platform get pods -l app=control-plane-api; kubectl logs -f deployment/control-plane-api -c api --tail 200
  - curl -v https://control-plane-api.internal/healthz || echo "down"
- Quick mitigations:
  - If pods are CrashLoopBackOff: kubectl describe pod <pod> to see OOM or config errors. Revert recent config change (kubectl rollout undo deployment/control-plane-api) if deploy timestamp aligns with incident.
  - If high CPU due to policy-store scan: scale up replicas temporarily: kubectl scale deploy/control-plane-api --replicas=4 (notify infra).
  - If external dependency (auth/KMS) failing: flip maintained feature-flag to allow unauthenticated local reads for emergency: POST to admin toggle endpoint (requires infra approval).
- Recovery steps:
  - Redeploy last known-good image: kubectl set image deployment/control-plane-api control-plane-api=registry.redwood/internal/control-plane-api:stable-20260201
  - Validate route-agents reconnected: check route-agent logs and policy version: kubectl logs -l app=route-agent -c agent | grep "policy_version="
- Post-incident:
  - Open PLAT JIRA ticket, attach timeline and last deploy id (PLAT-CONTROL-API-ERR-YYYYMMDD), run postmortem template, update changelog.

2) Policy drift or incorrect evaluation order deployed (bad rollout rules)
- Symptom: certain traffic unexpectedly hits a fallback model; regression alerts on quality (Rerank/quality evals) or sudden cost increase.
- Quick checks:
  - Check policy versions: curl https://control-plane-api.internal/v1/policies/versions last_3
  - Search for recent policy changes: git log --since="48 hours" -- platform-configs/policies
  - Query route-agent logs for "policy-eval" traces and decision path: kubectl logs -l app=route-agent | egrep "policy_eval|decision_path"
- Quick mitigations:
  - Push emergency policy patch that restores previous rule ordering. Use the policy-store admin UI to revert version or use API: POST /v1/policies/revert {"version":"v123"}
  - If automatic rollouts continue to apply bad policy, disable rollout engine: PATCH /v1/admin/settings {"rollout_enabled":false} (only for <30m).
- Recovery steps:
  - Validate behavior in canary region and run synthetic tests (see linked_artifacts). Promote fix to all regions after 30 minutes of stable metrics.

3) Regional split-brain / KV replication lag causing inconsistent policies across regions
- Symptom: region A has new policies, region B still uses older policies -> inconsistent routing; alerts: PLAT-POLICY-REPL-LAG.
- Quick checks:
  - Check policy-store replication status: kubectl -n platform exec -it statefulset/policy-store -- /bin/psql -c "SELECT * FROM replication_status;"
  - Check agent-sync metrics: route_agent_policy_sync_lag_seconds{region="us-east-1"}
  - Look for leader-election warnings in logs: kubectl logs -l app=policy-store | egrep "leader|raft|election"
- Quick mitigations:
  - If leader elected incorrectly, force leader stepdown to trigger re-election: kubectl exec -it pod/policy-store-0 -- /bin/consul operator raft remove-peer <peer-id> (follow infra runbook) or use etcdctl to promote leader.
  - Temporarily set global routing to prefer region with majority policy consistency: POST /v1/admin/routing/override {"global_prefer":"us-west-2"}
- Recovery steps:
  - Reconcile KV store: run the replication repair script from git (scripts/repair-kv-replication.sh) with oncall approval. Monitor sync lag and then lift routing override.

4) Route-agent high-latency evaluation causing end-to-end latency spikes
- Symptom: route-agent CPU usage high, p99 eval latency elevated, affecting latency SLOs.
- Quick checks:
  - route_agent_eval_latency_p50/p95/p99, route_agent_cpu_usage
  - Check rule set size: POST /v1/admin/policies/size for region to see number of rules loaded
- Quick mitigations:
  - Reduce policy complexity: enable emergency-compact policy set: POST /v1/admin/policies/compact {"reason":"latency_immediate"} to temporarily apply simplified ruleset.
  - Scale route-agent horizontally: kubectl scale deployment/route-agent --replicas=<current*2>
- Recovery steps:
  - Run policy pruning process to remove obsolete legacy rules (ticket PLAT-3120). Re-introduce full rule set gradually via canary.

Investigations / diagnostics cheat-sheet
- Verify control-plane health: curl https://control-plane-api.internal/metrics | egrep "control_plane_api|policy_store"
- Agent status per region: curl https://health-aggregator.internal/regions | jq . (look for last_synced_ts)
- Policy version reported to router: curl https://global-router.internal/status | jq '.policy_version'
- Example kubectl debugging commands:
  - kubectl -n platform exec -it deploy/control-plane-api -- curl -sS localhost:8080/debug/vars | jq .
  - kubectl logs -l app=route-agent -c agent --since=30m | egrep "warn|error|policy_eval"

Escalation and ownership
- First responder: oncall-platform (rotation). If control-plane API >15m, escalate to platform-sre lead and platform eng owner.
- Pager escalation policy: see PLAT-SOP-ESCL (Confluence link in linked_artifacts). Provide timeline, last_playbook_steps, and any admin toggles we exercised.

Safety knobs and feature flags (where to flip things)
- rollout_enabled (boolean) - disables automated rollouts when false. Admin API path: /v1/admin/settings
- policy_store_read_fallback - allows route-agents to use cached policies for longer TTL when set.
- global_routing_override - temporarily forces traffic to a single region or traffic tier. Use only for short windows and record justification.

Templates / quick commands
- Revert control-plane deployment: kubectl rollout undo deployment/control-plane-api -n platform
- Scale route-agent: kubectl scale deploy/route-agent -n platform --replicas=6
- Force policy-store leader election: kubectl exec statefulset/policy-store-0 -n platform -- /usr/local/bin/raftctl transfer-leader --target-id=<id>
- Emergency compact policy (API): curl -XPOST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://control-plane-api.internal/v1/admin/policies/compact -d '{"reason":"latency_immediate"}'

Post-incident checklist
- Create JIRA ticket with affected regions, start/end times, deploy ids, and mitigations taken (labels: incident, control-plane).
- Add timeline to ticket and link to this doc.
- Run policy audit: ensure no manual emergency edits remain. Archive emergency policy versions to policy-store/history.
- Update runbook with any new commands, gotchas, or learned metrics.

Known gaps / follow-ups
- No safe automated rollback from policy migrations that touch more than 500 rules. Action: implement transactional policy-apply with preflight dry-run (PLAT-4010).
- No RBAC approval flow for emergency admin toggles. Action: short-term Slack approval step required; long-term: implement approval queue.

Appendix: useful dashboards and tests
- Dashboards: Platform / Control Plane / Policy Store Replication; Platform / Routing / Agent Latency; Platform / Global Router Health.
- Synthetic tests: per-region policy-eval synthetic (synthetic/policy-eval) that runs every 30s; endpoint: https://synthetic.internal/policy-eval?test=basic-route

Contact list (oncall rotation owners)
- platform-oncall: @platform-oncall (pager), lead: Arjun Patel <arjun@redwood.com>, eng-owner: Maya Chen <maya.chen@redwood.com>

Notes to self (working area)
- Need to add TLS cert rotation steps for policy-store replication (deferred to infra).
- Double-check rollback image tags used in last 3 control-plane deploys.
- Follow up: add example logs for policy-eval decision_path so new oncall can grep them quicker.

End of doc.

Motivation: the OpenAI Responses API v3 introduces a seed/determinism flag and richer per-response metadata fields. Customers expecting parity through our OpenAI compatibility layer were hitting two classes of issues: 1) requests with deterministic seeds sometimes routed to fallback model variants causing non-deterministic behavior, and 2) streaming reassembly and function/tool-calling events lost user-supplied metadata (e.g., trace ids) on intermediate fragments. This PR: - Propagates the new 'seed' and 'determinism' fields from OpenAI-style Requests through our compatibility translation layer so upstream callers can control RNG determinism when we map to compatible model variants. - Adds per-request metadata passthrough: preserves and forwards top-level metadata and nested response-level metadata (user supplied) through streaming frames and the final assembled Response object. - Stabilizes streaming reassembly for mixed partials (text chunks, tool call fragments, structured JSON outputs) by introducing a sequence/frame id and last-frame markers in the compat layer; this avoids interleaving when a single call fan-outs to auxiliary model variants. - Ensures function/tool-calling events are emitted with the original 'metadata' and 'seed' fields intact so SDKs relying on tool traceability continue to work. - Adds exhaustive integration tests against the Responses v3 contract and extends streaming unit tests to emulate packet reorder and intermittent delivery. Implementation notes: - New compatibility translator: redwood/openai_compat/responses_v3_translator.py maps OpenAI fields to internal inference request flags (seed->rng_seed, determinism->sampling_profile). Translator is intentionally minimal: we preserve unknown fields in a passthrough map under compat_metadata for future extensions. - Streaming layer changes: redwood/api/streaming.py: implement frame_sequence_id and final_fragment bool. Reassembly uses (request_id, frame_sequence_id) ordering plus a small re-sequencing buffer gated by latency_slo to avoid head-of-line blocking. - Routing: routing/policy.py updated to prefer exact-architecture variants when determinism is requested; fallback still allowed if pinned variant unavailable. - Tests: tests/integration/test_responses_v3_compat.py includes deterministic-seed repeatability checks, metadata round-trip assertions, and simulated packet reordering scenarios. - Docs: docs/openai_compat.md updated with Responses v3 mapping and guidance for determinism semantics. Backwards compatibility: default behavior unchanged if seed/determinism not provided. We intentionally do not make determinism true by default because it impacts throughput. Checklist: - [x] Translator for seed/determinism fields - [x] Metadata passthrough in streaming frames - [x] Stable reassembly and ordering buffer - [x] Routing preference when determinism requested - [x] Integration + unit tests - [x] Docs update - [x] CI passing on rerun Rollout/rollback notes: feature gated behind a compatibility flag (OPENAI_COMPAT_V3=true) and an experiment toggle for routing. If customer issues are observed around tail latency with deterministic requests, the routing policy can be relaxed to fallback earlier while preserving seed values in logs for replay/diagnosis.

## Summary

This handbook defines a causal-first process for investigating model regressions (quality, latency, and cost) observed after a change (model version, quantization profile, infra, or prompt). It combines signals from the eval harness, production telemetry, and unit-level artifacts to form testable causal hypotheses and rapidly converge on root cause. This doc is intended for ML engineers, SREs, and applied ML owners performing triage on regression alerts.

## Scope

- Applies to regressions discovered via: continuous eval pipelines, production quality alerts, customer escalations, or automated regression bisect results.
- Covers causal graph design, hypothesis generation, experiment design, statistical testing, and actionable rollback/fix patterns.
- Not a replacement for the automated-bisect playbook; rather, this is the manual/analyst layer for ambiguous or cross-cutting regressions.

## Ownership and Escalation

- Primary owner: Applied ML - Model Quality team
- On-call SRE: for runtime/latency regressions
- Escalation: if causal analysis points to infra/serving runtime, escalate to Eng-Serving-Runtime within 4 hours.

## Definitions

- Regression: measurable degradation in an SLO or metric compared to baseline (pre-change).
- Change event: deploy, quantization profile change, router policy update, prompt set modification, or model promotion.
- Primary signals: evaluation harness results, production cost/latency/quality telemetry, example traces, token-level diffs.

## Signals and Data Sources (ordered by priority)

1. Eval harness: stable test-set metrics, per-slice breakdowns, and seed-fixed reruns.
2. Production telemetry: per-route token latency, error rates, kv-cache hit rates, and token counts.
3. Shadow traffic and A/B results (if available).
4. Client traces / transcript samples (anonymized).
5. Deployment metadata: model SHA, quantization profile ID, kernel selection log, GPU type, and routing policy.

## Causal DAG Templates

Use these canonical Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) templates to structure thinking. Draw the DAG and explicitly list assumed causal links before testing. Example templates (textual):

- Template A (Model-change-driven): ChangeEvent -> Weights/Quantization -> ModelBehavior -> OutputQuality
- Template B (Runtime-interaction): ChangeEvent -> KernelSelection/Batching -> Latency -> TimeoutErrors -> Quality
- Template C (Prompt/Context): ChangeEvent -> PromptSet/ContextTruncation -> KV-CacheHits -> EffectiveContext -> OutputQuality

Always annotate nodes that are observable vs latent and list available instrumentation for each node.

## Investigation Checklist (step-by-step)

1. Record the alert context: metric, threshold, time window, impacted slices (routes, languages, long vs short prompts).
2. Snapshot deployment metadata for the time window: model_id, model_sha, quant_profile, runtime_version, host region, and GPU type.
3. Replicate the failure in the eval harness with the same model and quantization profile, using the failing prompt slices. Use deterministic seeds where applicable.

   Example CLI to re-run a failing slice locally:
   
   curl -X POST https://eval-harness.internal/run -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"slice_id":"lang-en-long-context", "model_id":"m-v42", "quant_profile":"q8_4", "seed":42}'

4. Construct a concise causal DAG and list 2–3 competing hypotheses (e.g., quantization introduced a tokenization-sensitive bias; kernel fallback increased latency and triggered truncation).
5. Prioritize hypotheses by plausibility and ease-of-test. Run targeted ablations:
   - A/B run with float32 weights vs quantized profile on the same hardware.
   - Run with and without KV-cache enabled.
   - Run with controlled batch sizes to reproduce kernel selection differences.

6. Apply causal tests: difference-in-differences, regression adjustment, and when appropriate, causal-impact or DoWhy-style causal estimation.

   Minimal SQL snippet to prepare test/control cohorts:

   SELECT request_id, model_tag, quant_profile, prompt_slice, quality_score, latency_ms, kv_cache_hit
   FROM production_prompts
   WHERE event_time BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-02'
   AND prompt_slice IN ('lang-en-long-context', 'lang-en-short')

7. If initial tests are inconclusive, schedule targeted shadow traffic or a canary with enhanced telemetry for 2 hours covering the failing slices.
8. When confident in root cause, prepare remediation: rollback plan, targeted quantization tweak, kernel configuration change, or prompt update. Document the fix in the incident tracker.
9. Close the loop: add failing prompts to the prompt-sets-and-benchmarks suite and create a new quant-eval slice if quantization was causal.

## Statistical Decision Rules

- Minimum sample size: 500 requests per slice for high-variance tasks (chat/long-context); 100 for low-variance embeddings or deterministic reranks.
- Significance: two-sided p < 0.01 for primary SLOs. Use bootstrap CIs for non-normal metrics (BLEU-like or token-level fidelity).
- Effect size threshold: absolute quality-drop >= 2% or relative latency increase >= 20% is actionable by default. Adjust per-SLO tier.

## Example Causal Test (Python pseudocode)

# Example: Use DoWhy to estimate effect of quantization on quality_score

from dowhy import CausalModel
import pandas as pd

# load prepared cohort dataframe
df = pd.read_csv('cohort.csv')
model = CausalModel(data=df, treatment='quant_profile_q8_4', outcome='quality_score', common_causes=['prompt_length', 'route', 'seed'])
identified_estimand = model.identify_effect()
estimate = model.estimate_effect(identified_estimand, method_name='backdoor.propensity_score_matching')
print(estimate)

Note: include diagnostics and sensitivity analysis for unobserved confounding.

## Integrations with Automated Bisect and Eval Harness

- When bisect returns candidate change windows, attach a causal-analysis job that:
  - Replays failing trace samples across candidate model variants.
  - Runs the lightweight DoWhy/DiD tests on per-slice cohorts.
  - Produces a short causal report in the bisect output (delta metrics, p-values, suggested root causes).

- Hook names: eval-harness/replay, bisect/causal-report, telemetry/query-cohort.

## Required Instrumentation and Data Schema

Minimum columns for any cohort extract (plain text table):

| column_name | type | description |
| request_id | string | unique request identifier |
| event_time | timestamp | request time |
| model_tag | string | model identifier (e.g., m-v42) |
| quant_profile | string | quant profile id |
| route | string | API route or product feature |
| prompt_slice | string | slice label from prompt catalog |
| quality_score | float | chosen quality metric (0-1 normalized) |
| latency_ms | float | end-to-end token latency |
| kv_cache_hit | bool | cache hit flag |

Ensure all datasets are (a) anonymized, (b) token counts and sample prompts excluded from exported CSVs by default.

## Common Root Causes and Recommended Fixes

- Quantization-precision-bias: Re-run quant profile with per-layer fallback, raise precision on sensitive layers, add per-slice quant-tune.
- Kernel-fallback-latency: Pin kernel to earlier stable runtime for affected model length range; increase timeout SLOs temporarily.
- KV-cache-eviction-regression: Investigate policy, add explicit cache hold for long contexts or move to a larger shard.
- Prompt-truncation-shift: Add guardrail in prompt pipeline to preserve critical prefix tokens; add unit tests in prompt-sets.

## Playbook for Live Mitigation (fast timeline)

1. Within 30 minutes: if customer-facing degradations, enable fallback model variant (float or previous release).
2. Within 2 hours: collect reproducer examples and run targeted canary with enhanced telemetry.
3. Within 24 hours: implement permanent fix or schedule rollback.

## Post-Incident Actions

- Add failing prompts to permanent prompt regression suite.
- Create a quant-eval slice and add to nightly eval for that profile.
- Update the causal DAG library with the final root cause and evidence.
- Run a retrospective with owners (Applied ML, Serving Runtime, SRE) and record action items.

## Templates and Reporting

Use the following one-page template for causal-report attachments to incidents:

- Title: (short)
- Summary: 2–3 sentences
- Candidate hypotheses tested (list)
- Data used (cohort sizes, time windows)
- Statistical tests and results (p-values, CIs)
- Root cause (with confidence: low/medium/high)
- Action taken and follow-ups

description:
Motivation: Long-tail requests and multi-turn sessions make it hard to correlate expensive tokens with the actual prompt context. Alert noise for cost spikes often stems from superficially similar traces that differ in a few context tokens. This PR introduces two complementary observability primitives: (1) sampled context anchors — compact, privacy-safe snapshots attached to selected traces that let engineers inspect a representative prefix without storing full payloads; and (2) cost-delta annotations — span-level annotations that capture the incremental token cost relative to a baseline (baseline = first N tokens of the session or pinned model variant), enabling per-span cost-attribution and easy identification of regression candidates.

What this change does (high level):
- Adds a lightweight sampled-context store and recorder in the runtime that writes encrypted, k-anonymized anchors for 1% of long-tail sessions (configurable). Anchors include token fingerprints, anonymized prompt length buckets, and hashed prompt-context tags for grouping (no raw PII/token content stored).
- Adds cost-delta annotations into the tracing pipeline: each model-stage span now carries cost.delta and cost.baseline fields (numeric micro-units). These are added as span attributes and surfaced to OTEL and internal trace indexer.
- Dashboard updates: new dashboard panels on Console -> Observability that show per-route cost-delta distribution, anchor-cluster heatmap (session groups), and annotated trace + anchor join views.
- Alert tuning: new alerting rule that groups alerts by anchor-hash first and surfaces a single grouped alert for clusters of similar high-cost traces (reduces noisy duplicates). Added docs and runbook snippets for triage.

Implementation notes and constraints:
- Context anchors are generated at the runtime layer (redwood/service/runtime) before caching/quantization to avoid skew. Anchors emit a deterministic anchor-hash derived from a salted rolling-hash; the salt is customer-scoped to avoid cross-tenant correlation.
- Cost delta math: cost.delta = observed_token_cost - baseline_token_cost, baseline_token_cost is computed using a rolling median of the first 32 tokens for the route/model combo and periodically recomputed by a background aggregator.
- Privacy compliance: anchors are truncated and tokenized into fingerprint sketches; feature flags and customer-level opt-out is supported.
- Performance: profiling showed a 0.2% median p99 added latency on typical requests in our stage perf lab; batching and non-blocking flush paths mitigate the tail impact.

Doc purpose (Product Ops)
========================
We need a consistent set of internal remediation SLAs (time-to-mitigate / time-to-fix expectations) that:
- match what we can realistically execute across tiers (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)
- align with customer expectations and enterprise commitments (especially Dedicated/Private)
- can be implemented in tooling (ENG-4829 / SLA timers + breach alerts) without constant exceptions
- remains low-cardinality and understandable during live incidents

This is a working evaluation doc of options; final policy will live in Confluence in the Remediation SLA matrix.

Definitions
===========
- Remediation SLAs in this doc are internal operational targets and escalation triggers.
- We track two clocks:
  1) TTM (time-to-mitigate): time from incident declared (Sev assigned) to customer-impact mitigation in place (or credible workaround). Mitigation may include rollback, routing/fallback changes, traffic shaping, or isolating a bad region/model.
  2) TTF (time-to-fix): time from incident declared to a durable fix deployed OR a signed-off plan with committed ship date (depending on severity). For Sev0/Sev1, we typically expect a durable fix, not just a plan.

- “Tier” definitions:
  - Hosted: multi-tenant public API.
  - Dedicated: reserved capacity; stronger expectations for predictability and comms.
  - Private: VPC/on-prem control plane + data plane; sometimes customer-controlled networking and change windows.

- Severity (draft; matches on-call practice):
  - Sev0: broad outage / severe customer impact / safety risk / inability to serve core requests at scale.
  - Sev1: major degradation (e.g., high 5xx, severe latency) affecting meaningful customer set or a major enterprise customer; urgent.
  - Sev2: partial degradation; workarounds exist; limited scope.
  - Sev3: minor; limited impact; typically handled in normal on-call flow.

Decision principles
===================
1) Make the SLA actionable during incidents (what it forces us to do: staff, escalate, decide).
2) Keep differences by tier minimal, but acknowledge Dedicated/Private have different reality (capacity isolation, maintenance windows, customer networking).
3) Avoid a matrix so complex that incident-bot can’t enforce it.
4) “Pause/override” exists but must be auditable and rare.

Where tier differences are real (observations)
============================================
Hosted
- We control infra + routing + runtime deploys; can mitigate quickly via routing policies, throttles, or rollbacks.
- Customers accept “platform-wide” incidents but expect fast mitigation.

Dedicated
- Stronger expectations: named account pressure, high-touch comms, fewer acceptable repeated incidents.
- Mitigation sometimes means reallocating fleet capacity; can be constrained by GPU availability.
- Some mitigations require coordination with specific customer traffic patterns and agreed “degradation mode.”

Private
- Customer networking, DNS/TLS, firewalls, and change windows can dominate.
- “Mitigation” may require customer action; we can provide fix/instructions but can’t always execute.
- On-prem/air-gapped environments may block fast patching.

Key question: Do we set stricter SLAs for Dedicated/Private because customers pay more, or do we set realistic SLAs acknowledging dependencies and shift strictness into comms/escalation?

Option set
==========
Option A — Single SLA matrix (same targets across tiers) + comms escalation tiers
Pros: simple; consistent; easy to implement + dashboard.
Cons: risks being unrealistic for Private; breaches become noisy; forces frequent overrides.

Option B — Tier-adjusted TTF only (TTM consistent, TTF differs)
Pros: keeps the “stop the bleeding” behavior consistent; reflects reality that durable fixes take longer when customers control deploy windows.
Cons: still may be tight for certain Private classes; requires tier in SLA evaluator.

Option C — Tier-adjusted TTM and TTF (Dedicated stricter on TTM; Private looser on TTF)
Pros: matches customer expectation: Dedicated should be mitigated extremely fast; Private fixes can take longer.
Cons: more complex; risk of perceived unfairness (“why does private get longer?”).

Option D — Incident-type-aware SLA within severity (e.g., Private connectivity vs Control plane vs Runtime regression)
Pros: most accurate.
Cons: too complex for v1; high maintenance; taxonomy drift.

Recommendation (draft): Option B for v1
======================================
- Keep TTM targets consistent by severity across tiers (behavior we want in every incident: mitigate quickly).
- Allow tier-adjusted TTF targets (Private often needs customer maintenance window; Dedicated should still be fast but not necessarily faster than Hosted in all cases).
- In addition, define comms/escalation requirements by tier (Dedicated/Private proactive outreach thresholds), separate from remediation timers.

Proposed draft SLA targets (v1 candidate)
========================================
Notes:
- Times are proposed internal targets for breach alerting + leadership escalation.
- TTM measured to: restored SLO or reduced to acceptable degradation mode (documented).
- TTF measured to: fix deployed OR (Sev2/Sev3 only) fix scheduled with owner + date.

TTM (same across tiers)
-----------------------
Sev0: 30 minutes
Sev1: 2 hours
Sev2: 1 business day
Sev3: 5 business days (or next planned release train)

TTF (tier-adjusted)
-------------------
Hosted:
- Sev0: 24 hours
- Sev1: 3 business days
- Sev2: 10 business days
- Sev3: 30 business days

Dedicated:
- Sev0: 24 hours (same as Hosted; expectation is mitigation is faster, fix can be similar)
- Sev1: 5 business days (slightly longer than Hosted because some fixes involve fleet reshaping or customer-specific config review)
- Sev2: 15 business days
- Sev3: 30 business days

Private:
- Sev0: 48 hours (some fixes require customer coordination/change window; still want high urgency)
- Sev1: 10 business days
- Sev2: 20 business days
- Sev3: 45 business days

Rationale snapshots (to validate)
================================
- Private Sev0 TTF at 48h is the most controversial number. The intent is: if a Private incident is Sev0, we should be able to ship a fix quickly OR provide a validated workaround package quickly. But we may not be able to deploy it into the customer’s environment inside 48h. Proposed compromise: define “TTF = fix available” vs “TTF = deployed” for Private only.

Proposed adjustment for Private only:
- For Private tier: treat TTF as “fix available + customer delivery completed (artifact + instructions + support handoff)” rather than “fully deployed in customer environment.” Deployment tracking becomes a CS/Support deliverable.

This avoids constant SLA breaches from customer-controlled schedules, while still forcing Redwood to produce the fix quickly.

Edge cases + carve-outs (must be explicit)
=========================================
1) Cloud provider / upstream outage
- If root cause is confirmed upstream (AWS/GCP region/network, managed KMS outage, etc.):
  - TTM still applies (we should mitigate via failover/fallback where possible).
  - TTF may be waived or converted to “post-incident hardening actions” with due dates.
- Implementation requirement: incident-bot must allow “Upstream dependency” as a contributing factor and a “SLA exception reason” (audited).

2) Customer-caused or customer-controlled failures (mostly Private, occasionally Dedicated)
Examples:
- Customer rotated certs incorrectly; firewall blocks new endpoints; DNS misconfig; customer refuses recommended upgrade.
- TTM definition may be “workaround identified + communicated + support engaged.”
- TTF becomes a tracked action plan with customer owner and Redwood owner; SLA breach should not trigger paging.
- Implementation requirement: a controlled “Customer action required” exception reason.

3) Planned maintenance / change windows
- If incident is triggered by a planned change performed by Redwood:
  - SLAs still apply (we own it).
- If fix requires customer change window:
  - Private: allow “Fix available” measurement as above.

4) Multi-cause incidents
- Primary incident_type determines SLA class.
- Contributing systems recorded separately; do not create multiple SLA clocks.
- If reclassified, SLA clock should not reset (only severity changes reset behavior).

Comms and escalation requirements (separate from remediation timers)
===================================================================
We should not bake comms into remediation SLAs, but we do need consistent obligations by tier.

Draft comms rules (for CS alignment; see comms templates doc):
- Hosted
  - Sev0/Sev1: status page + initial update within 30 min; updates at least every 60 min until mitigated.
  - Sev2: case-by-case; internal update; status page optional.

- Dedicated
  - Sev0/Sev1: proactive outreach to affected accounts; initial customer-facing update within 30 min; updates every 60 min.
  - Sev2: proactive outreach within 1 business day if single account materially impacted.

- Private
  - Sev0/Sev1: proactive outreach; include “customer action required” assessment early.
  - Emphasize safe language: symptoms, mitigations, next update time.

Open issues / questions to resolve before signoff
=================================================
1) Private TTF definition: “available” vs “deployed”
- Need decision from SRE + Product Private (Vivek) + CS.

2) Dedicated Sev1 TTF: 3 vs 5 business days
- Dedicated product (Lauren) asked for realism: some changes require capacity rebalancing + canary.
- Counterpoint: enterprise expectation is faster. Maybe keep 3 BD but allow exceptions for capacity procurement work.

3) Severity-to-tier mapping clarity
- Can a Private incident be Sev0 if it affects only one customer? Yes, if it blocks core use case and is high urgency.
- Need crisp language in the incident process policy so on-call doesn’t under-severity enterprise incidents.

4) Implementation feasibility in tooling (ENG-4829)
- SLA evaluator needs tier + severity + type.
- Ensure we don’t create a combinatorial matrix. Proposed v1: severity x tier only, with optional overrides.

5) Reporting expectations

Based on last 2 quarters anecdotal review (see top-incidents analysis):

- Dedicated mitigations vary: quick when routing-only; slow when capacity constrained.
- Private “fix deployed” often exceeds 1–2 weeks due to customer windows; “fix available” is typically within a few days if we prioritize.

This PRD defines a product initiative to add first-class orchestration for multi-model pipelines in Redwood Inference. The goal is to let customers declare multi-step pipelines (e.g., embed -> rerank -> generate) composed of different model variants and to automatically optimize routing and instance selection for cost and latency tradeoffs while preserving per-pipeline SLOs.

Background and motivation:
- Customers commonly chain multiple model calls in a single feature (e.g., cheap encoder for retrieval, higher-cost reranker or generator).
- Current Redwood surface treats calls independently; customers must implement orchestration client-side or in application backends, leading to duplicated logic and missed opportunities for cross-request batching, KV cache reuse, and cost-aware routing.
- Providing a managed pipeline orchestration layer improves unit economics (lower cost per end-to-end request), reduces latency via coordinated batching and cache reuse, and centralizes rollout and variant management for pipeline steps.

5) Migration path for existing single-call customers to adopt pipelines with minimal code changes.

High-level design overview:
- Pipeline Descriptor: declarative JSON schema that describes steps (name, model selector, input mapping, resource hints), SLOs (p95 latency target, availability), and cost preference (aggressive-cost | balanced | aggressive-latency).
- Planner: Service that converts a descriptor into a per-request plan: assigns candidate model variants for each step, decides whether to colocate steps on the same instance/pool for cache reuse, and estimates cost/latency distributions.
- Execution Fabric: Extends existing serving runtime to accept multi-step request envelopes, enabling intra-request batching, KV cache rehydration, and shared IO handling.
- Adaptive Runtime Policies: Uses feedback (observed latencies, queueing) to swap in cheaper variants or add burst capacity when SLO violations are observed.

## Context
Audit events are becoming a hard requirement for enterprise (Hosted/Dedicated) and especially Private deployments. As we instrument more sensitive actions, we are seeing that the ingestion path is the limiting factor for reliability: transient sink outages, regional partitions, and backpressure can cause drops, long delays, or (worse) services blocking in unpredictable ways.

This ticket hardens the audit event ingestion pipeline with:
- bounded buffering (in-memory + durable where appropriate)
- explicit retry policy with jitter/backoff and retry classification
- clear backpressure behavior (what happens when buffers fill)
- failure-mode / chaos-style tests so we can prove behavior and avoid regressions

## Current behavior (summary of observed issues)
- Producers often do best-effort HTTP fire-and-forget to the ingestion API. On timeout/5xx we sometimes drop events without a consistent metric.
- Some producers retry aggressively (tight loops) causing thundering herd during outages; others never retry.
- During sink degradation (Kafka/stream backlog, exporter slowdown), ingestion API returns 429/503 but producer behavior is inconsistent.
- Private: installer/upgrade tooling sometimes runs in constrained environments; losing events during upgrades is common because there is no durable buffer.

## Goals / non-goals
### Goals
1) Define and implement the ingestion reliability contract for sensitive-action audit events (practical at-least-once) with bounded buffers.
2) Ensure services behave predictably when the audit sink is down/slow:
   - do not melt down core services
   - do not silently drop sensitive events
   - expose clear metrics so SRE can detect and respond
3) Provide failure-mode tests that simulate:
   - ingestion API down
   - sink backlog / slow downstream
   - network partitions / packet loss
   - producer restarts with buffered events

### Non-goals
- Building a customer-facing audit log UI
- Changing event schema/taxonomy (covered by ENG-4821/4822); we only add transport semantics + tests

## Proposed design (implementation direction)
### Producer-side library (preferred default)
- Add an async audit publisher in the shared audit library:
  - bounded in-memory queue (configurable, default sized by service QPS)
  - background worker(s) to publish batches
  - exponential backoff with jitter on retryable failures
  - classify retryable vs non-retryable (e.g., 400/validation error is non-retryable; 408/429/5xx retryable)
  - emit metrics: enqueue_rate, dequeue_rate, retry_count, drop_count, queue_depth, publish_latency

### Durable buffering (where required)
- For “must-audit” sensitive actions (RBAC changes, credential lifecycle, routing/policy changes, export config, retention/residency changes):
  - persist event to a local WAL (write-ahead log) before acknowledging the admin action where feasible.
  - publish from WAL asynchronously; on restart, replay.
- Hosted/Dedicated services: WAL on local disk (or ephemeral + backed by node disk), size-limited with rotation.
- Private installer/upgrade tooling: spool to a local file buffer (e.g., JSONL with checksums) and flush when ingestion is reachable.

### Backpressure behavior (explicit)
- When in-memory queue is full:
  - default: drop non-sensitive (or non-must-audit) events with a clear metric and log at WARN with rate limiting.
  - must-audit events: attempt WAL write; if WAL cannot be written (disk full / permissions / corruption), fail the admin action with 503 and a deterministic error code (so customers know this is “audit pipeline not healthy”).
- When WAL is full (size cap reached):
  - treat as must-audit failure for must-audit events (return 503 for the admin action)
  - for non-must-audit: drop with metric

### Delivery semantics and duplicates
- We assume at-least-once delivery is acceptable; duplicates must be expected.
- Require event_id presence (ENG-4830) so downstream and SIEM guidance can dedupe.
- Retries must not regenerate event_id.

### Ingestion API behavior (server-side)
- Return explicit status codes:
  - 202 accepted for async ingestion
  - 429 when throttling/backpressure (include Retry-After)
  - 503 when sink unavailable
- Add server-side buffering where appropriate (short-lived queue) to avoid rejecting brief spikes.

## Acceptance criteria
- When the downstream sink is unavailable for 30 minutes, producers with must-audit actions:
  - do not lose events (WAL replay after restart)
  - do not exceed configured disk cap; if cap reached, must-audit admin actions fail with 503 + documented error code
- When downstream is slow (p95 publish latency > 5s), producer queue depth increases but:
  - service CPU/mem remains within +10% of baseline
  - no request handler thread starvation / deadlocks
- Metrics and dashboards show:
  - drop_count = 0 for must-audit event types
  - end-to-end delivery latency p99 < 5 minutes under normal conditions
- Failure-mode tests run in CI (or nightly) and validate:
  - retry behavior conforms to backoff spec
  - WAL replay works after forced restart
  - backpressure returns expected status codes and does not produce unbounded memory growth

## Test plan (failure modes)
- Unit tests (library):
  - retry classification, jitter/backoff, queue overflow behavior
  - WAL append + replay + corruption handling
- Integration tests (local env):
  - run a fake ingestion server that returns sequences: 503 -> 202, 429 with Retry-After, timeouts
  - verify published count == enqueued count for must-audit types
- Chaos / staging:
  - temporarily block egress from a canary service to ingestion endpoint
  - inject sink latency/backlog (rate limit consumer)
  - verify alerts + runbook steps are actionable

## Rollout / migration
- Phase 1: ship producer library changes behind feature flag (audit.publisher.v2)
- Phase 2: enable for Control Plane + Console backend (highest customer impact)
- Phase 3: enable for API Gateway admin endpoints + Private installer
- Phase 4: enforce must-audit semantics for the sensitive action list (ties to coverage gating)

## Open questions
1) Which exact event types are “must-audit” (fail admin action if cannot persist)? Proposed set aligns with PM-938 list; confirm with Naomi/Olga.
2) WAL location/permissions in Kubernetes (Hosted/Dedicated) and disk sizing defaults.
3) Private installer identity: if operator identity is missing, do we still treat events as must-audit? (Proposed: yes; actor.type=system/operator_unknown but must log action.)

## Owners / reviewers
- Owner (SRE): Sean Gallagher
- Security Eng reviewer: Kevin Osei
- Platform reviewer: Ethan Park
- GRC consult: Olga Petrov

## References
- ADR: Audit Event Delivery Guarantees (Confluence)
- Related tickets: ENG-4835 (alerts), ENG-4830 (correlation IDs), ENG-4827 (exporter normalization)
- Customer signals: SUP-18510 (duplicate events on retries), SUP-18421 (Private missing events)

Summary: Introduces a smoothing layer in the Dedicated Autoscaler and a lightweight backpressure signal propagated from the gateway to fleet controllers. This reduces autoscaler thrash on spiky traffic and gives gateways a controlled way to shed load gracefully against per-pool soft capacity and throughput guarantees.

Motivation: Customers on Dedicated have reported oscillations when short bursts cross autoscaler thresholds and then recede; this leads to unnecessary GPU spin-ups and billing variance, as well as transient error spikes. The gateway currently responds with 429s or fallback heuristics; we need a first-class, observable mechanism that cooperates with autoscaling and preserves headroom for SLA-critical requests.

Changes in this PR:
- Autoscaler: add Exponential Moving Average (EMA) smoothing of utilization and request rate with configurable half-life per-pool. New config fields: smoothing_window_ms, smoothing_alpha (derived).
- Soft capacity & grace tokens: each pool now tracks a small ephemeral token bucket (grace_tokens) to allow short bursts without triggering scale-up, decaying over time and replenished by underutilization.
- Gateway backpressure: add a new X-Redwood-Backpressure header and a compact gRPC/backchannel (gateway->controller) event to advertise desired ingress rate reductions per-route when pool smoothed_utilization > threshold.
- Controller/gateway handshake: gateway subscribes to per-pool backpressure_quota updates; controllers include backpressure_rate in scheduling decisions and expose metrics.
- Telemetry: new metrics smoothed_utilization, grace_tokens_available, backpressure_rate, backpressure_rejections. Add Prometheus labels for pool_id, model_id, and region.
- API schema: extend dedicated pool spec with smoothing and backpressure knobs; added validation and defaults.
- Console/docs: admin UI now surfaces smoothing window and current backpressure state with guidance.
- Tests: unit tests for smoothing math, integration e2e that injects burst traffic and asserts reduced scale-up churn and controlled 429 behavior.

Context:
h1. Purpose
This policy defines what constitutes a production change at Redwood Inference and the minimum requirements to plan, approve, execute, and validate the change. The goal is to minimize customer impact while maintaining developer velocity.

h1. Scope
Applies to all production environments for the Hosted API and Console, including:
* Hosted API control plane and data plane services
* Console UI and backend
* Shared platform dependencies (routing, auth, billing metering, observability agents)

Out of scope: customer-managed environments for *Private deployments* (see the Private Deployment Change Policy), and vendor-managed changes outside Redwood’s control (cloud provider maintenance).

h1. Definitions
* *Production:* Any environment serving external customer traffic (including canary and regional production).
* *Production change:* Any change that can affect confidentiality, integrity, availability, latency, cost, or correctness for customer-facing workloads.
* *Change owner:* The person accountable for end-to-end execution and follow-through.
* *Approver:* A designated peer/manager/SRE/security reviewer depending on risk tier.
* *Change record:* A durable record (ticket + links) capturing intent, risk, approvals, execution, and validation results.

h1. Change types
|| Change type || When used || Required approvals || Notes ||
| Standard | Low risk, pre-approved pattern (e.g., doc-only, internal dashboard query fixes, non-prod config) | 1 peer approval | Must match an approved standard template |
| Normal | Most code/config deploys to production | 1 peer approval + (1) service owner approval | Requires pre-deploy verification, canary, and comms assessment |
| Emergency | Active incident mitigation or preventing imminent customer impact | On-call incident commander (IC) + service owner approval (as available) | Retrospective change record required within 24 hours |

h1. What counts as a production change (non-exhaustive)
* Any deployment to production clusters (including canary regions)
* Any change to routing policies, fallback policies, or model selection rules
* Any change to auth, RBAC, API keys, rate limits, quotas, or billing meters
* Any schema migration, backfill, or data retention configuration change
* Any infrastructure change that affects capacity, autoscaling, or failover
* Any change to observability pipelines that could reduce visibility (logs, metrics, tracing)

h1. Minimum required artifacts
For every production change, the change owner must create a change record that includes:
* Summary of change and customer impact assessment
* Rollback plan (explicitly stated, even if “re-deploy previous build”)
* Verification plan (how we will know it worked)
* Links to: PR(s), build(s), dashboards, runbook used, and any migration plan
* Approvals (captured in the change record)

h1. Risk assessment checklist
Answer these before requesting approval:
1. Could this change affect auth, data paths, encryption, logging, or retention?
2. Could this change change request routing, batching, caching, or model version selection?
3. Could this change materially change token accounting/billing?
4. Is there any data migration/backfill involved?
5. Is rollback fast and safe (< 10 minutes) and does it revert the customer experience?

If “yes” to any of 1–4, the change is *Normal* at minimum and may require Security Review (see Secure SDLC requirements).

h1. Approvals
* *Peer approval:* A reviewer from the same engineering org who is familiar with the subsystem.
* *Service owner approval:* The tech lead or on-call owner for the service being changed.
* *SRE gate:* Required when the change affects capacity, SLO-sensitive paths, traffic routing, or any failover config.
* *Security gate:* Required when the change touches auth, secrets, encryption, audit logging, PII, or data retention.

h1. Change windows and freezes
* Default window: weekdays 09:00–16:00 local time for the primary owning team.
* Changes are prohibited during declared change freezes.
* Additional restrictions apply when error budgets are low (see “Change Freeze and Risk Assessment”).

h1. Execution requirements
All production changes must:
1. Use the documented runbook for the target system (Hosted API or Console).
2. Perform a canary rollout for traffic-bearing services unless explicitly exempted in the change record.
3. Confirm observability before and after (golden signals and specific dashboards).
4. Have a clearly defined rollback trigger and a “stop the line” principle.

h1. Communications requirements
Change owner must determine if customer communications are required:
* *Planned maintenance:* Status page notice and direct customer comms if any material impact is expected.
* *No expected customer impact:* Internal announcement in #eng-releases and on-call awareness if during core hours.
See “Planned Maintenance and Change Communications” for templates and required lead time.

h1. Post-change validation and closure
Within 60 minutes after completion, the change owner must:
* Validate key SLO metrics and error rates are within normal bounds
* Confirm canary is healthy before full rollout
* Update the change record with results and attach screenshots/links
* File follow-ups for any issues discovered

h1. References
* Prod Deployment Gates (Hosted API + Console)
* Hosted API Deploy Runbook
* Console Deploy Runbook
* Rollback and Post-change Validation
* Change Freeze and Risk Assessment
* Secure SDLC: Security Review Requirements for Prod Changes
* Planned Maintenance and Change Communications

Provisioning helper script (setup_local_policies.sh) exits with non-zero when system locale uses legacy Unicode collation normalization (NFKD) or certain non-default LC_CTYPE/LC_COLLATE values. This stops the imaging task sequence mid-run and prevents Intune check-in/enrollment on a subset of repaired devices.

Impact:
- ~8 machines in the last two depot batches failed imaging and never completed Intune enrollment; users received a partially provisioned workstation (local accounts only, no corp certs).
- Blocks fast-redeploy for depot repair queue; increases turnaround time.

Environment:
- Affected devices repros on prod imaging pool in us-east.
- OS: Windows 11 22H2 corporate image (with latest platform patches as of 2026-03-01)
- Provisioning artifact: provisioning-scripts v2026.02.28 (bash + PowerShell wrapper)
- Managed via SCCM task sequence that runs setup_local_policies.sh late in the image.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Boot a test device (Dell Latitude 7440) into SCCM task sequence in the us-east imaging pool.
2) Set system locale environment to one of the affected collations (example repro used: LC_COLLATE="fi_FI@collation=NFKD" exported in cmd before running the script).
3) Allow task sequence to reach the provisioning-scripts step.
4) Observe that setup_local_policies.sh aborts with an encoding/collation exception and the task sequence halts.

- C:\Windows\Temp\provisioning\setup_local_policies.log:
  [2026-03-09 14:07:02] INFO: starting local policy setup
  [2026-03-09 14:07:03] ERROR: fatal: string normalization failed when writing registry key: "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\\SOFTWARE\\Redwood\\Provision"
  [2026-03-09 14:07:03] ERROR: exit code 1
- SCCM smsts.log shows task sequence step 'Run Command Line' returning 1 and aborting sequence.

Hypothesis and root cause (initial):
- The helper script uses Python 3.9 subprocess invocation and writes UTF-8 strings to the Windows registry using a small C# helper compiled during the build. Under certain LC_COLLATE/LC_CTYPE values the runtime performs Unicode normalization (NFKD) on strings and strips combining characters; combined with our registry write helper's unsupported normalization mode this results in an exception thrown by the helper (System.ArgumentException: Invalid character in registry value).
- This only triggers when a depot-repair process re-applies device-specific locale settings prior to provisioning (we see this on repaired devices that retain OEM locale overrides).

Temporary workaround applied:
- Imaging team added a wrapper to forcibly set LANG and LC_COLLATE to en_US.UTF-8 before running the provisioning step in the task sequence. This is in place for the current depot batch and prevents the failure.

- Imaging ops to roll the temporary LANG/LC_COLLATE wrapper into the standard task sequence until the patch is deployed.
- Confirm fleet-wide by running a small canary set of 20 repaired devices with the patch and removing wrapper after two successful batches.

Context:
Purpose:
This doc describes a targeted probe-suite for embedding sets intended to catch regressions that specific upstream changes (quantization, tokenization tweaks, batch-kernel swaps) can introduce in noisy or length-varied input distributions. Focus is multilingual (5 langs), and pragmatic search / clustering scenarios. The suite is designed for quick PR smoke runs (< 30s if cached) and a heavier nightly battery for regression detection.

Design goals:
- Cover realistic noise types engineers see in production search queries and user content: typos, punctuation stripping, emoji/code switching, url/email patterns, concatenated sentences, truncation.
- Measure sensitivity to input length extremes (very short 1–3 tokens; long 128–2048 tokens) and mid-range distributions observed in product telemetry.
- Multilingual parity checks: English, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Japanese. Include script- and morphology-sensitive probes (e.g., tokenization boundary noise for Japanese/Hindi).
- Fast-to-run smoke tests + detailed regression metrics for nightly.
- Provide clear pass/fail thresholds and expected failure modes for triage.

Probe matrix (high level):
- Noise types: typo-insert (random character delete/insert), keyboard-substitution (q->w style), punctuation-strip, whitespace-collapse, emoji-insert, code-switch (insert 10–30% words from other language), url/email-masking (replace with token), repetition-attack (duplicate sentence), concatenation (2 distinct queries glued without separator).
- Length buckets: tiny (1–3 tokens), short (4–16), medium (17–128), long-seq (129–512), ultra-long (513–2048).
- Tasks: semantic-search (query→doc ranking), clustering (k-means purity), cross-lingual-retrieval (EN query → non-EN doc), neighbor-isotropy checks (nn distance distributions).

Datasets included in the suite:
- curated-qrels-5lang: 2k queries per language, relevance judgments derived from FAQ and support logs (de-identified).
- synthetic-noise-sweep: 400 canonical queries per lang x 8 noise types x lengths (constructed deterministically to be reproducible).
- multilingual-paraphrase-pairs: 3k pairs covering translation parity and paraphrase density (source: internal translation memory + CC-aligned subset).
- cluster-sanctum: 600 short documents per language arranged into 20 known clusters (topic-level), used for silhouette/purity checks.

Metrics collected:
- Retrieval: NDCG@10, MRR, Recall@100, mean reciprocal rank delta vs baseline.
- Clustering: Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), cluster purity, Silhouette score per-language and cross-language.
- Embedding diagnostics: pairwise cosine distribution (mean/std), nearest-neighbor language contamination rate (fraction of top-k neighbors from different language when they should be same), isotropy score (variance of singular values / top-eig ratio).
- Robustness deltas: relative change in metric vs pinned baseline model/version. We report absolute metric and percent change and flag regression when metric drops beyond threshold.

Pass/Fail thresholds (example):
- Smoke (quick PR): median cosine NN distance within +/- 6% of baseline; NDCG@10 drop < 3% absolute on curated-qrels-5lang; cluster purity drop < 5 percentage points.
- Nightly (heavy): NDCG@10 drop < 1.5% absolute; ARI drop < 0.03 absolute; isotropy change < 8% (unless model intentionally changed).
Notes: thresholds chosen to balance sensitivity to real regressions and avoid noisy false alarms; teams may tighten for canary/dedicated rollouts.

Implementation notes and reproducibility:
- All noise injectors are deterministic with fixed RNG seed and documented mutators in /eval/embedding-noise-mutators. Avoid non-deterministic augmentations in smoke runs.
- Use same tokenization pipeline as serving runtime for the eval (this catches tokenization drift). Test harness runs both raw-text pipeline and tokenized-stage embeddings to localize regressions (tokenizer vs encoder).

Motivation: Production teams increasingly ask for safe, explainable defaults for batching, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles tuned to their unit-econ targets. Manual tuning is slow and error-prone; naive defaults either leave money on the table or cause latency regressions. This PR introduces the 'Batch-Cache Policy Synthesizer' — a small service and integration that synthesizes conservative, runbook-driven defaults and optional suggestions for aggressive cost-saving profiles, backed by workload traces and unit-econ objectives.

What this changes:
- New service: internal/optimizer/policy_synthesizer that consumes sampled request traces, cost/latency SLO goals, and historical model perf profiles to output a ranked set of policy candidates (batching window, max batch size, prefix cache TTL, kv-cache-hotlist-size, quantization profile id).
- CLI: tools/cost-synthesizer/bin/rcs (runbook-config-synth) for operators to generate profiles locally from a trace file and preview expected token-cost and p50/p95 latency deltas.
- API: /v1/internal/policy_synthesizer/generate (protected) to request on-demand policy suggestions for a customer or model route.
- Redwood Console integration: Add a lightweight Recommendations drawer that surfaces the top-3 candidates along with estimated saving, expected latency impact, and confidence score.
- Safeguards: Every suggestion includes a conservative fallback policy and an automatic canary rollout plan (10% traffic -> 50% -> 100%) with automatic rollback on latency or quality regressions.
- Tests: unit tests for candidate scoring, integration tests for the CLI path, and e2e smoke that runs a small synthetic trace through the service and validates metrics emitted to metrics.redwood (new metric: optimizer.synthesized_policy.{applied,rolled_back}).

Design notes (short):
- Scoring model: multi-objective heuristic that combines estimated per-token cost delta, expected p95 latency delta (from per-op instrumentation), and an uncertainty penalty derived from sample size. Operators can pick a unit-econ target multiplier (e.g., 0.8x cost target) and the synthesizer returns candidates that meet the target while keeping p95 within a user-configured latency window.
- Quant profiles: the synthesizer references the model-registry quant profiles and recommends the lightest quant that has a validated quality delta < configured threshold (default 1% BLEU/ROUGE-style surrogate). If no profile passes, quant recommendations are omitted.
- Safety floor: all policies include a required minimal TTL and max_batch safeguards to avoid excessive batching for latency-sensitive routes.
