Motivation: under high-concurrency, the paged KV cache freelist would fragment after repeated allocations/frees of mixed-size blocks, increasing allocation latency and causing more frequent slow-path compaction. This PR adds an opportunistic freelist defragmenter that compacts adjacent free pages on free-paths and a lightweight hot-prefix selective pinning policy so frequently-accessed key prefixes avoid costly eviction. Goals: reduce p99 allocation latency, lower background compaction pressure, and improve tail latency for workloads with hot prefixes (chat sessions, long contexts).

Summary of changes:
- Opportunistic freelist defragmenter run inline on frees when a small threshold of contiguous free segments is observed (configurable).
- Compact-on-free path that coalesces adjacent free pages into larger blocks to improve reuse for larger token sequences.
- Adaptive reuse scoring: tracks short-term reuse frequency per page bucket and prefers reuse of high-score pages.
- Hot-prefix selective pinning: a small resident pin set for top-N hot key prefixes with LRU eviction; pins are persisted across ephemeral reconnects to stabilize performance.
- Scheduler hint: allocator exposes a gentle backpressure hint to the request scheduler when fragmentation crosses configured thresholds so the scheduler can delay batch growth and avoid thrashing.
- Tests and microbenchmarks: new unit tests for defragmenter invariants and a throughput/latency benchmark demonstrating behavior across workload mixes.

Compatibility: fully opt-in via runtime config flags (defaults are conservative).

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc linked in PR
- [x] Unit tests
- [x] Microbenchmark
- [x] CI green after flake fix
- [x] Perf measurements attached

Motivation: We have multiple downstream needs that couldn't be satisfied by the legacy model capability schema: (1) lightweight, per-request runtime hints that the routing layer and serving runtime can use without deserializing the full model profile; (2) a transparent metering knob for tool/function calling (customers asked for per-invocation crediting separate from token billing); and (3) richer guidance for streaming fallbacks so clients can degrade more gracefully when a model variant switches to a lower-throughput tier. This PR introduces three related surfaces: capability_headers, function_call_credit, and streaming_degradation_policy, alongside an OpenAI-compatible shim that surfaces structured-output hints in /v1/models list responses.

Summary of changes (high level):
- API: Add optional capability_headers map to /v1/models and /v1/models/:id responses. These are short key/value runtime hints intended for fast routing decisions (examples: "supports_prefix_cache": "true", "max_prefetch_tokens": "256").
- Catalog schema: Deprecate legacy capability_schema.v1 (kept as legacy_capabilities for migration) and introduce capability_schema.v2 that references compact headers + full capability document. Migration docs added.
- Billing: Introduce function_call_credit as a first-class optional numeric field on model profiles and endpoints. This allows the billing system to attribute cost for tool/function call ops independently; SDKs and console will display credits usage.
- Streaming: Add streaming_degradation_policy on model profiles to expose a list of ordered fallbacks and suggested partial-output tokens thresholds (helps clients decide when to switch to a summarized streaming path). Also include preferred_prefetch_hint to suggest prefix caching window.
- OpenAI compat: Update the /v1/models listing returned by the OpenAI-compat shim to include capability_headers and structured_output_hints under the "capabilities" umbrella so downstream OpenAI-compatible clients can discover behavior without touching Redwood-specific endpoints.
- Docs & SDK: Docs page describing migration, examples for reading capability_headers and consuming streaming_degradation_policy; Python and TypeScript SDK surfaces to parse new fields.

Commits (summary):
- commit 1: api: extend model list + get handlers to populate capability_headers and streaming_degradation_policy (handlers and serializers)
- commit 2: catalog: add models_v2 schema, migration script to copy legacy_capabilities into full_profile and generate default headers
- commit 3: billing: record function_call_credit into usage events and expose in billing UI (console changes)
- commit 4: sdk/docs: parse helpers and docs for migration and examples

Files changed (representative):
- src/api/handlers/models_list.go (updated serializer and OpenAI-compat shim)
- src/catalog/schemas/models_v2.json (new compact schema)
- tools/migrations/migrate_capabilities_v1_to_v2.go (migration script)
- services/billing/credits.go (add function_call_credit aggregation)
- console/src/components/model/ModelDetails.tsx (show capability headers and credits)
- sdk/python/redwood/models.py (new fields + helper parser)
- docs/migrations/capability_headers_migration.md (migration and rollback guide)

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests: added for serializer and parser behavior (capability_headers omitted vs present), billing aggregation tests for function_call_credit.
- Integration: end-to-end test in perf-canary that validates streaming_degradation_policy is honored by the router under simulated capacity pressure; canary shows no increase in 95p latency on main model variants.
- Backwards compatibility: /v1/models still returns legacy_capabilities field for consumers that haven't migrated; the OpenAI-compat shim prefers capability_headers but will fall back to legacy_capabilities when capability_headers is absent.

Migration strategy & rollout:
- Stage 1 (canary): populate capability_headers from existing full capabilities via migration script; run canary for 2 days to ensure no regression in routing or billing.
- Stage 2 (gradual): expose new headers to 20% of API responses; monitor routing decisions and SDK parsing errors.
- Stage 3 (opt-in enforcement): allow customers to opt-in to strict schema validation via a console toggle (default off).
- Final: Deprecate legacy schema via announcement; grace period until 2026-06-01, after which legacy_capabilities may be removed for new write operations.

Review conversation (condensed):
- Owen Park: "Large change — please ensure migration script is idempotent and add a safety flag so we can revert on dataset problems." — Author: "Migration is idempotent; added --dry-run and --cutover flags in migrate_capabilities_v1_to_v2.go; documented in migration md."
- Lina Gomez: "Need to ensure function_call_credit can't be negative and that default is 0 where absent; also clarify how it interacts with token billing." — Author: "Validation added; billing pipeline will emit both tokens and function_call_credit events. Release notes updated to clarify pricing semantics."
- Harriet Zhao: "Does the streaming_degradation_policy open us up to oscillation if multiple routers act on hints?" — Author: "Router change includes a small randomized jitter and a dead-time to prevent oscillation; added comment in routing code and unit test."
- QA (Slack): reported one flaky test in console snapshot related to ModelDetails layout — fixed by stabilizing test data ordering in the SDK.

CI summary: initial run had lint warnings (long line in models_list.go) and one flaky integration test; both addressed in follow-up commits. Final status: all checks passed (unit, lint, integration, e2e canary). Performance canary showed stable tail latency; billing integration tests validated function_call_credit emitted for simulated tool calls.

Rollout notes for operators:
- The migration tool writes a migration_log to S3; if any migration errors occur, the --rollback flag will reverse schema updates made to the catalog DB.
- Feature gate: runtime.capability_headers (default: enabled for all API nodes in next release). If issues appear, ops can disable gate per region to return legacy behavior immediately.

Decision rationale and follow-ups:
- We intentionally kept capability_headers compact and stringly-typed to avoid heavyweight schema churn; full capabilities remain available for deep inspection and compatibility with existing tooling.
- Follow-ups: ENG-2639 to add UI visualization for streaming_degradation_policy, ENG-2670 to instrument per-function-call credit telemetry in the billing dashboard, and ENG-2692 to add a half-life cache invalidation for capability_headers to support fast rollbacks.

Merge outcome: Squash merge by Lina Gomez on 2026-02-19 after approvals from all reviewers and green CI. Release note entry drafted and scheduled for the 2026-02 minor release.

Context:
description:
Motivation: Developers repeatedly hit vague runtime errors when streams failed (auth handshake, transient network) and had to implement ad-hoc parsing logic to decide whether to retry, resume, or surface an error. This PR introduces language-native typed error classes across the three SDKs (Python/TypeScript/Go) and a unified ergonomic iterable reconnect API for stream consumers.

What this change does: 
- Introduces TypedError/StreamError subclasses with machine-friendly error_code, retriable, and suggestion fields across SDKs.
- Adds a new StreamIterable API (python: StreamIterable, ts: createStreamIterable, go: StreamIterator) that yields typed result objects and automatically attempts a single reconnect on retriable failures by default with backoff tuning. Reconnect behavior is configurable by the caller.
- Deprecates low-level sync callback hooks (on_chunk/on_error) in favor of async iterables/promises/iterators to improve ergonomics and parity.
- Adds structured telemetry hooks (opt-in) so apps can key metrics by error_code without brittle string matching.
- Small refactors: move common auth-retry utility into internal/sdk-common, update changelogs and bump SDK package versions.

Backward compatibility and migration: 
- Old callback APIs are still present but marked deprecated; they will emit one deprecation log per process and are scheduled for removal in the next major. Migration notes are added to each SDK CHANGELOG.
- Typed error shapes are additive; existing code catching broad exceptions will continue to work but can opt-in to typed handling for clearer logic.

Testing and rollout: 
- Unit tests added for typed error construction, serialization, and iterable reconnect edge cases. Integration tests simulate transient auth failures with a test double of the runtime.
- Canary rollout to Dedicated region us-west-2 for 72 hours before full merge.

Checklist: 
- [x] Python implementation and tests
- [x] TypeScript implementation and tests
- [x] Go implementation and tests
- [x] Changelogs and version bumps
- [x] Docs snippet in quickstarts repo pointing to new API example

References: Linear ENG-1987, SUP-402 (customer-facing incident), internal design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-1987/stream-reconnect-typed-errors (internal link).

Context:
Overview

This playbook bundles three tightly related areas that frequently cause onboarding friction for new integrations: SDK localization (i18n) readiness, docs-site operational procedures (staging/canary/translation pipelines), and a compact set of canonical fixes for the top support issues we see from developer onramps. The goal is a one-page operational reference that engineering, Docs, and Support can use during new SDK ship weeks and customer trials.

Goals
- Reduce mean-time-to-first-success (MTTFS) for new SDK adopters by 30% through localized examples and a repeatable docs deploy pipeline.
- Provide concise canonical fixes for the top 8 devx support issues so Support can resolve 60% of triageable tickets without engineering intervention.
- Maintain a low-friction docs release process (canary -> staged -> prod) with clear rollback semantics and telemetry hooks.

Audience
- Developer Experience engineers and tech writers shipping SDK examples and docs.
- Support engineers handling integration issues and reproductions.
- Product engineers owning SDKs or client libraries.

Scope and non-goals
- Included: JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, and Go SDK snippets; docs-site content lifecycle; translation handoff and CI checks; canonical fixes for common API/SDK errors.
- Excluded: full localization of legal or marketing copy; mobile SDKs beyond sample snippets.

Prerequisites
1) Repo layout: all SDK examples live under repo: redwood/devx-examples (branch: main).
2) Docs-site: hosted via docs.redwood-inference.internal, uses static site generator with i18n plugin (locales in /i18n/*.json).
3) CI: GitHub Actions with workflows: docs-canary.yml, docs-staged.yml, docs-prod.yml.
4) Telemetry: snippet telemetry.events.example_load, telemetry.tags.locale, and telemetry.context.sdk_version must be emitted by sample harness.

Quickstart: Localized SDK Example Bundle (developer flow)
1. Clone examples: git clone git@github.com:redwood/devx-examples.git && cd devx-examples
2. Install toolchain (node/pip/go): ./scripts/bootstrap-dev.sh
3. Generate locale-specific examples: ./scripts/generate-localized-examples --locales=en,es,fr --sdk=python
4. Run local docs server including translations: npm run docs:local -- --locale=fr
5. Verify telemetry events appear in staging stream (kinesis-devx-staging): 
   - Expected event: {"event":"example_load","locale":"fr","sdk":"python","version":"0.12.0"}
6. Submit PR to docs-examples with i18n diffs and request docs-site canary deploy via label: docs-canary-request

SDK Localization Checklist (per release)
- [ ] Confirm sample text keys are externalized (no hard-coded English strings in code examples).
- [ ] Provide translation-ready README and example captions in /i18n/{locale}.json.
- [ ] Localized code comments: keep English primary, add short localized caption lines under // LOCAL: ... to avoid syntax churn.
- [ ] Add locale-specific smoke tests: tests/smoke/{locale}/example_test.py (asserts example runs and emits telemetry).
- [ ] Bump telemetry schema version if adding fields: TELEMETRY_SCHEMA: v2 -> notify analytics@redwood.com.

Table: Supported Example Locales and Priority
Locale | Priority | Owner | Notes
------ | -------- | ----- | -----
en (English) | high | devx-eng | baseline; all CI gates run against en
es (Spanish) | medium | intl-ops | customer-facing regions: LATAM, EU-ES
fr (French) | medium | intl-ops | EU-FR customers
de (German) | low | intl-ops | add on request
ja (Japanese) | low | intl-ops | APAC pilot only

Docs-site Operating Procedure (canary -> staged -> prod)
1) Authoring and PRs
   - Create content branch in docs-content repo and include locale JSONs under /i18n.
   - Attach smoke test run output to PR (artifact: smoke-{sha}.zip).
   - Tag PR with labels: [docs-canary-request] or [docs-staged-request] as appropriate.
2) Canary deploy (automatic with label docs-canary-request)
   - Action: GitHub Action docs-canary.yml runs build and deploys to docs-canary.redwood-inference.internal.
   - Checks (must pass): build (exit 0), i18n-linter (no missing keys), smoke-tests (artifacts present), telemetry sanity (at least one example_load event during smoke test).
   - Rollback: manual; revert PR or trigger docs-canary-rollback workflow.
3) Staged deploy (after 48h of Canary uptime and signoff)
   - Add label docs-staged-request. Ops lead runs gated promote: ./tools/promote_docs.sh --from=canary --to=staged --approve="<approver>"
   - Staged URL: docs-staged.redwood-inference.internal. Run translation QA with translator team.
4) Prod promote
   - Window: M-F 9:00-17:00 PT. Approvals: 2 reviewers (author + docs eng). Run promote script with --to=prod and monitor SLOs for 30min.

Operational SLOs for Docs-site during promote windows
- Build success rate >= 99% (30-day rolling).
- Canary smoke-tests pass within 15 minutes after deploy.
- No production downtime > 1 minute caused by new docs push.

Canonical Support Issues and Fixes (top issues during onramp)
Issue A: SDK example fails to authenticate (401)
- Detection: error pattern in logs: "error=unauthorized, code=401, hint=apiKey"; Support: run reproduction script with -v flag.
- Root cause: sample uses environment variable REDWOOD_API_KEY unset or using expired demo key.
- Canonical fix steps:
  1. Confirm env var exists: echo $REDWOOD_API_KEY
  2. If missing, instruct customer to create API key via console (link: internal:product-docs/create-api-key).
  3. For expired keys, rotate and confirm permission scopes: scopes must include: [inference:invoke, metrics:read].
  4. Add small code snippet to sample that fails fast with helpful error message (example below).
- Owner: Support -> escalate to SDK owner if repro fails.

Code snippet: fail-fast auth check (Python)
```python
import os
api_key = os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')
if not api_key:
    raise RuntimeError('Missing REDWOOD_API_KEY environment variable. Create one at https://console.redwood-inference.internal/settings/api-keys')
# proceed with client
```

Issue B: Streaming responses stall mid-stream
- Detection: client receives first tokens then stalls; metrics show open connection but no bytes.
- Root cause: client-level keepalive mismatch or proxy buffering (common with corporate proxies).
- Canonical fix steps:
  1. Ask customer to test with curl -N to confirm raw stream: 
     curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" -N \"https://api.redwood-inference.internal/v1/stream?...\"
  2. If curl works, recommend SDK change: prefer chunked transfer decoding and set socket keepalive: true.
  3. Provide fallback example using poll-based generation with polling timeout 5s.
- Owner: SDK eng + DevX docs for the streaming troubleshooting page.

Issue C: Localized examples missing strings or have placeholders ("__MISSING__")
- Detection: i18n-linter failure in CI; smoke test asserts replaceable keys remain.
- Root cause: upstream translations not merged to branch or translation key mismatch after refactor.
- Canonical fix steps:
  1. Run i18n-linter locally: npm run i18n-lint -- --locale=es
  2. Check missing keys report: ./tools/i18n-report --sha <pr-sha>
  3. If keys changed upstream, rebase PR and run ./scripts/merge-i18n.sh
  4. If translation missing, create placeholder and flag translator for fast-turn merge.
- Owner: Docs + Intl-ops.

Issue D: SDK telemetry not appearing in staging (no example_load events)
- Detection: telemetry dashboard shows zero events for smoke-run timeframe.
- Root cause: SDK example uses wrong telemetry endpoint, or telemetry schema mismatch.
- Canonical fix steps:
  1. Confirm telemetry endpoint env var: TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT points to staging ingestion.
  2. Run smoke tests locally with verbose flag and inspect emitted payloads: ./scripts/run-smoke --verbose | jq .
  3. If schema mismatch, check TELEMETRY_SCHEMA in repo and bump analytics contract.
- Owner: DevX instrumentation owner.

Emergency rollback recipe (docs-site)
- Trigger: Canary or staged build causes widespread example breakage or production regressions.
- Steps:
  1. Revert offending PR or tag immediately. Use GitHub UI or: git revert --no-edit <merge-commit> && push.
  2. Run docs-canary-rollback action: ./tools/docs_rollback --env=canary --commit=<last-good-commit>
  3. Notify #devx and #sre-channels with incident summary template (include commit, author, time).
  4. Run postmortem within 72 hours if > 15 developer-impacting incidents occurred.

Telemetry and Monitoring (what to watch)
- Telemetry events: example_load, example_error, docs_build_status
- Dashboards: DevX -> Examples Overview, Docs -> Build Health, Support -> Top SDK Errors
- Alerts: Build failure rate > 5% in 1h (PagerDuty to Docs oncall), Missing telemetry events for a deployed smoke run (Slack alert to #devx-monitor).

Owner matrix and contact points
- DevX Docs (authoring + i18n): Marisol Vega (owner)
- Intl-ops (translation & QA): Sana Ribeiro
- SDK engineering (runtime fixes): Evan Park
- Support triage lead: Luis Moreno

Appendix: Example file layout (minimal)
- /devx-examples/
  - /python/
    - example_quickstart.py
    - README.md
    - /i18n/en.json
    - /i18n/es.json
  - /js/
    - example_quickstart.js
    - /i18n/en.json

Contact and escalation
- For blocked promotes contact: #devx-ops on Slack and add pager: docs-oncall@redwood-inference.internal
- For telemetry contract questions: analytics@redwood-inference.internal

Revision history
- 2025-09-12: Initial draft by Marisol Vega
- 2025-11-03: Added streaming troubleshooting and telemetry checks (review: Evan Park)
- 2026-02-20: Finalized canary/staged procedure and rollback script path updates

Related artifacts and snippets
- Scripts referenced live in repo: https://github.com/redwood/devx-examples/tree/main/scripts
- Translation handoff template: /templates/translation-handoff.md

End of playbook

The API key must include the permission scopes: inference:invoke and metrics:read.

Motivation: INT8 inference for large decoder models showed suboptimal memory layout overhead and extra dequant steps when combined with smoothquant-style per-channel scaling. This PR introduces a weight prepack path and a small kernel-lane allocator that lets the runtime fuse smoothquant dequantization into the kernel dispatch without materializing intermediate dequant tensors. Goals: 1) lower wall-clock latency for first-token and steady-state by removing memory-bound dequant copies, 2) reduce peak GPU memory for multi-tenant workloads by prepacking int8 weights in a compact layout and sharing lane metadata across batches, 3) keep compatibility with existing KV cache and continuous-batching pipelines. What changed (high-level): - New weight prepack module (src/runtime/kernel/int8_weight_prepack.cc/h) that produces a packed INT8 layout with per-channel scale/zero-point metadata optimized for our vectorized GEMM kernels. - Kernel adapter hooks (src/runtime/kernel/kernel_adapter.cc) to accept packed weights and apply smoothquant per-channel scaling on-the-fly inside the GEMM launcher when the model has smoothquant metadata. - Kernel lane allocator (src/runtime/scheduler/lane_allocator.cc/h) that assigns model weight lanes to worker threads/GPU streams so packed weights can be reused across microbatches without copying. - KV cache coordinator updates (src/runtime/scheduler/kv_cache_coordinator.cc) to pin KV cache blocks to the same lane affinity when the request uses pinned weights, avoiding cross-lane synchronization. - A shortfall fallback: when model uses dynamic shape patterns incompatible with lane reuse, runtime falls back to previous dequant-copy path automatically. Performance: microbenchmarks on a 32B decoder model (batch sizes 1..8, seq len 1..1024) show median token latency improvement of 9-16% at steady state and 18-28% for first-token latency on Ampere A100, with peak memory reduction of ~12% at high concurrency. Compatibility/risks: The change touches low-level kernel dispatch. We limited the surface by gating packed-weight paths behind a model feature flag and added runtime checks for per-channel metadata version. Rolling plan: staged canary rollout on Dedicated pools with a 2-hour canary window, monitor latency, token error-rate regressions, and memory counters. Intermittent cases where per-key priority overrides combined with per-org and per-route policies result in transient under-enforcement (requests allowed when they should be throttled). Observed as short windows of elevated usage for a small set of tenants after shard reassignment and policy hot-reload. This ticket captures investigation, repro, short-term mitigation, and a long-term fix plan.

impact:
Transient over-allow for small number of tenants leading to underbilling and potential customer perception issues; visible as short-lived bursts up to ~2x expected throughput for affected keys. Affects hosted and dedicated clusters during rolling updates or instance restarts.

reproduction_steps:
1) Create two tenants T1 and T2 sharing a shard (sticky-shard assignment enabled).
2) Configure per-org policy: default priority = low, per-route quota = 1000/min.
3) Configure per-key override for a service key K1 belonging to T1: priority = high, burst credits = +200.
4) Start a steady stream of requests from T1 at near-quota rate; verify enforcement hitting quota windows.
5) Trigger a shard reassignment for one edge node (simulate instance bounce or maintenance) while simultaneously applying a policy hot-reload that changes route fallback behavior.
6) Observe a ~10-30s window where requests for K1 are allowed beyond quota; metrics show credits attributed to the wrong in-memory bucket and enforcement checks returning allow from fast-path cache.
7) Collect tracer spans and edge logs for the window; reproduce locally using the shard-reassignment harness and time-accelerated policy reloads.

logs_snapshot:
edge: allow decision fastpath: key=K1 shard=sh-23 cache_hit=true priority=high quota_window_id=2026-03-12T10:04:00Z
shard-reassign: lease=renewal failover->sh-27 old_owner=sh-23 new_owner=sh-27
policy-hot-reload: version=v2026-03-12-1 route-fallback=enabled
meter-commit: credits_applied target_bucket=org:T2:key:Kx unexpected=true amount=200

hypothesis:
A race between sticky-shard mapping update and policy hot-reload causes fast-path cache entries (priority and credit pointers) to be re-keyed incorrectly. Per-key overrides store a pointer to a tenant-scoped credit bucket; during reassignment we are dereferencing a stale pointer and applying credits to the wrong tenant's bucket. Enforcement uses the fast-path decision if cache present, so the wrong credits cause an allow where a deny should occur.

experiment_results:
Replayed the sequence in staging using the shard-reassign harness. With no policy reload the issue did not occur. When timed policy reload coincided with reassignment, we reproduced the over-allow consistently. Enabling stronger pointer validation (temporary patch) eliminated the over-allows in the harness.

root_cause:
Sticky-shard pointer (in-memory bucket reference) is validated only by shard id but not by tenant id during fast-path credit application. Policy hot-reload mutates the route/priority indices while a shard transfer copies pointers; combined these can produce a transient pointer that points at an unrelated tenant's bucket. Enforcement fast-path accepts the cache without full tenant-level validation.

mitigations:
Short-term patch deployed to staging: on fast-path cache hit, perform tenant-id validation on the cached credit pointer before applying credits. Also increased grace period on shard handoff to reduce overlap. Rolled patch to canary edge fleet.

rollout_plan:
1) Canary for 2 hours on low-traffic region with added telemetry (done). 2) Gradual ramp to 30% of traffic with continued trace sampling for next 24 hours. 3) Full rollout after 48 hours if no regressions. 4) Follow with a database reconciliation backfill job to detect credits misapplied in last 7 days and create accounting fixes if needed.

long_term_fix:
Refactor in-memory credit pointer representation to be immutable and namespaced by tenant+shard+route. Replace pointer dereference fast-path with a lightweight validation token check (versioned binder). Add unit and property tests for concurrent shard handoff + policy reload scenarios.

regression_test_plan:
Add deterministic concurrency tests to runtime-policy-simulator: combinations of shard reassignment, policy hot-reload, per-key overrides, and burst credit application. Add e2e test in CI harness that exercises rolling updates with randomized interleavings. Add a smoke check after canary verifying no over-allow traces in last 10 minutes.

notes:
PM (Aisha Kapoor): prioritize mitigation; billing reconciliation may be needed if misapplied credits persist beyond 24h.
Security (Rajiv Patel): no PII involved in pointers but ensure tracing does not expose tenant ids in public dashboards.
Observation: reproduces more reliably when policy reload contains route fallback toggles rather than pure priority edits.

Question:
What caused the brief period where a few tenants were not being throttled correctly after a shard reassignment happened at the same time as a runtime policy reload?

A race condition between the sticky-shard mapping update during shard reassignment and a runtime policy hot-reload caused fast-path cache entries for per-key overrides to reference a stale in-memory credit pointer. Because the pointer was only validated by shard ID (not tenant ID), burst credits could be applied to the wrong tenant's bucket, and the fast-path cache would incorrectly return "allow," leading to a brief under-enforcement window.

Context: Teams repeatedly ask for sensible defaults for batching, cache TTLs and quantization when onboarding models to Redwood. Currently defaults live in multiple places and require manual tuning with evals and internal heuristics. Goal: ship a small, auditable suggestion system that observes recent workload signals and proposes conservative default profiles for batching.window_ms, batch_size caps, prefix/KV cache TTLs, and quantization presets. The suggester is opt-in by default and produces human-readable suggestions surfaced in the Console and via a new API endpoint.

What this PR does: 1) Adds a lightweight offline heuristic engine (defaults-suggester) that consumes short-term aggregated telemetry (per-route QPS, median latency, 50/95/99 latency quantiles, token length distribution) and maps to a ranked set of suggested profiles. 2) Introduces a new API: POST /optimize/v1/suggestions which returns JSON suggestions with confidence scores and an explanation string. 3) Wire up Console: a Suggestions panel on per-route settings with an Apply & Preview flow that shows estimated unit-cost delta and latency impact. 4) Add a gated runtime flag so the runtime can accept a profile payload for immediate application (useful for Dedicated/Private workflows). 5) Provide a small set of canonical profiles (conservative, balanced, aggressive) for batching and quantization, plus TTL presets for prefix/KV caches. 6) Add end-to-end test coverage and benchmark harness runs comparing before/after for representative traffic shapes.

For Private installs the suggester can be run locally against their telemetry export. - Suggestions include an estimated unit-cost delta computed from our unit-econ model; we expose the formula in the Console and include the prompt/eval link so teams can validate quality impact.

Context:
Summary

This ADR defines a company-wide standard for declarative contract tests and a complementary "schema fencing" discipline to prevent schema drift between services and the Redwood platform (APIs, telemetry, and model-serving payloads). The goal is to make API and model I/O contracts machine-testable, versioned, and CI-gated, minimizing production surprises and simplifying rollback and compatibility reasoning.

Context and motivation

Recent incidents and near-misses were traced to silent schema changes that allowed malformed or unexpectedly shaped requests/telemetry to flow into the runtime. Ad-hoc unit tests are insufficient for cross-service contract guarantees because:

- Contracts span teams (edge proxies, gateways, runtime, and client SDKs).
- Behavioral compatibility is not captured by type checks alone (e.g., field deprecation with semantic changes).
- Runtime routing fallback and model-variant compatibility require an explicit, testable matrix.

This ADR proposes:

1. A declarative, YAML-first contract-test spec that lives next to service code and in a central conformance repo for cross-service scopes.
2. A "schema fencing" lifecycle that fences allowed shape changes via explicit change proposals, automated conformance checks, and CI gates.
3. A conformance status ledger and telemetry for contract drift and failed-matrix cell SLI.

Scope

Applies to:

- Public and internal HTTP/GRPC REST endpoints (edge, control-plane, telemetry ingestion).
- Model-serving input/output schemas (prompts, structured responses, embeddings metadata).
- Streaming/session protocols where message schemas are negotiated.

Out of scope:

- Internal-only helper functions that are never consumed by other services.
- Ad-hoc developer prototypes until they are promoted to a supported service.

Key concepts

Declarative contract test spec (DCTS):
- A human-friendly YAML format that describes request/response shapes, example inputs, success/failure predicates, and conformance categories (strict, tolerant, deprecated).
- DCTS entries can be unit-run (local), CI-run (service-level), and cross-service-run (integration conformance matrix).

Schema fencing:
- Every change to a DCTS schema field must be accompanied by a Change Proposal (CP) file and an automated compatibility check.
- CPs are accepted automatically if they pass compatibility rules or fail open for manual review if they are breaking.

Conformance matrix and ledger:
- A centrally aggregated matrix that tracks which service versions (and model variants) satisfy which DCTS cells.
- Each matrix cell has a pass/fail history and a conformance SLI aggregated daily.

Rules and compatibility classes

Fields are labeled with one of: required, optional, deprecated, extension. Compatibility rules:

- required -> optional: allowed but requires explicit CP and CI signal.
- optional -> required: breaking change; requires canary/rollout plan and staged opt-in.
- remove deprecated field: allowed only after 3 release cycles and >95% conformance across callers.
- add new field marked extension: always allowed if receivers ignore unknown fields (tolerant mode).

Change proposal workflow (brief)

1. Author creates a CP file in the service repo under docs/contracts/cps/<pr>.yaml describing intent, compatibility class, rollout plan, and rollback criteria.
2. CI runs: unit tests, DCTS local run, contract linters, and cross-service dry-run against the latest conformance snapshot.
3. If auto-check passes (non-breaking or safe extension), merge proceeds. If flagged as potentially breaking, the CP moves to manual review by contract stewards and product owners.
4. After merge, integration conformance jobs run nightly to validate callers and receivers.

Example DCTS snippet (YAML)

# Example: /v1/generate request/response
# Save as service/docs/contracts/dcts/generate.v1.yaml
---
endpoint: POST /v1/generate
scope: public
version: 1.0.0
mode: strict
request: 
  content-type: application/json
  schema: |
    type: object
    properties:
      prompt:
        type: string
      features:
        type: object
        additionalProperties: true
    required: [prompt]
examples:
  - name: simplest
    request: {"prompt": "Summarize the following text..."}
response:
  schema: |
    type: object
    properties:
      id: {type: string}
      output: {type: string}
      tokens_consumed: {type: integer}
    required: [id, output]
predicates:
  - description: output must be non-empty
    jq: ".output | length > 0"
conformance_category: strict

Automation and CI integration

CI responsibilities (service repo):
- Run local DCTS validation (schema validity, example conformance).
- Run contract linter: enforces required metadata fields (owner, risk_level, test_coverage_min).
- Publish DCTS artifact to conformance-bucket/<service>/<version>/dcts.yaml on successful merge.

Cross-repo conformance job (central):
- Nightly job that pulls the published DCTS artifacts and runs pairwise checks across known callers and receivers.
- Failing cells create RFC-style issues in the responsible service repo and update the conformance ledger with failure signals.

Conformance ledger and dashboard

The ledger is a time-series-friendly table with columns described below and exposed in the Redwood Console and an internal dashboard. Store as rows in our metrics DB and index in the conformance service. (Table described in prose below.)

Required columns (ledger row): timestamp, service_a, service_a_version, service_b, service_b_version, endpoint, dcts_version, test_case_id, result (pass|fail), failure_reason, run_id.

Operational SLOs and alerting

- Nightly conformance pass rate for critical public endpoints >= 99.0%. Alert if < 98.0% over a 24-hour rolling window.
- Any new CP that causes a regression in an existing passing matrix cell triggers a P1 review if the affected client is production and >= 10% traffic.

Gating and release policy

- Service merge gating: Non-breaking CPs are mergeable. Breaking CPs require manual approval and a staged rollout with canary conformance verifying client behavior.
- Platform releases (runtime, SDKs): must maintain 100% conformance for official SDK bindings across supported minor versions.

Rollout and rollback playbook (high level)

1. Pre-merge: author runs smoke DCTS locally and creates CP with rollout notes.
2. Merge: DCTS published and cross-repo nightlies scheduled.
3. Canary: route 5% traffic to new service variant for 2 hours while conformance checks run.
4. Monitor: observe ledger and user-facing errors for regressions.
5. If failure SLI breached or critical callers fail, execute rollback to previous version and open an incident review.

Telemetry and observability requirements

Each contract-test run must emit:
- conftest.run_id (UUID)
- conftest.service (service name/version)
- conftest.endpoint
- conftest.test_case_id
- conftest.result (pass|fail)
- conftest.duration_ms

Motivation: We observed intermittent correctness regressions and KV-cache divergence when nodes opportunistically switched to lower-precision kernels under load. These issues were most pronounced during warm-up phases and when continuous-batching mixed short warm-up sequences with steady-state traffic. The goal of this PR is to make the low-precision fast path reliable in production by adding conservative checks and an automatic, observable annealing mechanism that trades small amounts of peak throughput for deterministic correctness.

Summary of changes: add a light-weight per-node kernel stability probe that runs microbenchmarks on model startup and periodically during low-utilization windows; expose a configurable 'kernel_stability_threshold' that gates transitions to low-precision kernels; implement a precision-annealing state machine that steps precision down gradually (fp32 -> fp16 -> int8) only when stability and latency criteria are met; add a kv-sync-guard which attaches short-lived checksums to KV cache snapshots and prevents applying a cache state if checksum mismatch or stale-timestamp detected; update continuous-batching heuristics to avoid batching sequences observed during the warm-up probe and to prefer homogeneous-decoded sequences to reduce cache churn.

Configuration and defaults: default kernel_stability_threshold=0.92 (fraction of microbench runs that must pass), anneal_step_interval=30s, min_stable_window=2m. Operators can override in runtime config or via console per-cluster. Canary rollout automatically enables annealing on 10% of nodes by default.

Design notes: stability probe is intentionally lightweight (per-model token-limited runs) and runs on a background worker with a low scheduling priority. We capture simple metrics: decode latency variance, kernel success/failure, and checksum of produced KV updates. The precision-annealing state machine records a rollback count and will automatically revert to the last-known-good precision if a regression is detected for two consecutive evaluation windows. KV-sync-guard uses a small 64-bit checksum and timestamp to detect divergent updates; it prevents a stale or corrupt cache from being applied and triggers a re-fetch path that is more conservative (sequential KV application with verification).

Performance and correctness: measured on internal perf-lab with a mix of 1k short-chat and 200 long-generation traces: baseline (optimistic fp16 fastpath without probes) showed +12.3% token/sec vs safe fp32 but a 2.8% rare correctness/regression signal on our eval set and occasional KV-invalidation incidents during canary. With this PR enabled (default canary), we observe +9.1% token/sec, p95 token latency improved by 6ms relative to safe fp32, and correctness regressions dropped to 0.12% (within noise). CPU/GPU telemetry indicates a ~7% reduction in wasted kernel restarts during warm-up.

description:
Problem: During regional disruptions we currently perform blunt traffic drains or full cutovers that can truncate long-lived streaming sessions and lose in-flight KV state. This causes visible client disconnects, token replays, and SLO violations for tail latency and availability.

Goal: Implement a gateway bifurcation pattern that enables graceful takeover between two active regions that share a coordinated per-connection KV checkpointing mechanism, short token-grace window, and circuit-decay policy. The mechanism should: preserve active streaming attachments where possible, reduce user-visible interruptions, maintain SLOs for p95/p99 latency, and allow progressive traffic rebalancing with automated load-shedding triggers and circuit breakers for overloaded endpoints.

acceptance_criteria:
New gateway bifurcation control plane can execute staged traffic split 100% -> 80/20 -> 50/50 -> 0% with per-connection checkpointing applied during each stage
Active streaming sessions can resume on target region with KV checkpoint replay within token-grace window for >= 95% of test sessions in canary
Circuit-decay policy triggers and drops low-priority background requests while preserving high-priority tokens; measured p99 latency remains within SLO (<= 800ms) during 70% simulated surge
Automated rollback when telemetry shows error-rate delta > 2% or SLA budget burn > 30% in 10m window
End-to-end observability: dashboards for per-connection handoff success rate, checkpoint latency, token-grace expirations, and circuit-breaker activations are available in Console
Runbook updated with step-by-step operator commands and emergency cutover procedure

design_notes:
Bifurcation model: introduce a light-weight control plane API that instructs edge gateways to enter a 'bifurcate' mode where connections are tracked and checkpoints emitted at defined safe boundaries (e.g., sentence boundaries or invocation end for non-streams)
KV checkpointing uses existing prefix cache format but augments with 'handoff-metadata' containing sequence id and minimal opaque resume token
Token-grace window: short TTL (default 45s) during which requests with valid resume token are allowed on destination region before full auth revalidation, configurable per-customer
Circuit-decay: instead of hard reject on threshold breach, reduce priority of non-interactive routes progressively using weighted drop and backoff so that interactive sessions retain headroom
We will avoid synchronous cross-region KV replication; instead use per-connection snapshot + opportunistic async pre-warm on destination to keep overhead low

technical_approach:
Edge changes: gateway will emit checkpoint artifacts to S3-backed artifact store (or internal blob cache) keyed by connection-id and region, with signed short-lived pointer visible to target region
Control plane: bifurcate controller service with APIs: /start-bifurcate, /advance-stage, /rollback, /finalize. Controller computes staged percentages and pushes policies to gateways via gRPC config streams
Resume flow: destination gateway receives resume token, fetches checkpoint, rehydrates KV cache and replay last few tokens to restore deterministic decoder state; if checkpoint unavailable or stale, fallback to canonical stateless retry path
Load-shedding triggers: telemetry-driven rules based on queue depth, GPU headroom, and p99 latency; rules feed into controller which adjusts split and activates circuit-decay rules
Safety nets: global circuit-breaker per-customer that can instant-fail new sessions to protect cluster and prevent cascading failures
Backwards compatibility: non-streaming and stateless flows unaffected; default behavior for customers not opted-in remains original cutover path

rollout_plan:
Phase 0 - Internal Canary: deploy bifurcate controller and edge code to test cluster; run synthetic suite with deterministic streams (2/10 - 2/24)
Phase 1 - Limited Canary: enable feature for internal services only, monitor handoff success and token-grace expirations, iterate on checkpoint size and pre-warm thresholds (3/1 - 3/8)
Phase 2 - Customer Canary: opt-in 3 low-risk customers with long-lived streams; run staged splits with progressive % increases (3/9 - 3/16)
Phase 3 - Ramp: enable auto-split for broad traffic with conservative defaults and telemetry thresholds; maintain human-in-loop for first 48 hours (3/17 - 3/24)
Rollback: emergency commands in runbook to abort and redirect all bifurcate traffic back to original region and invalidate resume tokens

telemetry:
Per-connection metrics: checkpoint_size_bytes, checkpoint_emit_latency_ms, resume_fetch_latency_ms, resume_success_bool
Handoff metrics: handoff_attempts_total, handoff_success_rate, handoff_fallback_rate
SLOs: p95/p99 latency pre/post-handshake, availability per-region, error-rate by route
Circuit metrics: circuit_open_count, average_decay_rate, dropped_requests_by_priority
Alerting: conservative alerts for handoff_success_rate < 90% in 5m and p99 latency regression > 20% vs baseline

test_plan:
Automated unit tests for checkpoint serialization/deserialization and token signing
Integration tests with simulated cross-region resume using local artifact store
Chaos tests: introduce network partitions and verify controller rolling advance/rollback semantics
Load tests: synthetic streams plus background embedding/ingest traffic to evaluate circuit-decay efficacy
Canary dashboards and SLIs tracked during each stage; automatic gates for phase transition

risks:
Resume token leakage: mitigated by short TTLs and signature verification; requires security review
Large checkpoints may add storage/IO pressure during mass handoffs; mitigation: cap checkpoint size and prefer incremental diffs
Checkpoint replay may diverge for non-deterministic model serving paths (e.g., sampling); mitigation: restrict replay to deterministic sampling or force deterministic mode during handoff windows
Increased control plane complexity and blast radius if controller miscomputes split — mitigations: rate limits, circuit-breakers, and manual abort
SLO trade-off: during surge the system may favor availability of interactive sessions by dropping background work; this needs clear product communication

Context:
Summary:
This PRD defines the Quantization & Fidelity Experimentation Lab (the Lab): a reproducible, service-backed environment for running targeted fidelity experiments when introducing quantized model variants, pruning, or other cost-saving serving techniques. The Lab's outputs are deterministic experiment artifacts, decision signals (pass/fail/gated), and standardized reports used by Product, Applied ML, and Serving Runtime to decide rollouts and fallback strategies.

Goals:
- Provide a single source of truth for fidelity impact of any automated compression or quantization profile across representative tenant workloads.
- Produce machine-readable experiment results (quality deltas, latency/cost deltas, statistical significance) and a human-readable report with recommended rollout gating (allow, canary, block).
- Support experiment types: full-model quantization, per-layer mixed-precision, activation pruning, low-rank adapters, and forced KV-cache eviction behaviors.
- Integrate with the Optimize and Serving Runtime rollout pipelines to automatically recommend safe rollouts and guardrail thresholds.

Non-goals:
- The Lab will not itself perform live production A/B rollouts. It produces evidence and artifacts consumed by the rollout systems.
- The Lab does not replace long-term model quality monitoring (that remains in Console/Optimize).

Success metrics (first 6 months):
- 90% of candidate quantization profiles produce a deterministic Lab report within 48 hours of submission (on standard profiles).
- >=75% reduction in manual evaluation time for quantization-related rollouts (measured via engineering survey).
- Fallbacks triggered by Lab-approved rollback policies reduce customer-seen quality regressions by >60% vs ad-hoc rollouts.

Stakeholders and owners:
- Product (owner): Ivy Chen (product lead) — defines acceptance criteria and experimental matrix templates.
- Applied ML (owner): Rafael Ortega — curates evaluation sets and quality metrics per workload/domain.
- Eng: Serving Runtime (owner): Arjun Malhotra — provides runtime hooks and cost/latency telemetry, implements automated rollout integration.
- Eng: DevEx — SDK/CLI for experiment submission and artifacts retrieval.

User stories:
1) As an Applied ML engineer, I want to submit a quantization profile and a list of evaluation prompt sets and receive a standardized fidelity report (metrics, significance, artifact links) so I can recommend rollout policy.
2) As a Product manager, I want a summary dashboard showing pass/fail across customer segments, so I can prioritize safe rollouts.
3) As an SRE, I want experiment artifacts to include traceable request IDs and telemetry so I can audit regressions that reach production.

Experiment runner requirements (functional):
- Accept experiment definitions as YAML or JSON via SDK/REST and return a job id.
- Run experiments against: canonical test harness (deterministic RNG seeds), a configurable subset of model variants (float32, int8, 4-bit mixed), and a set of workload slices (chat, code, long-form completion, embeddings).
- Capture and persist: per-example outputs, token-level latencies, resource utilization (GPU RAM, kernels used), and per-example quality scores.
- Produce a structured report containing: aggregated metrics (mean, median, p99), delta vs baseline, 95% confidence intervals, A/B test p-values, and an automated pass/fail recommendation based on policy.

Experiment runner requirements (non-functional):
- Turnaround: typical small experiments complete within 24 - 48 hours; pilot-level experiments (large prompt sets) within 5 days.
- Reproducibility: experiments run with immutable seeds, pinned model binaries, and environment hashes.
- Multi-tenant safety: experiments run in an isolated namespace, with no customer data used unless explicitly authorized and scrubbed.

Quality metrics and gating logic:
- Primary metrics per workload:
  - Chat/Completion: semantic similarity (embedding cosine) vs baseline, normalized F1 when applicable, and response length parity. Gate: mean embedding cosine drop <= 0.012 AND 99th-percentile semantic delta <= 0.02.
  - Code generation: pass@k and compilation success rate. Gate: pass@1 drop <= 1.5 percentage points and compile-failure delta <= 0.5pp.
  - Embeddings: mean cosine similarity drop <= 0.015; downstream retrieval MAP drop <= 0.8%.
  - Latency/Cost: p50 latency must not increase more than 8% for the target serving configuration; cost/unit must be reduced by >= 12% to be considered.
- Automated pass/fail decision algorithm:
  1. Compute per-workload deltas and CIs.
  2. If any primary metric breaches gate thresholds -> FAIL.
  3. If primary metrics pass but secondary metrics (edge-case slices) show regressions above 95th-percentile thresholds -> WARN (manual review).
  4. Produce recommendation: allow | canary (10% traffic) | block.

Experiment definition schema (example YAML):
  ---
  experiment_name: "int4-mixed-prune-v2"
  model_variant: "redwood-open-7b-v2"
  baseline_variant: "redwood-open-7b-fp16"
  profiles:
    - name: "int4-mixed"
      quantization: "mixed-int4"
      per_layer_overrides: ["attn-16:8", "mlp-5:4"]
  workload_slices:
    - name: "customer-chat-small"
      sample_set: "canonical/chat-1000"
      metrics: ["embed_cosine","mean_length","toxicity_rate"]
  eval_repeat: 3
  rng_seed: 41321

Telemetry and artifact requirements:
- Events captured: experiment.submitted, experiment.started, example.{id}.inference.start, example.{id}.inference.end, experiment.completed, experiment.report.generated.
- Telemetry must include: job_id, model_variant, profile_hash, seed, environment_hash, worker_version, and timestamps.
- Artifacts stored: raw outputs (per example), normalized metric table (CSV), aggregated report (JSON and human-readable markdown), and an immutable experiment metadata file.

Data handling and PII policy:
- No customer PII may be used in Lab experiments unless explicitly consented and processed in a restricted workspace.
- When customer data is approved, the Lab will apply automated scrubbing per the Data Management policy: remove names, tokens matching credit-card patterns, and PII heuristics.

Integration points and automation:
- Rollout Integration: Lab will call the Rollout Recommendation API with pass/canary/block and attach experiment artifact links. Serving Runtime will annotate model variants with experiment ids.
- Console: Add a new page type "Experiment Report" where product and applied-ml can browse experiments, filter by model, and export PDFs.

Operational requirements and infra sizing:
- Baseline test cluster: 8x A100(80GB) equivalent nodes for parallel small experiments; ability to burst to 32 nodes for large sweeps.
- Storage: lifecycle retention of experiment artifacts: 90 days hot, 1 year cold archive.
- RBAC: roles: lab-admin, lab-runner, lab-viewer. lab-runner may execute jobs but cannot delete artifacts.

Reporting and human-readable output (example):

| chat-1000 | 0.872 | 0.861 | -0.011 | ±0.003 | PASS |
| legal-slice | 0.790 | 0.760 | -0.030 | ±0.010 | WARN |
Notes: The legal-slice regression is concentrated in documents with very long citations (see artifact: /artifacts/12345/legal-edge-cases.csv). Recommend a canary to 5% with automated fallback to fp16 for flagged tenant tags.

2. Applied ML reviews WARNs; if minor, mark canary; if block, require engineer to iterate.
3. If canary approved, schedule a 2-week canary at 5-10% traffic with monitoring alerts configured (quality delta, token-level fraud checks).
4. If canary succeeds (no production quality regression for 14 days), promote to gradual rollout.

Purpose and scope:
This is a lightweight scratchpad for thinking about 'fractured context' strategies: when a long session is assembled from multiple interleaved short interactions (multi-document chat, task switching, user sessions with gaps) and how to keep latency and cost predictable while preserving retrieval/continuity quality.

Motivation (quick):
- Users expect context continuity across ephemeral turns and across background tasks (e.g., user edits doc A, then does a quick search, comes back).
- Full prefix replay is expensive at 1k+ tokens per turn; naive KV cache growth or repeated retrievals blow cost/latency.
- Need heuristics or micro-protocols to anchor session state cheaply and recover context when needed.

Reading roundup (notes + immediate takeaways):
1) "Session Anchors for Long Conversational State" (arXiv:2403.01234) - skimed
   - idea: create compact anchor vectors at decision points (every N tokens or after topic change).
   - anchors are small (128–512 dims), stored per-session; on context switch, retrieve nearest anchors and rehydrate partial KV cache via learned projector.
   - takeaway: anchor projection noise likely high for factual detail; works better for topical continuity + procedural cues.

2) "KV-summarize: fragment summarization to compress attention state" (internal notes + related work)
   - offline summarization of stale KV segments to 1–2 sentence summaries that are kept in prompt context rather than expanding KV cache.
   - tradeoff: lossy summaries reduce token cost but can break exact retrieval for code/legal stuff.

3) "Interleaved Context Scheduling (ICLR workshop slides)"
   - scheduling requests by urgency: low-urgency turns can be batched and served with cached summaries; high urgency uses full KV rehydration.
   - practical: annotate requests with "urgency" metadata from client SDK.

Open questions / hypotheses:
- H1: Anchors + light projection will preserve >80% topical coherence while cutting rehydration tokens by 60%.
- H2: For factual fidelity (exact names, code), anchors will fail; need hybrid: anchors for discourse, fetch original KV for critical segments indicated by metadata.
- H3: User-visible latency SLO improves if we precompute anchors on idle CPU/GPU cycles and keep a small LRU of recent anchor->KV mappings.

Experiment sketch (priority ordering):
A) Benchmark anchor retrieval vs full KV rehydration (toy dataset)
   - Dataset: 200 synthetic sessions (mix edits, searches, code) assembled from public chatlogs + internal anonymized sessions.
   - Metrics: continuity_score (human-rated 1-5), token_cost, average_latency, factual_precision@k for retrievals.
   - Implementation notes: reuse kv-playground repo branch from linked PR; add anchor projector model (2-layer MLP) and serialization format.
B) Urgency-based scheduler prototype (client + server hooks)
   - Add "urgency" header in SDK, default low. Server policy: if low and session > N tokens, return summary placeholder and queue background rehydration.
   - Measure user-perceived latency and number of follow-up rehydrations.

Edge cases to capture:
- Multi-document merges (two docs referenced across a session) -> anchors need multi-anchor composition, or metadata indicating document ids to pull exact KV when necessary.
- Hallucination risk when relying on compressed anchors for facts; include fallback that detects high-entropy model outputs (logprob heuristics) and triggers full fetch.

Summary
-------
This document summarizes the Redwood Optimize 1.3 release (GA: 2026-02-20). Optimize 1.3 introduces Performance Profiles, Telemetry-based Cost Estimator, latency-tier presets for the Console, and several SDK/CLI usability improvements. The release targets customers using Redwood Optimize to tune Dedicated and Hosted inference for predictable unit economics and simplified rollout of quantization/batching recommendations.

Highlights
----------
- Performance Profiles (feature flag: optimize.performance_profiles): per-model, per-workload profiles that capture measured latency/throughput/cost at multiple sequence-length distributions. Profiles power auto-suggestion rules and the new cost estimator.
- Telemetry-based Cost Estimator: end-to-end estimator that uses historical request shape telemetry (prefix length, tokens-per-request, hit rates) to produce monthly cost projections and sensitivity analyses.
- Latency-tier Presets in Console: new predefined profiles (S0: <50ms p95, S1: <120ms p95, S2: <250ms p95) that automatically tune batching and cache TTL recommendations.
- SDK v0.18.0: new Optimize client with async estimate_cost() and get_performance_profile() helpers; breaking rename of estimate() -> estimate_cost().
- CLI: redwood optimize export-profile <model> -> writes a reproducible YAML profile used for Dedicated scheduling.
- Migration & compatibility: recommended default quantization profiles unchanged; deprecated optimize.legacy_hint removed (see Migration notes).

What’s new (detailed)
---------------------
1) Performance Profiles
   - Description: Profiles record observed stat distributions for: sequence_length, tokens_generated, request_rate (qps), prefix_cache_hit_rate. Each profile stores measured p50/p95 latencies and per-token GPU time across representative buckets (short/medium/long).
   - Storage: profiles are stored in the customer namespace (s3-backed), versioned, and visible via Console and API.
   - API preview: POST /v1/optimize/profiles {"model":"redwood-7b-v1","workload":"chat-short"} -> returns profile id and recommendations.
   - Owner: Optimize team (owner: Deepa Nair).

2) Telemetry-based Cost Estimator
   - Inputs: time window (default 30d), model(s), deployment mode (hosted/dedicated), commitment tier, sequence-length histogram.
   - Output: month-over-month projection (USD), token breakdown (input/system/output), sensitivity table (how cost changes if average tokens/request increases by +10/25/50%).
   - Accuracy caveats: estimator factors in measured batching efficiency and prefix cache hit rate; for cold-start or sparse telemetry customers, the estimator uses conservative defaults (see config below).
   - Console: new "Cost Projection" panel on Optimize pages with download CSV button.

3) Latency-tier Presets
   - Presets: S0 (ultra-low latency), S1 (balanced), S2 (cost-efficient). Each preset maps to batching window targets, max batch size, and prefix_cache_TTL suggestions.
   - Implementation: presets are applied as heuristics on top of Performance Profiles and can be overridden by route-level policy.

4) SDK & CLI changes
   - SDK v0.18.0: function rename estimate() -> estimate_cost(); new async wrapper; returns structured CostEstimate object. See SDK guide for migration snippet.
   - CLI: new export-profile command produces a YAML suitable for Dedicated scheduler. Example: redwood optimize export-profile redwood-13b-v2 --window 7d --out profile.yaml

Migration notes and breaking changes
----------------------------------
- Deprecated field removed: optimize.legacy_hint (previously used for heuristic-only recommendations). Action: remove any usages in saved route configs. Failure to remove will return 400 in API calls that include the field.
- SDK rename: update code references estimate() -> estimate_cost(). Simple search-and-replace sufficient for most codebases.
- Profile format changes: profile v1 -> v2 adds buckets for "prefix_cache_hit_rate". Dedicated scheduler accepts both v1 and v2, but v1 profiles will be automatically converted on import with a best-effort fill (read-only). We recommend re-exporting profiles after conversion.

Configuration snippets and examples
----------------------------------
- Console: Toggle Performance Profiles via Admin -> Optimize feature flags -> optimize.performance_profiles (default: off for existing tenants; on for new tenants).

- Example API request (cost estimate):

  # after

Motivation: observed high peak GPU workspace usage for mixed-sequence inference (short+long requests) and multi-query fanout workloads. Existing arena tuning + static activation checkpointing provided good average memory savings but left headroom in two patterns: (1) transient scratch buffer spikes from kernels that allocate per-op temp buffers, and (2) suboptimal kernel choices when the operator fanout (key/value heads * queries) changes runtime characteristics. This PR implements two complimentary mechanisms to reduce peak workspace: 1) dynamic scratch reuse: a runtime scratch allocator that tracks short-lived temp regions by lifetime buckets and reuses buffers across operators within the same execution frame, avoiding repeated allocations and reducing fragmentation; 2) fanout-aware kernel selection: extend the kernel-selector to consider request fanout and KV cache reshaping costs when choosing between tiled/packed attention kernels and the low-memory fused attention kernels.

Summary of changes: implemented a lightweight scratch manager in runtime/scratch_manager.{cpp,h} with a lock-free free-list per-sizeclass and lifetime-tagging. Hooked the scratch allocation path into the kernel interface and modified critical kernels (attention, rotary, layernorm) to request scratch via the manager. Added a fanout heuristic in runtime/kernel_selector.cpp that uses observed Q*K fanout counters (collected per-model) to pick kernels that trade compute for lower transient memory. Added a compatibility path so that models pinned to older kernel profiles will continue to run the legacy selector. Integrated unit and microbenchmarks under benchmark-lab/ with a new benchmark script fanout_memory_profile.py and an end-to-end e2e memory test that simulates interleaved short/long requests.

Performance results: on A100-40GB with GPT-2 style model (1B params) and mixed workload (50% seq_len=32, 50% seq_len=1024) peak workspace dropped from 16.8GB to 12.1GB (~28% reduction). For high-fanout Q=16 tests the transient peak reduced by ~34% when the fanout-aware kernel was selected. End-to-end latency impact: median latency for long requests increased ~2.3% in a worst-case knob-on scenario where the low-memory kernel is used; this is within the SLA tradeoff and we expose a config flag to prefer latency vs memory at policy-level.

Compatibility and rollout strategy: feature gated behind runtime flag runtime.scratch_reuse.enabled=false by default in this PR; we plan a phased rollout: enable on non-production clusters for 2 weeks, then opt-in for Dedicated clusters with memory pressure, finally flip default after one week of metrics monitoring. Kernel selection heuristic is additive and can be disabled with runtime.kernel_selector.fanout_heuristic=false. Added telemetry metrics: runtime.scratch_reuse.alloc_reuse_ratio, kernel_selector.fanout_decision_count and memory.scratch_peak_by_model.

Testing: added unit tests for scratch manager lifecycle and size-class reuse; added integration tests that assert no OOM on synthetic high-fanout scenarios; ran infra e2e-bench and observed stable results. CI: linux-unit-tests, cuda-smoke, and e2e-bench run green in the final run. Created a small fuzz harness to ensure lifetime tagging prevents use-after-free across frames.

Backward compatibility: no breaking API changes; the kernel interface signature extended with an optional scratch_token but remains backward-compatible with default nullptr behavior. Documentation: runtime/README.md updated with configuration knobs, and redwood-docs/ops/gpu-memory-tuning.md includes recommended settings for Dedicated customers.

Notes: this PR intentionally avoids changing global arena sizing heuristics in this iteration — that will be a follow-up to measure impact of scratch reuse on arena fragmentation (ENG-1919). Also, we identified a secondary opportunity to compress KV cache layout when fanout>8; tracked separately under ENG-1875.

Quick takeaways (TL;DR):
- For conversational short-turn workloads (turns <= 40 tokens) the H100 + small-batch multiplexing gives best p50 and p90 at moderate cost; p99 is highly sensitive to background session churn.

- Hardware: H100x1 (80GB), A100x1 (40GB), A10Gx1 (24GB) — note: these are single-GPU node profiles run under the same runtime image.
- Network: intra-region, measured client RTT mean 5ms.
- Workloads: three profiles (interactive-nano, interactive-short, long-generate):
  * interactive-nano — 1–8 tokens output per turn, arrival Poisson lambda tuned for 400rps sustained, 10% bursts.
  * interactive-short — median 35 tokens output, targeted for chat UIs with quick replies.
  * long-generate — median 300 tokens, used by summarization/batch-response flows.

- Two modes tested per workload: fastpath (no batching, low-latency multiplexer), and windowed-batching (batch-window 25ms, max-batch 32).

Purpose: This handbook describes a focused, repeatable Ten-Step Restoration Sprint used during multi-system outages and pairs that operational flow with a structured shadow-mentor program to accelerate oncall proficiency. Scope: Applies to production incidents that meet SLO-impacting criteria (see SLO thresholds section). Not intended for low-severity config errors or scheduled maintenance.

Owner: Eng SRE team. Primary contact: oncall-lead@redwood.example.com.

Quick links: runbook library, status page templates, postmortem template, incident evidence checklist.

Audience and roles

- Incident Initiator: the first person to acknowledge the alert and call the bridge.
- Bridge Operator: facilitates the incident bridge, coordinates comms, and enforces the Ten-Step Sprint cadence.
- Primary Resolver: service owner(s) leading technical work for the impacted service(s).
- Secondary Resolvers: cross-functional engineers called in to assist (networking, infra, runtime).
- Shadow: junior responder who observes and documents actions during the sprint.
- Mentor: senior SRE who leads post-incident coaching and retro facilitation.

How to use this document

- Use the numbered Ten-Step Sprint for initial restoration (first 60–90 minutes).
- Run the shadow mentoring checklist in parallel to create training artefacts.
- After containment, follow the Post-Incident Evidence & Draft Postmortem template included below.

SLO thresholds that trigger Ten-Step Sprint

| Severity | Symptom | SLO impact | Trigger |
|---------|---------|------------|---------|
| Sev1 | Total region outage for hosted API | >= 99.5% reduction in success rate for 5+ minutes | Auto-trigger after 3x alert flood or manual bridge |
| Sev2 | Significant latency increase | > 200ms p95 increase across customer requests for 15+ minutes | Review/bridge by oncall |

Ten-Step Restoration Sprint (primary runbook)

1) Acknowledge & Bridge (0–5m)
   - Incident Initiator: acknowledge the alert in PagerDuty and create a bridge (Zoom/Google Meet).
   - Bridge Operator: open the incident channel (#inc-xxxx) and post initial status: impacted services, region, estimated blast radius, primary contact.
   - Shadow: note timestamps, alert IDs, and initial metrics snapshot.

2) Quick Impact Triage (5–10m)
   - Primary Resolver: confirm service(s) affected using dashboards (console/model-serving, ingress, and edge metrics).
   - Bridge: classify impact (regional vs. global, data plane vs. control plane).
   - Output: short impact statement to stakeholders.

3) Stabilize Traffic (10–20m)
   - If applicable, apply graduated traffic control: rate-limits, scaled back routing policies, or traffic-division to healthy regions.
   - Use fallback model variants or reduced sequence length mode where supported to temporarily reduce CPU/GPU pressure.

4) Hotfix Window (20–40m)
   - Primary Resolver and Secondary Resolvers: run validated mitigation steps from specific service runbooks (see related runbook IDs).
   - Keep changes small, reversible, and documented in the incident channel.

5) Validate Restoration (30–50m)
   - Run synthetic probes against restored endpoints. Confirm p95/p99 latency and error-rate trends returning to baseline.
   - Shadow: capture pre/post metric snapshots and the commands used.

6) Customer Status & Tiered Notifications (immediately after validation)
   - Bridge Operator: publish customer-facing status update using the template below.
   - For enterprise customers impacted by the incident, trigger account-level outreach per the escalation matrix.

7) Stabilization Monitoring (50–90m)
   - Maintain increased sampling and tracing for 3x normal volume for 90 minutes.
   - Set temporary alerts at tighter thresholds (e.g., 50% of SLO slack) to catch reversion.

8) Evidence Collection & Triage for Postmortem (start while stabilizing)
   - Collect logs, traces, config diffs, rollout metadata, and full command history. Attach artifacts to the incident ticket.
   - Shadow: curate a short evidence index with direct links.

9) Restore Normal Ops & Runbook Handover (90–120m)
   - Roll back temporary mitigations and revert traffic controls when confident.
   - Primary Resolver: schedule a 60-minute triage deep-dive with the mentor and product owner within 48 hours.

10) Close Bridge & Draft Postmortem (post sprint)
   - Bridge Operator: move the channel to read-only and create a draft postmortem using the included template.
   - Mentor: assign action owners with clear SLAs for mitigation items.

Shadow-Mentor Program (parallel process)

Purpose: Turn incidents into repeatable learning opportunities and accelerate new responder ramp.

Shadow checklist (during sprint):
- Record timestamps for each decision and action.
- Note who is contacted and the exact commands or consoles used.
- Capture any runbook gaps or ambiguous steps.
- Collect a short list of 3 teachable moments for the retro.

Mentor responsibilities (post sprint):
- Within 48 hours: review the evidence index and draft postmortem with the shadow.
- Within 7 days: run a 30–60 minute learning session with the wider oncall rota covering the teachable moments and suggested runbook updates.
- Ensure at least one runbook edit or clarification is merged per incident for which the shadow prepared artifacts.

Escalation matrix (quick reference)

- Local service issue -> Primary Resolver -> Service Lead (15 min)
- Cross-service or infra -> Add Secondary Resolver(s) + SRE oncall (10 min)
- Prolonged SLO loss > 1 hour -> Paging to Eng Director + Product Ops (escalate at 60m)
- Customer-impacting > 4 hours -> Executive status + CS/AE briefing (escalate at 4h)

Enterprise account brief (email/Slack DM):

3) Root cause hypothesis / final root cause: technical summary.
4) Contributing factors: people, process, tooling, and telemetry gaps.

7) Evidence index: links to logs, traces, recordings, rollout IDs, and config diffs.

- Runbook review cadence: quarterly for high-risk services, bi-annual for others.

- Shadow simulations: monthly 60-minute labs where a shadow leads a mini-restoration and a mentor grades the artifacts produced.

- Mean Time To Restore (MTTR) — target: reduce by 20% year-over-year.
- Shadow ramp time — % of shadows qualified to be solo oncall within 4 months.
- Runbook churn — number of runbook edits per incident (target: >=1 edit/incident).
