Context:
Summary

This document describes the step-by-step oncall protocol for performing an inter-account GPU warm-pool handoff when the primary tenant capacity is exhausted and a cross-account burst is required. It covers preflight checks, the handshake sequence between warm-pool-manager instances, IAM role chain assumptions, Terraform/IaC changes required for emergency handoffs, verification, rollback, and observability. This runbook is intended for oncall engineers (infra SRE and GPU fleet owners) who manage multi-account GPU bursting and warm-pool orchestration.

When to run this

- Automatic trigger: capacity-sentry signals a sustained 90th-percentile queue time > 2.5s and warm-pool saturation for 3 minutes.
- Manual trigger: customer-facing latency incidents, region outage, or when the allocation controller requests cross-account burst.

Preflight (5 minutes)

1) Confirm incident context and scope: affected tenant(s), region(s), and SLO impact.
2) Check SLO dashboard:
   - 99th-pct latency target: 500ms token-serving
   - Queue-time SLO: 95th-pct < 1.2s
3) Verify warm-pool health in both accounts: runbook-owner should check warm-pool-manager metrics for: active leases, available-gpus, preheat-success-rate.

Quick commands (run from the oncall bastion with appropriate MFA)

- Check capacity-sentry alerts: curl -s https://prometheus.internal/api/v1/query?query=capacity_sentry_alert
- List warm pool instances (k8s): kubectl -n infra get pods -l app=warm-pool-manager -o wide
- Inspect lease table: psql -h leases-db.internal -U infra_user -c "select * from leases where state='handshake' order by created_at desc limit 20;"

Roles and architecture notes

- warm-pool-manager: service running in every account responsible for preheating GPUs, tagging instances, and performing handshake.
- burst-orchestrator: global controller that decides target account for overflow.
- capacity-sentry: SLO monitor and alerting signal source.
- egress-shim: per-account egress proxy that performs bandwidth-aware stamping for cross-account traffic.
- lease-daemon: lightweight agent on compute nodes that accepts ephemeral leases and streams KV-cache seeds.

Handshake protocol overview (high level)

1) burst-orchestrator determines target account and issues an ephemeral handshake token (valid for 3 minutes).
2) warm-pool-manager in target account validates the token via IAM role chain and creates a placeholder Lease record in read-only state.
3) Source warm-pool-manager begins KV-cache seed transfer using the lease token and a TLS-auth channel to the target account's lease-daemon.
4) After successful seed receipt, the target upgrades the Lease to Active and updates routing tables so the router sidecar can route tenant requests into the new pool.

Detailed emergency handoff procedure (approx. 18–30 minutes)

Step 0 — Notify stakeholders (2 minutes)
- Announce on #infra-oncall and page the oncall rotation in PagerDuty with priority P2. Include region, tenant, and current capacity metrics.

Step 1 — Confirm IAM and trust boundary (3 minutes)
- Validate the target account has the cross-account role configured: role name "redwood/warm-pool-handoff".
- Quick check (from source account):
  aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::TARGET_ACCOUNT_ID:role/redwood/warm-pool-handoff --role-session-name handoff-check
- If assume-role fails: escalate to cloud-accounts team (page Slack: @cloud-accounts). Do not proceed.

Step 2 — Issue ephemeral handshake token (1 minute)
- From burst-orchestrator console: POST /api/v1/handshake {"source_account":"A","target_account":"B","ttl_s":180} -> returns token.
- Record token id and TTL in the incident timeline.

Step 3 — Reserve capacity in target pool (3 minutes)
- In target account run: kubectl -n infra exec deploy/warm-pool-manager -- /bin/warmctl reserve --token <TOKEN_ID> --count <n_gpus>. Aim to reserve 10–20% above predicted peak for safety.
- If reserve fails due to account quotas, run the quota increase quick path (see Quota quick path below).

Step 4 — Seed transfer and KV-cache sync (6–12 minutes)
- Initiate transfer from source warm-pool-manager: /usr/local/bin/warmctl transfer-seed --token <TOKEN_ID> --target-endpoint https://lease-daemon.target.internal:8443 --profile fast
- Watch transfer metrics in Prometheus: warm_seed_transfer_duration_seconds, warm_seed_transfer_error_count.
- Expected durations: 90% < 90s for a 4GB seed over inter-region link (with typical egress-shim compression enabled).
- If transfer stalls > 180s: reduce concurrent shards (--shards 4) and retry. If repeated failures, abort and fall back to DNS-level routing (see Fallback options).

Step 5 — Activate lease and switch routing (2 minutes)
- On target: kubectl -n infra exec deploy/warm-pool-manager -- /bin/warmctl activate --token <TOKEN_ID>
- Update router sidecar config: POST /router/configs/apply with route override: route { tenant: "TENANT_ID", pool: "target-account-pool" }
- Wait for 1 minute for caching to propagate.

Verification (5 minutes)

- Confirm incoming requests are served from target pool: query per-request trace header x-redwood-pool in the last 100 requests.
- Confirm token billing tags and cost attribution are set: check cost-annotator logs for token_id tag.
- SLO check: observe latency and queue-time dashboards for the affected tenant for a 10-minute window; expect queue-time to drop by >= 40%.

Rollback and fallback options

- If KV-cache transfer fails irrecoverably: run fallback DNS-level routing to a best-effort cached model in a regional pool: runbook command: /usr/local/bin/warmctl fallback-dns --tenant TENANT_ID --region REGION_CODE.
- To fully rollback (deactivate target pool): kubectl -n infra exec deploy/warm-pool-manager -- /bin/warmctl deactivate --token <TOKEN_ID> --force
- Post-rollback: ensure that lease state in leases-db is set to "aborted" and trace ids are added to the incident record.

Quota quick path (when target reservation fails)

1) Check current quota: aws service-quotas get-service-quota --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-ABCDEFGH --region <REGION>
2) If instantaneous quota bump is configured (emergency-bump role): assume role: aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::TARGET_ACCOUNT_ID:role/redwood/instant-quota-bump --role-session-name qb
3) Run Terraform apply against iac/quotas/emergency-bump.tf with variables: --var 'account=TARGET_ACCOUNT_ID' --var 'delta_gpu=+X' and set -auto-approve. Only the cloud-accounts engineer should execute this; page them if necessary.

Observability and dashboards (ongoing)

- Prometheus metrics to watch:
  - warm_pool_active_leases{account,region} (target should increase)
  - warm_seed_transfer_rate_bytes
  - capacity_sentry_queue_time_seconds
  - egress_shim_bandwidth_utilization
- Logs: lease-daemon logs (stdout) aggregated in kibana index leases-logs-*/_search. Look for "seed-received" and "seed-commit" events.
- Traces: sampling key x-redwood-trace-token in Jaeger should show cross-account hops.

Post-incident tasks (owner: GPU-Fleet)

1) Create postmortem within 48 hours if handoff was non-trivial or if SLOs were missed. Include timeline and seed-transfer traces.
2) If quota bumps were used, reconcile cost center tags and submit billing adjustment within 5 business days.
3) If transfer retries occurred >2x, open a backlog ticket for transfer optimization and include transfer artifacts (logs, histogram).

Security considerations

- Handshake tokens are single-use and TTL-limited (default 180s). Never copy tokens into external channels.
- All cross-account transfers must happen over mTLS endpoints; confirm cert fingerprint before starting (see cert-check below).

Cert check (one-liner)

- openssl s_client -connect lease-daemon.target.internal:8443 -servername lease-daemon.target.internal | openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256
- Confirm fingerprint matches entry in keyring: kubectl -n infra get configmap handoff-keyring -o yaml | grep <fingerprint>

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: GPU-Fleet (pager oncall alias: #gpu-fleet-oncall).
- Secondary (cloud accounts): @cloud-accounts.
- Escalation path: after 10 minutes of blocked handoff, escalate to SRE manager and run a P1 bridging call if customer impact is P1.

Change control and IaC notes

- Any permanent changes to the warm-pool-handoff role, token TTL, or the transfer protocol must be implemented in Terraform and go through the infra GitHub repo CI/CD gates. PRs must include: unit test for token TTL enforcement, integration test that mocks assume-role, and a canary rollout policy for warmctl binary.
- Quick emergency IaC patch (only cloud-accounts): update terraform/modules/iam/roles.tf and run: terraform plan -var 'account=TARGET_ACCOUNT_ID' && terraform apply -auto-approve. Always run terraform fmt and run the policy-as-code checks before apply.

Appendix: common failure modes and remediation

| Symptom | Probable cause | Remediation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Seed transfer stalls at 0% | Egress-shim throttling | Reduce parallel shards; enable compressed profile; contact networking if sustained >5min |
| Assume-role fails | Missing trust policy | Validate role ARN and trust relationship; escalate to cloud-accounts |
| Router override not applied | Config propagation error | Reapply router config and check config-version in /router/status; restart router sidecar if necessary |

Change history

- 2024-11-12: Initial draft (Marisol Ortega)
- 2025-02-08: Clarified quota quick path and added cert-check (Ethan Kwan reviewer)

Related reading

- See the GPU capacity runways and warm-pool sizing whitepaper for sizing heuristics.
- See the egress-shim operational runbook for bandwidth shaping and compression settings.

Contact matrix

- gpu-fleet-oncall: pagerduty/@gpu-fleet-oncall
- cloud-accounts: slack/#cloud-accounts
- networking: slack/#infra-networking

End of runbook

implementation_notes:

Context:
Purpose:
This is a working sketch of a lightweight, self-contained manifest format intended to capture everything needed to deterministically replay an inference session (or a set of requests) across model rollouts, runtime variants, and quantization changes. The goal is to make postmortems, regression triage, and model A/B comparisons reproducible without requiring full environment cloning.

Non-goals (for v1):
- Not attempting to capture private customer data; manifests should be able to reference redacted payloads or point to secure storage locations.
- Not a full provenance ledger; this is focused on deterministic playback for debugging/regression.

Design principles:
- Minimal: small manifest that references artifacts rather than embedding bulk blobs.
- Deterministic intent: include all inputs that can affect output (tokenizer, seed, model artifact id, runtime config, injected policies).
- Portable: JSON-compatible, human-readable, and easy to attach to support tickets or GitHub issues.
- Privacy-aware: fields that may contain PII must be flagged and optionally replaced with redaction pointers.

Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)
- created_by: name/email of the authoring agent (person, system)
- created_at: ISO date
- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots
- privacy_policy: small token describing redaction level (none, partial, strict)
- signature: optional signed blob for integrity verification (OIDC/JWKS compatible)

Request descriptor (ordered list element):
- request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)
- timestamp: ISO timestamp of original request
- api_route: e.g., \"/v1/generate\" or \"/v1/chat/completions\"
- client_sdk: client library and version (if applicable)
- raw_payload_ref: pointer to stored payload (S3/GCS/secure-store) OR inline (redacted) string
- input_checksums: list of checksum objects (tokenization checksum, raw text checksum)
- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks
- fallback_policy_trace: if fallback occurred during original call (e.g., switched to smaller model), record decisions and timestamps

Environment (examples):
- host_os: ubuntu-22.04
- runtime_image: redwood/runtime-infer:2025-10-21
- gpu: a100-80gb (or cpu)
- region: us-west-2
- concurrency_profile: \"single-req\" | \"batched\"

Telemetry references:
These are URIs (or internal artifact ids) pointing to:
- structured trace (jaeger/span id)
- token-level metrics (latency per token)
- server logs (filtered range)
- resource utilization snapshot (GPU memory thread dump)

Privacy notes:
- raw_payload_ref should be used in combination with privacy_policy. For strict privacy, manifest contains only a redaction pointer that trusted ops can use to fetch the unredacted artifact.
- tokenizer checksums avoid including raw text; a small mapping table may be included for debugging if permitted.

Example (toy manifest snippet as text):
{
  \"manifest_id\": \"m-3c9f2d4b\",
  \"created_by\": \"aisha@redwood.ai\",
  \"created_at\": \"2025-11-02T15:04:12Z\",
  \"source_context\": \"support-ticket #12345 - user reported hallucination on invoice extraction\",
  \"model_artifact\": \"gptx-4-quant-v2:sha256=abcd1234...\",
  \"tokenizer\": \"tokenizer-v3:sha256=ef56...\",
  \"requests\": [
    {
      \"request_id\": \"r1\",
      \"timestamp\": \"2025-11-01T22:10:03Z\",
      \"api_route\": \"/v1/chat/completions\",
      \"raw_payload_ref\": \"s3://redwood-playback/12345/payload-r1.json.redacted\",
      \"input_checksums\": [\"tok:sha256:fff...\", \"raw:sha256:aaa...\"],
      \"sampling_config\": \"temp=0.0;seed=42\"
    }
  ],
  \"runtime_flags\": [\"use_kv_cache=true\", \"kv_prefetch=on\"],
  \"deterministic_seeds\": [\"global_seed=42\"],
  \"telemetry_refs\": [\"jaeger://spanid/abc123\", \"s3://redwood-playback/12345/token_metrics.json\"]
}

Repro playback flow (implementation notes):
1) Validate: check manifest signature (if present), model artifact checksum, tokenizer checksum. Bail if missing required artifacts.
2) Acquire artifacts: pull model variant + tokenizer. If quantization profile mismatch with available runtime, follow policy: either simulate (not ideal) or fail fast and record mismatch in report.
3) Materialize inputs: fetch raw_payload_ref (honoring privacy) and apply pre_hooks in order. Recompute tokenization checksum and assert equal to manifest's checksum.
4) Configure runtime: apply runtime_flags and sampling_config. Seed RNGs.
5) Execute: run request(s) single-threaded in deterministic mode (disable nondeterministic kernels where possible) and capture token logs + timings.
6) Compare: compute response fingerprint and compare with expected_response_signature. Record diffs at token, sentence, and semantic (embedding distance) levels.
7) Report: output an artifacts bundle (resulting tokens, metrics, delta report) and attach back to the manifest.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is the exact fingerprint algorithm for responses? (sha256 on normalized tokens vs embedding similarity)
- How to best represent batched vs multiplexed traces in a compact way?
- Policy for model mismatches: fallback simulation? automatic shim?
- Integration with onboarding flow: ergonomic UI in Console to upload manifest and run playback with controlled cost limits.

Notes to self (implementation cadence):
- v1: implement minimal server tool that accepts manifest, validates artifacts, runs single-request deterministic playback, emits delta report (Q1 2026).
- v2: support multi-request sessions, integrated debugger UI, signed manifests for customer upload (Q2 2026).

Short checklist for next sync with SRE/Serving Runtime:
- confirm which runtime knobs are accessible via API and which require image rebuilds
- verify deterministic kernel availability across GPU types
- prototype small corpus of manifests from recent incidents for validation

End of sketch.

(Loose, rough — meant as a personal draft for discussion. Will refine schema into a JSON Schema and example artifact layout after feedback.)

The earlier draft instead listed an optional embedded `signature` field for integrity verification.

Context:
description:
This PRD defines a production-ready evaluation harness for Optimize that: (1) uses cohort-driven and sentinel prompt sampling; (2) gates A/B rollouts with statistical and business thresholds; and (3) implements a graded rollback/failover policy that escalates from automated throttles to full traffic rollback. The goal is to reduce undetected regressions while keeping rollout velocity high for model and configuration updates.

background:
We have recurring incidents where model/config rollouts pass coarse checks but produce regression in specific customer cohorts or long-tail prompts. Current canaries are per-model and global; they miss cohort-specific quality regressions and provide coarse binary pass/fail decisions. Optimize needs a more granular, actionable evaluation contract that ties observable signals to deterministic remediation steps and human-in-the-loop triage when necessary.

goals:
Detect cohort-specific degradation with >90% recall for regressions causing >5% business-impact metric change
Prevent silent regressions by introducing sentinel prompt detection and progressive gating across traffic slices
Define deterministic rollback/playbook actions that reduce mean time to mitigation (MTTM) to under 20 minutes for high-severity regressions
Enable safe rapid rollouts: initial canary to 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100% with objective pass criteria at each stage

non_goals:
Improve underlying model training processes (this is a serving/eval policy change, not an ML re-training initiative)
Replace manual post-deploy human QA for complex policy/regulatory cases
Provide full auto-rollback for noisy low-signal metrics without human review

requirements:
Create a library of sentinel prompts organized by cohort (customer persona, region, latency-sensitive flows, regulatory flows)
Define cohort definitions and labeling rules so traffic is deterministically bucketed at request time
Implement an evaluation pipeline that computes per-cohort metrics in near-real-time (max 5 minute lag)
Provide configurable A/B gate rules in Console for: min sample size, minimum detectable effect, alpha, beta, and max allowed regression
Ship a staged rollback engine that can: gradually throttle traffic, divert to previous model version, or full rollback; each action tied to clear trigger conditions
Integrate HIL (human-in-the-loop) notification and approval steps for ambiguous signals
Expose evaluation results and runbook links in per-release Console UI and in Slack/PagerDuty alerts

acceptance_criteria:
Sentinel library with >= 500 prompts covering at least 8 predefined cohorts exists and is versioned in Optimize
Per-cohort metrics (accuracy proxy, hallucination rate, latency P95, token cost) are computed and stored with <=5 minute latency
A/B gate config supports: alpha=0.05, beta=0.2 defaults and allows override per-release
Minimum sample size calculator included in UI and enforced for gating decisions
Automated rollback triggers implemented: (a) immediate throttle if a safety sentinel > 0.5% absolute regression, (b) automatic 50% traffic revert if composite quality score drops >3% sustained for 10 minutes, (c) full rollback if business KPI regression >5% for 5 minutes
Playbook linked in Console for each trigger with owner, checklist, and communication templates
End-to-end test harness that simulates cohorts and verifies gating/rollback behavior in staging

rollout_strategy:
Phase 0: Staging validation with synthetic traffic (2 weeks) -> Phase 1: Internal canary (1%) for 48 hours -> Phase 2: Beta customers (5%) for 72 hours -> Phase 3: Gradual ramp (20% for 24 hours, 100% if gates pass). Each phase requires passing cohort-specific gates. If any cohort fails a gate, automated action is applied per remediation_playbook and the release is paused pending investigation.

statistical_tests:
Default statistical test: two-sided proportion test for binary signals (e.g., sentinel hit rate) and t-test (Welch) for continuous scores (e.g., quality score). Default alpha=0.05. Enforce minimum detectable effect calculation in UI: MDE = z_{1-alpha/2}*sqrt(p*(1-p)*(1/n1+1/n2)). Minimum n computed and must be met for the gate to be valid. For low-signal cohorts use sequential analysis with alpha spending (e.g., Pocock boundary) to allow earlier decisions while controlling Type I error.

remediation_playbook:
Level 1 (Transient noise): Auto-throttle new release traffic by 50% and notify on-call; retry observations for 15 minutes
Level 2 (Cohort regression): Divert failed cohort traffic to previous stable variant, create high-priority investigation ticket, and open a dedicated War Room channel
Level 3 (Business KPI impact): Immediate full rollback of the release, notify customers via status page and account reps, schedule postmortem within 48 hours
Human-in-the-loop: For signals classified as ambiguous by the composite detector, create a Hold state pending reviewer approval; reviewers have 30 minutes SLO to act for P1 releases

monitoring_signals:
Sentinel hit rate per cohort
Composite quality score per cohort (weighted accuracy + hallucination penalty + latency penalty)
Business KPIs: conversion rate, retention signal (as provided by customer integrations)
Infrastructure signals: token cost variance, GPU latency P95, request error rate
Anomaly detectors: drift in distribution (embedding distance) and abrupt change in output length

Console: Release details page gains a Cohort tab (per-cohort metrics, sentinel breakdown, sample viewer) and a Gates panel showing pass/fail status and confidence intervals. Gate configuration page allows setting alpha/beta, MDE, and remediation actions. Notifications configuration for slack/PagerDuty integrated into release flow.

Storage for per-request metadata and evaluation events (retention 90 days)
Streaming pipeline (Kafka) to route sampled requests to evaluation workers
Evaluation workers to run controlled prompts and compute metrics; need autoscaling profile and quotas
Dashboard endpoints and Console API to surface near-real-time cohort results

This PR adds a resilience layer that: 1) performs backpressure-aware chunking and reassembly for streaming frames to avoid partial json/toolcall corruption on slow clients, 2) proxies a lightweight 'tool-signal' envelope so function/tool-calling boundaries are deterministic across retries and reconnections, and 3) forwards seed/determinism flags and a subset of user metadata transparently through the compatibility layer.

Compatibility notes: We keep the OpenAI-compatible surface stable for existing callers. Default behavior is identical unless callers set determinism/seed or rely on streaming reconnects; in those cases the bridge guarantees idempotent framing (replay-safe chunk markers) and consistent toolcall reassembly. There are small opt-ins: the 'tool-signal' envelope is only applied when callers include a 'enable_tool_signal' flag (default true for our hosted API). For private deployments customers can opt-out via config.

Context:
h1. Purpose
This runbook describes how to perform an *emergency rollback* of the Serving Runtime release across *Hosted* and *Dedicated* fleets. It focuses on restoring SLOs safely and quickly while preserving evidence for later analysis.

h1. When to rollback (triggers)
Rollback is appropriate when one or more is true and mitigation is not available within ~30 minutes:
* p95 *time-to-first-token (TTFT)* regression > 30% in 2+ regions for 10+ minutes
* error rate > 2% on generation routes due to runtime (5xx, timeouts, OOM)
* canary cohort shows sustained degradation and traffic shift cannot be halted cleanly
* repeated GPU OOM or kernel crash loops attributable to the new runtime build

*If unsure*: declare an incident and page Runtime + SRE (see incident process) and start preparing rollback steps in parallel.

h1. Preconditions
* An incident has been declared if customer impact is confirmed or likely (see SEV process page).
* Runtime oncall has identified *candidate rollback target* (prior runtime release tag).
* Release engineer or infra oncall is available to execute the pipeline rollback (see CI/CD rollback doc).

h1. Ownership and roles
* Incident Commander (IC): owns the decision to rollback and comms cadence.
* Runtime oncall: validates technical root cause hypothesis and rollback target.
* Release/Infra oncall: executes the rollback in deployment tooling.
* SRE: monitors fleet-level SLOs and regional health signals.

h1. Rollback decision checklist
Before executing rollback, capture in the incident channel:
# Current runtime release identifier (e.g., runtime-release-2025.02.01)
# Intended rollback target (e.g., runtime-release-2025.01.17)
# Blast radius (Hosted regions; Dedicated clusters/tenants)
# Primary symptom (TTFT, throughput, 5xx, OOM)
# Confirm the prior release is known-good (at least 24h stable in prod)

h1. Step-by-step procedure

## 1) Freeze rollout / stop further progression
* If a rollout is in progress, *pause* it immediately (do not continue canary expansion).
* Ensure no automated progressive delivery job will re-advance the rollout.

## 2) Hosted rollback (global fleets)
Follow the CI/CD rollback doc to pin the Hosted runtime to the rollback target, then:
* Roll back in this order:
  # non-critical region (if any still on canary only)
  # remaining canary cohort
  # all regions currently on the bad release
* After each region completes, verify:
  * 5xx rate normalizes
  * GPU utilization returns to expected
  * TTFT and token/s recover to baseline

Hosted verification queries (Console):
* Dashboard: "Hosted Inference / Runtime Release Health"
* Metrics to watch: request_error_rate, ttft_p95_ms, tokens_per_sec, gpu_oom_count

## 3) Dedicated rollback (tenant clusters)
Dedicated rollbacks must consider customer-specific change windows and comms. In emergencies, proceed under the emergency change policy.
* Identify impacted Dedicated clusters/tenants:
  * Check "Dedicated / Runtime Release Adoption" dashboard
  * Confirm whether each tenant is on the bad release
* Execute rollback per cluster using the pipeline rollback procedure.
* For high-sensitivity tenants, coordinate with CS for outbound comms and approvals (see comms guide).

## 4) Post-rollback validation
* Keep the incident open until metrics are stable for 30 minutes (Hosted) / 60 minutes (Dedicated)
* Confirm request latency distributions return to baseline and no new error modes appear
* Ensure autoscaling stabilizes (watch for over-provisioning due to the regression)

h1. Guardrails and common failure modes
* If rollback target also shows elevated OOMs, stop and reassess (may be traffic pattern or model mix).
* If only one model family is impacted, consider temporarily routing to a compatible variant instead of fleet rollback (requires IC approval).
* Avoid rapid flip-flopping between releases; if you must re-roll forward, document the reason and require runtime lead approval.

h1. Required artifacts (for later review)
Capture links in the incident channel:
* CI/CD job link(s) for rollback
* Affected regions / clusters
* Metrics screenshots or dashboard permalinks
* Any customer comms sent

h1. References
* SEV process for runtime regressions (incident roles, paging, timelines)
* Runtime release pipeline rollback procedure (exact CI/CD steps)
* Emergency change policy (approvals and documentation)
* Customer/status comms guide (templates and approval chain)


Question:

For an emergency rollback of a Serving Runtime release in Hosted and Dedicated, first pause/freeze any in-flight progressive rollout so it cannot auto-advance, then re-pin the runtime to a known-good prior runtime release tag, trigger a redeploy, and verify fleet health (e.g., 5xx rate, p95 TTFT, GPU OOMs) before closing the incident/change record. Context:
# Overview
This standard defines how Redwood Inference stores, uses, and rotates **secrets and credentials** for production services. The objective is to reduce the blast radius of credential compromise and ensure rotation is routine and low-risk.

# Definitions
- **Secret**: any value that grants access (API keys, database passwords, service tokens, signing keys, OAuth client secrets, private keys).
- **Credential rotation**: replacing a secret with a new value and updating all consumers.
- **Emergency rotation**: accelerated rotation performed due to suspected compromise or active incident.

# Approved storage systems
Production secrets must be stored in one of the following:
- Redwood Vault (primary)
- Cloud KMS/HSM-backed secret store where required by compliance (Private deployments may vary)

Prohibited:
- plaintext in Git repositories
- plaintext in Confluence/Google Docs
- long-lived secrets in CI logs
- hard-coded values in container images

# Secret classification
- **Tier 0**: root/admin credentials, signing keys, KMS master operations.
- **Tier 1**: service-to-service auth tokens, database credentials, message bus credentials.
- **Tier 2**: third-party API keys with limited scopes, internal read-only tokens.

# Rotation requirements
Minimum rotation cadence (unless documented exception):
- Tier 0: every **30 days** + after any personnel change impacting privileged access
- Tier 1: every **90 days**
- Tier 2: every **180 days**

Immediate rotation is required if:
- a secret is exposed in logs, tickets, or a public repository
- a workstation is compromised and had access to Vault tokens
- an access anomaly is detected in audit logs

# Design requirements for rotatable secrets
Services must be designed to support rotation with minimal downtime:
- Support dual-read / dual-verify where possible (accept old+new for a bounded window)
- Prefer short-lived tokens derived from an identity provider rather than static shared secrets
- Avoid single shared credentials across unrelated services

# Logging and auditability
- Access to Tier 0 and Tier 1 secrets must be auditable (requester identity, time, action).
- Rotation events must be recorded in a change record (or incident record for emergency).

# Ownership
- Secret owner is the owning service team; Security sets minimum standards and reviews exceptions.
- On-call teams may execute emergency rotations but must follow the break-glass process.

# Exceptions
Any exception to cadence or storage must be documented with:
- rationale and compensating controls
- expiration date
- Security approval

# References
- See the Production Secret Rotation Runbook for execution steps.
- See Break-glass and Emergency Access for emergency access controls.

Question:
What is Redwood Inference's end-to-end process for rotating secrets and credentials used by production services (including emergency rotation)?

For planned rotation, the owning service team identifies the secret (Vault path) and **all consumers** via the Credential Dependencies inventory, confirms tier/cadence and access, then rotates using a repeatable pattern: preferably **dual-valid overlap** (generate new credential → write as a new Vault version without deleting old → deploy/update consumers to read latest and, if applicable, accept old+new → monitor auth/health for ≥30 minutes (≥60 for Tier 0) → disable/deprecate the old credential at the issuer → remove the old Vault version after the overlap window, default 7 days) or, if overlap isn't possible, a **cutover** (scheduled change window → change issuer-side credential → immediately update Vault → restart/redeploy all consumers → validate/rollback if needed). After any rotation, they complete the verification checklist (ensure all rollouts/reloads completed, monitor auth/dependency metrics, run critical canaries, confirm audit logs and that any break-glass access is revoked) and record the event in a change record.

For **emergency rotation** (suspected compromise/exposure/anomalies), an incident is opened and "emergency secret rotation" is declared (secret names/paths only), break-glass may be used via the approved workflow for **time-limited (60 min)** Tier 0/1 rotate access with full audit logging; the IC/Security/SRE prioritize and rotate **Tier 0 then Tier 1**, selecting dual-valid where possible or cutover otherwise, updating issuer + Vault and restarting/redeploying all consumers, pausing to reassess if impact worsens, recording exact timestamps, then revoking break-glass immediately and documenting rotated secrets/services plus any follow-up rotations (derived/cached tokens) in the incident timeline and post-incident summary for Security review.

## Summary
On 2026-01-12, streaming responses intermittently stalled for a subset of chat completion requests. Affected clients observed streams that paused mid-response for 10–45 seconds, then resumed or timed out. The incident correlated with a traffic surge and increased concurrent connections on the edge streaming gateway.

## Customer impact
- Duration: 41 minutes (peak impact window)
- Symptoms: stalled Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams; elevated client timeouts
- Scope: ~9% of streaming requests in us-east-1

## Detection
- Alert: "stream-gateway open connections" exceeded threshold
- Secondary signals: increased 499/504 rates at the edge; elevated p95 time-to-first-token

## Timeline (UTC)
- 16:02: First alerts triggered (p95 TTFT + edge 5xx)
- 16:07: On-call confirms stalled streams in synthetic checks
- 16:15: Mitigation: reduce max concurrent streams per gateway pod; scale gateway
- 16:29: Runtime team rolls back a connection reuse optimization
- 16:43: Metrics return to baseline

## Root cause
A recently enabled connection reuse optimization increased head-of-line blocking within the streaming gateway under high concurrency. Combined with an overly permissive keepalive and a missing backpressure guard, the gateway accumulated slow clients and delayed flushes to the network.

## Contributing factors
- SRE alerting did not include a direct SLO for "stream stall duration"
- The runtime canary did not cover high-concurrency streaming workloads
- Gateway autoscaling policy used CPU only; connection count was the real driver

## What went well
- Synthetic streaming checks helped confirm impact quickly
- Scaling the gateway immediately reduced new stalls

## What didn’t go well
- Rollback decision took longer than expected due to unclear ownership between gateway vs runtime
- Lack of a dedicated runbook step for diagnosing SSE buffering

## Follow-up action items
(Each item counts toward the owning team’s total.)
1. Add an SLO/alert for "stream stall duration" derived from periodic flush timestamps. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P0.
2. Add connection-count based autoscaling to stream-gateway (HPA on open_conns). Owner team: SRE. Priority: P1.
3. Implement explicit backpressure guard in stream-gateway to drop/slow overly slow consumers. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P0.
4. Add load-test scenario for 20k concurrent streaming connections to perf-canary suite. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P1.
5. Update runbook: "Streaming issues" to include tcpdump/flush tracing steps and known failure modes. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P1.
6. Document gateway/runtime responsibility boundaries and escalation path. Owner team: Platform. Priority: P2.

## Lessons learned
Streaming incidents are often connection-management incidents. We need first-class metrics for stream health (stall duration, flush frequency) and scaling signals tied to open connections.

A sustained burst in long-context chat workloads coincided with a delayed capacity scale-up. The scheduler began queuing requests beyond safe limits. Backpressure increased, and the API gateway started returning 429s. When queue timeouts were exceeded, the runtime returned 503s.

- 19:05: Capacity restored; error rate returns to baseline

# Root cause

**Contributing factors:**
- Capacity forecast underweighted long-context workload mix shift
- Queue depth alert existed but was not paging Eng Infra (warning-only)

- Temporarily increased routing weight to us-west for long-context requests
- Raised max concurrent replicas for the hosted scheduler in us-east

## Purpose
This checklist is the required go/no-go gate for upgrading an *enterprise* Redwood Private deployment (VPC or on-prem). It defines the minimum validations, evidence, and sign-offs required before starting the maintenance window, and the stop/rollback criteria during execution.

## Scope
Applies to any customer production Private environment upgrade of: (a) control plane components (operator, controller, API gateway), (b) serving runtime/data plane images, (c) cluster dependencies shipped by Redwood (ingress, cert-manager bundles, logging agents), or (d) installer/upgrade tooling.

> Policy dependencies: This page is the operational gate, but approvals/comms requirements are defined in the Change Management Policy and Planned Maintenance Comms SOP. Security-specific sign-off requirements are defined in Secure SDLC: Security Sign-off for Customer Deployments. SLO/error budget checks are defined in Planned Change SLO / Error Budget Review Requirements.

---

## Pre-window requirements (must be complete 24h before window)
### A) Change record + ownership
1. Create a change request ticket using the Private Upgrade Change Request template (Jira internal-support).
2. Name a single *Change Owner* (usually Private Deployments on-call or the assigned Solutions/Delivery engineer).
3. Confirm customer-side *Change Approver* and *Operator* contacts (who will be present in the window).

### B) Version + compatibility
1. Record current versions: installer, operator/controller, runtime images, chart versions.
2. Confirm target versions and the exact upgrade path (no skipping major versions unless explicitly supported).
3. Confirm model/runtime compatibility notes for the customer’s pinned models.

### C) Backups + rollback readiness
1. Confirm backups exist and are recent for:
   - Control plane config state (values files, helm releases, operator CRs)
   - Any Redwood-managed persistent volumes (if present)
   - Customer-provided external dependencies are documented (DB, SSO, KMS)
2. Validate rollback artifacts are available locally: previous installer bundle, previous image tags, and prior values files.
3. Ensure a rollback decision point is explicitly called out in the window plan (see “In-window gates”).

### D) Preflight validations (attach evidence)
Run the standard preflight and attach the output to the change ticket:
- Cluster capacity and node readiness checks
- Storage class/PV health
- DNS and egress reachability (if images are pulled during window)
- TLS/certificate expiration checks
- Required Kubernetes API versions present (no deprecated APIs that will break charts)

### E) Observability readiness
1. Confirm dashboards/alerts are visible to Redwood during the window (temporary access granted if needed).
2. Confirm the following signals are available:
   - Control plane API error rate
   - Inference request error rate (5xx)
   - P95 latency for primary routes
   - GPU utilization and OOM/restart rates

---

## Go/No-Go gate (must be completed at window start)
The Change Owner must explicitly record “GO” in the change ticket after confirming all items below.

### 1) Required sign-offs (links required)
- Change Management approvals completed (see policy for approvers by risk level).
- SRE SLO/error budget review completed (or documented risk acceptance).
- Security sign-off completed if triggered (auth/RBAC/audit/TLS/dependency changes).
- Customer Success owner acknowledges comms plan and customer readiness.

### 2) Customer communications ready
- Maintenance notice sent according to comms SOP (timing + channel).
- During-window escalation path confirmed (Redwood + customer).
- “All clear” message drafted for post-window.

### 3) Final technical readiness
- Preflight output has no *red* blockers; any *yellow* warnings have an owner and mitigation.
- No open P0/P1 incidents on Redwood side that would reduce ability to respond/rollback.
- If a change freeze is active, an exception is approved and linked.

---

## In-window gates (stop points)
### Gate A: Post-control-plane upgrade health
Proceed only if all are true within 10 minutes:
- Operator/controller pods Ready
- Control plane API healthy (no sustained 5xx)
- No unexpected restart loops

### Gate B: Post-data-plane rollout health
Proceed only if all are true within 15 minutes:
- Runtime pods Ready and stable (no crashloops)
- Can complete a synthetic inference request on each region/cluster segment
- Customer confirms application-level smoke test passes

### Gate C: Verification window
Hold for 30 minutes of steady state with alerting enabled and monitored.

---

## Rollback criteria (immediate NO-GO / trigger rollback)
Rollback should be initiated if any of the following occurs and cannot be resolved quickly:
- Sustained inference 5xx above customer’s baseline +5% for >5 minutes
- P95 latency regression >30% for >10 minutes on the primary routes
- Authentication failures (SSO/JWT validation) or RBAC denial spikes
- Audit log pipeline breaks (if contractual requirement)
- Control plane cannot reconcile/upgrade further

---

## Evidence to attach to the change record
- Preflight output
- Version matrix (from/to)
- Rollback plan (commands + expected time)
- Links to SLO/error budget check and any risk acceptance
- Security sign-off (or “not required” rationale)
- Copy of customer comms and confirmation of receipt

## Ownership
Primary: Private Deployments
Consulted: SRE, Security & Compliance, Customer Success

Context:
h1. Purpose
This policy defines what constitutes a production change at Redwood Inference and the minimum requirements to plan, approve, execute, and validate the change. The goal is to minimize customer impact while maintaining developer velocity.

h1. Scope
Applies to all production environments for the Hosted API and Console, including:
* Hosted API control plane and data plane services
* Console UI and backend
* Shared platform dependencies (routing, auth, billing metering, observability agents)

Out of scope: customer-managed environments for *Private deployments* (see the Private Deployment Change Policy), and vendor-managed changes outside Redwood’s control (cloud provider maintenance).

h1. Definitions
* *Production:* Any environment serving external customer traffic (including canary and regional production).
* *Production change:* Any change that can affect confidentiality, integrity, availability, latency, cost, or correctness for customer-facing workloads.
* *Change owner:* The person accountable for end-to-end execution and follow-through.
* *Approver:* A designated peer/manager/SRE/security reviewer depending on risk tier.
* *Change record:* A durable record (ticket + links) capturing intent, risk, approvals, execution, and validation results.

h1. Change types
|| Change type || When used || Required approvals || Notes ||
| Standard | Low risk, pre-approved pattern (e.g., doc-only, internal dashboard query fixes, non-prod config) | 1 peer approval | Must match an approved standard template |
| Normal | Most code/config deploys to production | 1 peer approval + (1) service owner approval | Requires pre-deploy verification, canary, and comms assessment |
| Emergency | Active incident mitigation or preventing imminent customer impact | On-call incident commander (IC) + service owner approval (as available) | Retrospective change record required within 24 hours |

h1. What counts as a production change (non-exhaustive)
* Any deployment to production clusters (including canary regions)
* Any change to routing policies, fallback policies, or model selection rules
* Any change to auth, RBAC, API keys, rate limits, quotas, or billing meters
* Any schema migration, backfill, or data retention configuration change
* Any infrastructure change that affects capacity, autoscaling, or failover
* Any change to observability pipelines that could reduce visibility (logs, metrics, tracing)

h1. Minimum required artifacts
For every production change, the change owner must create a change record that includes:
* Summary of change and customer impact assessment
* Rollback plan (explicitly stated, even if “re-deploy previous build”)
* Verification plan (how we will know it worked)
* Links to: PR(s), build(s), dashboards, runbook used, and any migration plan
* Approvals (captured in the change record)

h1. Risk assessment checklist
Answer these before requesting approval:
1. Could this change affect auth, data paths, encryption, logging, or retention?
2. Could this change change request routing, batching, caching, or model version selection?
3. Could this change materially change token accounting/billing?
4. Is there any data migration/backfill involved?
5. Is rollback fast and safe (< 10 minutes) and does it revert the customer experience?

If “yes” to any of 1–4, the change is *Normal* at minimum and may require Security Review (see Secure SDLC requirements).

h1. Approvals
* *Peer approval:* A reviewer from the same engineering org who is familiar with the subsystem.
* *Service owner approval:* The tech lead or on-call owner for the service being changed.
* *SRE gate:* Required when the change affects capacity, SLO-sensitive paths, traffic routing, or any failover config.
* *Security gate:* Required when the change touches auth, secrets, encryption, audit logging, PII, or data retention.

h1. Change windows and freezes
* Default window: weekdays 09:00–16:00 local time for the primary owning team.
* Changes are prohibited during declared change freezes.
* Additional restrictions apply when error budgets are low (see “Change Freeze and Risk Assessment”).

h1. Execution requirements
All production changes must:
1. Use the documented runbook for the target system (Hosted API or Console).
2. Perform a canary rollout for traffic-bearing services unless explicitly exempted in the change record.
3. Confirm observability before and after (golden signals and specific dashboards).
4. Have a clearly defined rollback trigger and a “stop the line” principle.

h1. Communications requirements
Change owner must determine if customer communications are required:
* *Planned maintenance:* Status page notice and direct customer comms if any material impact is expected.
* *No expected customer impact:* Internal announcement in #eng-releases and on-call awareness if during core hours.
See “Planned Maintenance and Change Communications” for templates and required lead time.

h1. Post-change validation and closure
Within 60 minutes after completion, the change owner must:
* Validate key SLO metrics and error rates are within normal bounds
* Confirm canary is healthy before full rollout
* Update the change record with results and attach screenshots/links
* File follow-ups for any issues discovered

h1. References
* Prod Deployment Gates (Hosted API + Console)
* Hosted API Deploy Runbook
* Console Deploy Runbook
* Rollback and Post-change Validation
* Change Freeze and Risk Assessment
* Secure SDLC: Security Review Requirements for Prod Changes
* Planned Maintenance and Change Communications


Question:
What is Redwood Inference's end-to-end process for making a production change (definition, required approvals, pre-deploy verification, deploy execution, customer/internal communications, and rollback/post-change requirements) for the Hosted API and Console?

For the **Hosted API and Console**, a **production change** is **any change in any environment serving external customer traffic (including canary/regional prod)** that could affect **confidentiality, integrity, availability, latency, cost, or correctness** (e.g., prod deploys, routing/model-selection policies, auth/RBAC/quotas/billing, schema migrations/backfills, capacity/failover, or observability changes that reduce visibility). The change owner must create a durable **change record** (ticket) with **summary + customer impact assessment, risk checklist, verification plan, explicit rollback plan, links to PRs/builds/dashboards/runbooks/migration plan, and captured approvals**, and schedule within the default **weekday 09:00-16:00 local** window while obeying **error-budget/incident change control** (Green: normal approvals; Yellow: add **SRE on-call**; Red: freeze except incident/security fixes requiring **IC + service owner + SRE on-call**).

**Required approvals depend on change type and risk:** *Standard* needs **1 peer**; *Normal* (most deploys) needs **peer + service owner** and additionally **SRE gate** for capacity/SLO-sensitive/traffic routing/failover changes and **Security review** for auth/session/RBAC/secrets/encryption/audit logging/PII/retention/network exposure or security-relevant dependency upgrades (with threat summary, affected assets, security verification, safe rollback, and reviewer approval recorded); *Emergency* changes require **IC + service owner (as available)** and a completed change record/retrospective within **24 hours**.

**Pre-deploy verification (gates) for every release (unless an approved, documented exemption):** provide build identifiers (image digest/build #), release-notes snippet, change record link, PR/test links; ensure **green unit + integration tests** (exceptions approved by service owner), **perf sanity** when request-path/caching/batching changes, confirm **current SLO posture** (p95 latency/error rate normal), **capacity headroom ≥20%** or an **SRE-approved** plan when changing scaling/concurrency/batching, ensure **backward-compatible migrations** with rollback/forward plan, and complete any required **security gate** checks.

**Deploy execution:** always follow the relevant runbook and **announce internally in `#eng-releases`** (change record, owner/approvers, services/regions, canary plan, rollback trigger). For **Hosted API**, perform pre-deploy checks (dashboards, no conflicting incidents, error-budget posture), deploy a **mandatory canary** (typically **1 region or 1% traffic**) and hold **≥15 minutes** steady-state; pass criteria include **≤0.2% absolute error-rate regression**, **≤10% p95 latency regression**, and no sustained saturation (GPU/CPU/memory/queue depth), plus smoke tests (e.g., **/v1/chat/completions** streaming & non-streaming, **/v1/embeddings**) and metering validation if billing changed; then roll out region-by-region (default order **us-west-2 canary → us-east-1 → eu-central-1**) avoiding concurrent multi-region/router+gateway rollouts unless explicitly approved. For the **Console**, deploy **console-api first, then console-web**, prefer **feature-flag dark launches** and (when feasible) canary to an **internal staff cohort**; validate key workflows (login, org switching, API key creation, usage dashboard, settings), flag evaluation health, and watch for auth errors (401/403); publish the new web bundle with cache invalidation while keeping the prior bundle available for fast revert.

**Customer and internal communications:** internal heads-up in `#eng-releases` is **always required**; **customer comms** (status page notice and, for major impact, direct email) are required for expected downtime/degradation, breaking API/SDK/auth/quota changes, billing/usage reporting risk, or maintenance reducing redundancy-using **≥24h lead** for minor and **≥72h + email** for major maintenance (emergency: ASAP), including what/impact/times/regions/products/mitigations/status-page link/support contact, with updates at least **hourly** during the window and a final completion update.

**Rollback and post-change requirements:** "stop the line" and **rollback immediately** if canary/post-deploy gates fail or if there's plausible Sev2+ impact (including the explicit triggers: **>0.2%** sustained error-rate increase, **>10%** sustained p95 latency increase, saturation/timeouts, or customer reports); rollback by **pausing further rollout**, reverting **highest-leverage toggles first** (feature flags, routing/policy bundles), then **redeploying the last known-good image digest/bundle** (Hosted API typically region-by-region starting with the most impacted), with special handling/escalation for **schema migrations** and validation of **positive/negative authz** for auth/RBAC changes. After any change (successful or rolled back), perform **functional smoke tests**, verify **observability** (dashboards/logs/alerts), validate **billing integrity** if relevant, and keep **enhanced monitoring for ≥60 minutes**; only close the change record once it documents final build state (or rollback), evidence/links of observed outcomes, timestamps, and any follow-up tickets.

Context:
h1. Purpose
This policy defines the minimum change-management requirements for production changes that affect model versions, routing policies, serving runtime configuration, or customer-facing inference behavior.

h1. Scope
This applies to all production environments across:
* Hosted API
* Dedicated capacity
* Private deployments (VPC and on-prem)

Examples in-scope:
* Introducing a new model version behind an existing model alias
* Changing default routing/fallback policy
* Changing runtime settings that alter batching/caching/quantization
* Adjusting context-length limits or tool-calling behavior

Out of scope (but still recommended): documentation-only updates and non-production experiments in isolated sandboxes.

h1. Change classes
* Class 0 (Low risk): no customer traffic, no routing changes, no behavioral change (e.g., internal benchmarking).
* Class 1 (Moderate risk): canary to <= 5% traffic with immediate rollback.
* Class 2 (High risk): > 5% traffic impact, new default version, or changes to safety/tool calling/formatting behavior.
* Class 3 (Critical): global default changes, broad customer impact, or changes that can violate contracts/compliance commitments.

h1. Required artifacts (all classes 1–3)
A production rollout plan MUST include the following sections (link to template is mandatory):
1. Summary (what is changing, why now, customer impact)
2. Scope (which environments, regions, and customer tiers are included)
3. Success criteria and guardrails (explicit thresholds)
4. Monitoring plan (dashboards, alerts, owners)
5. Rollout steps (canary, ramp schedule, decision points)
6. Rollback and fallback rules (what happens automatically vs manually)
7. Customer communications plan (who, when, channels)
8. Approvals and change window

h1. Approvals
Approvals depend on class. Approvals MUST be recorded in the rollout plan under the “Approvals” section.

Required approvers by class:
* Class 1: Oncall Eng Manager for affected service OR Platform Eng TL
* Class 2: Platform Eng Manager + SRE oncall delegate + Product Manager for inference
* Class 3: VP Engineering (or delegate) + Security (if any policy/compliance implication) + Product (Director+)

Additional approval triggers (any class):
* Private deployments: Solutions Engineering lead + Private Deployments Eng TL
* SLA/contract impact: Customer Success Director
* Data residency/retention impact: Security & Compliance

h1. Change window
* Hosted + Dedicated: preferred Tue–Thu, 09:00–14:00 PT (unless explicitly approved).
* Private: must align with customer change window; document customer-specific windows in the plan.

h1. Pre-change checklist (minimum)
* Confirm rollout plan is published and linked from the change ticket.
* Confirm dashboards and alerts are configured and owned for the duration of the rollout.
* Confirm rollback path has been tested in staging or perf-canary.
* Confirm “blast radius” controls are available (traffic caps, customer allowlist/denylist, per-region routing controls).

h1. Post-change requirements
Within 48 hours of completing a model-version rollout:
* Add a short “rollout outcome” note to the plan (final ramp %, any issues, any follow-ups).
* File follow-up tasks for any threshold violations or customer escalations triggered during rollout.

h1. Record retention
Rollout plans and approval records are retained for 2 years (minimum).

This page documents lightweight guidelines for installing office art, plants, and temporary desk decorations at Redwood Inference offices. It is intended to balance aesthetic expression with safety, accessibility, and shared workspace norms. These notes are informal and maintained by People Ops.

Scope:
- Applies to common areas (kitchen, lounges, corridors) and individual desks in open offices.
- Does not replace formal safety or building management policies for structural changes or electrical work.

Guiding Principles:
1. Safety first: no obstructing egress, fire alarms, or emergency equipment. Avoid tripping hazards.
2. Respect shared spaces: avoid strong scents, noisy installations, or items that monopolize common areas.
3. Accessibility: ensure signage/art is hung at a height that does not impede mobility or visibility.
4. Temporary & reversible: most installations should be removable without tools or wall damage.

Approval & Ownership:
- Small desk plants and framed prints: no formal approval required.
- Larger items (floor-standing planters, freestanding sculptures, wall-hung installations > 30" in any dimension): submit a short request to people-ops@redwood.com with location, dimensions, weight, and installation method.
- People Ops is the owner for approvals and coordination with building management.

Installation Guidelines:
- Mounting: prefer adhesive strips rated for drywall where appropriate; for heavier fixtures require building-approved anchors and sign-off.
- Electrical: any installation requiring power must be scheduled with facilities and IT; do not run extension cords across walkways.
- Plants: prefer low-allergen, low-light tolerant species for shared spaces (e.g., snake plant, pothos). Avoid high-fragrance plants in kitchens and meeting rooms.
- ID tags: label any communal plant with owner name and watering cadence if not centrally maintained.

Maintenance & Removal:
- Owners are responsible for upkeep. Facilities may remove items that create hazards or persistent nuisances after one week's notice.
- For space reconfigurations, owners will be asked to relocate or remove personal/communal items within two weeks.

Summary

This page documents a lightweight, experimental set of guidelines for beanbag seating and ambient noise considerations in Redwood Inference shared spaces (cafeteria, lounge, and overflow areas). The goal is pragmatic: improve employee comfort and informal collaboration while keeping operational burden low.

Scope

- Applies to: cafeteria, adjacent lounge, satellite huddle areas on main campus and leased offices.
- Does NOT apply to: focus rooms, phone booths, secure rooms, or private customer meeting rooms.

Guiding principles

1. Respect for teammates: conserve shared spaces for implicit consent — assume people nearby prefer moderate noise levels.
2. Minimal ops: prefer low-maintenance furniture and sensors; avoid complex approvals for small purchases.
3. Data-informed: measure and iterate; use a simple decibel sampling process before large rollouts.

Furniture guidelines (beanbags and soft seating)

- Quantity: limit beanbag count per room to 6 units or 25% of casual seating, whichever is smaller.
- Placement: require at least 1.5m clear circulation path; do not block egress or access to kitchen equipment.
- Materials: choose wipeable, flame-retardant covers rated for commercial use.
- Procurement checklist (sample):
  1. Model spec and SKU
  2. Flame retardant certificate (pdf)
  3. Supplier lead time and return policy
  4. Estimated cost per unit
  5. Maintenance plan (wipe schedule)

Ambient noise guidance

- Target levels: daylight cafeteria 45-55 dB typical; lunchtime peaks allowed up to 65 dB for short periods.
- Quiet windows: designate 11:30-12:30 on Tuesdays as a quiet-lunch pilot in one lounge for two quarters and evaluate.

Quick decibel sampling procedure

1. Tools: smartphone with a basic dB meter app (note: consumer apps vary).
2. Sampling: take 6 samples across a 30-minute window during a target time (e.g., Wednesday 12:00-12:30).
3. Record: document median and max values. Store sample note on the facilities ticket with a short comment.

Example CLI-style sample (for reference in case teams use a measurement device):

# pseudo-command for a USB mic logger (example only)
# record 30s segments and write a simple CSV of RMS dB values
# recorder --device /dev/audio1 --interval 30 --out cafeteria-sample.csv

Operational checklist for pilot rollout (one-month pilot)

1. Facilities ops to order up to 4 beanbags for Pilot Location A.
2. People Ops to publish the pilot notice and expectations (quiet windows, cleanup).
3. Facilities to execute sampling on week 1 and week 4 and upload notes.
4. Survey: send a 3-question pulse survey after week 4 (comfort, noise impact, cleanup).

Safety, maintenance, and waste

- Cleaning: wipeable covers weekly; deep-clean monthly.
- Disposal: follow office recycling guidelines; avoid foam landfill where programs exist.

Decision and escalation

- If complaints > 10% of local headcount in pilot area, pause and review.
- Escalation owner: Facilities Lead (email: facilities@example.com).

Ownership and review cadence

- Document owner: People Ops (Aisha Khan).
- Review cadence: pilot review at month 1, full review at month 3.

Related artifacts and references

- See: Office space guidelines (Confluence) for building rules and safety.
- See: Facilities procurement template (Drive) for ordering checklist.

Attachments and sample forms

- Procurement sample checklist (attach to ticket)
- Decibel sampling notes (CSV)

Notes and known limitations

- This is intentionally lightweight and experimental. It is not a binding policy for client-facing meeting rooms or regulated spaces. If a space is used for interviews or customer meetings, revert to formal meeting-room standards.

Revision history

- 2024-11-07 initial draft by Aisha Khan
- 2025-01-15 pilot parameters updated after facilities review

Meeting header: 2026-03-21 16:00 UTC, duration ~58m. Attendees: Priya Narayanan (Redwood), Samir Chen (Redwood), Jordan Lee (candidate).

[00:00] Priya: Hi Jordan, thanks for making time. We're going to do a systems-forward interview — about 50 minutes — and then 5–10 minutes for questions. Sound good?
[00:10] Jordan: Yep that works for me. Excited to talk through some of the infra stuff.
[00:18] Samir: Quick note — feel free to use screen share, we can draw. If you prefer whiteboard verbal, that's fine too.
[00:25] Jordan: I can share a quick diagram, let me know when.

[00:30] Priya: Great. Let's start with a scenario: you have a multi-tenant LLM inference service. Customers have mixed latency requirements; some are small chat responses, some are long-form generation. How would you design the request routing and batching strategy to balance latency and throughput?
[00:50] Jordan: Okay, so first cut, separate by SLO tier — fast-path for low-latency customers, batch-path for bulk. Use an upfront router that tags requests with expected token length and priority. For batching you run continuous batching window, but you also have a max-wait timeout, like 5–10ms for the low-latency tier, and larger for throughput.
[01:20] Samir: When you say continuous batching, are you thinking synchronous queues per worker or a global scheduler?
[01:27] Jordan: I'd go with hybrid — local worker-level queues for micro-batching to reduce cross-host coordination, and a global coordinator for balancing load and moving batches if workers are idle. The coordinator can reshuffle by affinity and memory footprint (KV cache locality).
[01:45] Priya: How would you incorporate KV cache behavior? For large chat histories the KV cache grows — what tradeoffs do you consider?
[01:55] Jordan: If the KV cache (kay-vee cache) is per-model shard, you want to minimize cold-cache misses. Techniques: pin recent active conversations to same GPU, use LRU eviction tuned by sequence length, and optionally offload cold-kv to host memory with on-demand fetching. But that increases latency, so prefer sharding customer affinity.
[02:20] Priya: What about memory-limited GPUs; how would you handle quantized models and cache memory?
[02:28] Jordan: Quantization reduces model size but KV cache still consumes a lot. I'd explore 4-bit quantization for weights and mixed precision for activations. For KV caching, you could compress keys or use 8-bit storage for cached kv pairs; there's a tradeoff with decode cost. Also tiered caching: hot kv stays on GPU, warm kv on fast host RAM, and cold kv in a slower store.
[02:55] Samir: Do you have experience with specific quantization libraries or tooling?
[03:00] Jordan: I've used bitsandbytes for 4-bit and a custom offline quantizer for 6-bit experiments. I haven't used Redwood-specific tooling but I worked on a similar stack at OpenEmbeddings.
[03:12] Priya: Cool. Follow-up: suppose a customer sends 200 concurrent short requests — how does your scheduler avoid head-of-line blocking?
[03:22] Jordan: Use priority lanes and per-customer concurrency limits. Implement fairness via weighted round robin between tenants and preemption for high-priority requests. Also allow small fast-path shards that bypass large batching windows.
[03:35] Samir: You mentioned preemption — how do you implement preemption at the GPU kernel level?
[03:41] Jordan: Full kernel preemption is hard; prefer request-level scheduling: if a queued large batch is waiting, you can reorder queues before dispatch, or split large batches into smaller micro-batches. Use CUDA streams to overlap work where possible, though synchronization is tough.
[03:58] Priya: Let's pivot to a whiteboard: design a scheduler that decides which model variant to route to when capacity is constrained — e.g., you have full-precision, quantized, and distilled variants.
[04:10] Jordan: Okay — objective: maximize throughput while meeting latency SLOs and minimizing cost. Have a multi-armed routing policy that considers: estimated latency on variant, quality delta, customer tier, and current load. For each request compute expected utility = quality_weight*quality - cost_weight*latency_estimate and pick highest utility under SLO constraints.
[04:45] Samir: How do you estimate latency for a given request?
[04:49] Jordan: Use a learned model or empiric histograms: features include sequence length, batch size, model variant, and GPU utilization. Keep online calibration.
[04:58] Priya: Any thoughts on rollback/fallback if quality regressions happen?
[05:02] Jordan: Maintain a canary pool and do shadow traffic to evaluate quality metrics. If regressions detected, fallback to next-best variant and trigger alerts. Also use prompt-level checks where applicable.
[05:15] Samir: Let's surface an ambiguity: how do you measure 'quality' programmatically?
[05:20] Jordan: Use task-specific metrics — perplexity for language models, BLEU/ROUGE for summarization, or cosine similarity for embeddings. For chat, may need human evaluations or downstream signal like user satisfaction.
[05:35] Priya: Good. Quick behavioral: tell us about a time you had an incident in production and how you resolved it.
[05:42] Jordan: At my last role we had a GPU OOM cascade after a recent release that increased sequence-length handling. Root cause was a regression in a padding calculation that duplicated KV entries. We mitigated by throttling ingress and rolling back the deploy, then patched the padding logic and added e2e tests for long sequences.
[06:05] Samir: Nice. Any telemetry changes you added?
[06:08] Jordan: Added a long-tail sequence length histogram, per-request KV size metric, and an alert when average KV per request exceeded threshold.

[06:20] Priya: We're about halfway; let's do a short coding/design exercise: outline an API and data model for a take-home that tests batching logic. What would you ask?
[06:30] Jordan: I'd ask them to implement a simple router that ingests requests with (tenant_id, priority, expected_tokens) and outputs batch assignments with a max batch size and max wait. Provide a simulator of incoming load and assert latency percentiles under different scenarios. Also include unit tests for edge cases like starvation.
[06:50] Samir: How would you validate correctness and fairness?
[06:54] Jordan: Validate with synthetic workloads, check p50/p95 latency per tenant, and enforce per-tenant concurrency caps. For fairness, compute Jain's fairness index across tenants' latencies.
[07:10] Priya: Perfect. Final 10 minutes for candidate questions. Anything you'd like to ask us?
[07:16] Jordan: Yeah — how tightly coupled is the inference runtime to the control plane? Are rollouts handled automatically by the platform or handled by SRE?
[07:26] Priya: Our platform provides routing policies and rollout primitives, but SRE owns infra-level rollouts and emergency fallbacks. Engineers can set policies in the control plane and manage model variants.
[07:38] Jordan: Nice. Also curious about hybrid on-prem/private deployments — do teams usually run the same runtime?
[07:44] Samir: Yes, same runtime with optional private deployment packaging; differences are in networking and key management.

[07:52] Priya: Thanks Jordan. We'll send a take-home exercise; expect it by Tues. Any final notes?
[07:58] Jordan: No, thanks for the thoughtful questions.

Notes: transcript contains some disfluency and occasional word substitutions (kay-vee for KV). Action: Priya to send exercise. End of transcript.
